Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: The 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.92
Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita: An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay You can sleep over at this historic mountain refuge straddling the Italy-Switzerland border – but only if you're willing to undertake a days-long, high-altitude icy mountain trek. I'm roped to four strangers, concentrating on the light cast by my headtorch, as I wend my way through the icy labyrinth of crevasses tearing across the Alpine Lys Glacier. We've been here since 05:00, tugging each other ever higher up the Monte Rosa mountain massif towards the highest altitude building in Europe. We've just reached a giant mountain bowl filled with clouds of snow. The milky blue twilight fades to the soft glow of dawn. Our guide squints into the distance. "Up on that ridge" he says, "Do you see it? That's the Margherita refuge." I can't see anything, but the peak he's pointing towards is so sheer sided that I'm convinced he must be mistaken. We press on and, by midday finally arrive at the summit, 4,554m (14,941ft) above sea level. The crystal frosted world of the Punta Gnifetti peak is revealed. I can see the refuge now. I gasp. Somewhat resembling a giant tin can, the narrow three-storey metal building is not so much built onto the mountain as it is balanced on the edge of a precipice. On one side is a steeply falling snow slope and on the other, there's just a vertical kilometre of thin air. A refuge fit for a queen Sharing the Alpine border between Italy and Switzerland, the Monte Rosa massif contains some of the highest peaks in the Alps, including Monte Rosa itself, which at 4,634m (15,203ft) is behind only Mont Blanc. Punta Gnifetti (also called Signalkuppe) comes in sixth. It's here where an Italian scientific research facility and mountaineers' shelter was constructed and named for the then-queen of Italy, Margherita of Savoy. The queen, famed for her adventurous, athletic nature, insisted on climbing to the refuge herself for its 1893 inauguration and spending the night. Plan your trip: When to go: The Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita is staffed only between mid-June and early September. This is a very popular hike, so make guided tour, accommodation and travel reservations well in advance. The refuge sleeps 70 in summertime. How to do it: Most people climb with a qualified local guide on organised tours, which depart daily in summer. To stay overnight at the rifugio, choose the three-day climb. What you need: Winter clothing, sturdy mountain hiking boots and crampons (not micro spikes). More than a century later, the refuge still supports scientific research while also operating as a mountain hut (rifugio) offering rustic accommodation and thrilling panoramic views. Hiking the massif's eternal winter landscapes has become a popular trek in its own right. Roughly 30,000 hikers summit the peak each year and 4,000 stay overnight, ready like me – and Queen Margherita – to say they've slept in the continent's highest beds. I opted for a three-day guided hike, which requires crampons and ropes. As a frequent hiker, this didn't faze me. If anything worried me, it was the altitude. The hike to the refuge involves a dramatic gain in altitude, from 1,200 to 4,554m (3937 to 14,941ft) in just two days, so steady acclimatisation is essential. More than 4,000m into the air My journey began a day earlier in the Italian mountain village of Alagna Valsesia, at the slopes of the Monte Rosa massif – the literal end of the paved road before the mountainous ascent. From here, a series of cable-car rides whizzed me uphill to Punta Indren, (3,275m/ 10,745ft) where I met my guide and the four other members of our climbing group. Since we were all still acclimatising, our first day involved little more than an hour's hiking across rock and ice to where we would spend our first night, the Rifugio Città di Mantova (3,498m/ 11,476ft), a large wooden mountain refuge set just below the start of the Lys Glacier. There was a marked difference in temperature from Alagna Valsesia, but by wrapping up warm from the biting wind, I could enjoy the panoramic terrace with views of the green valley far below. Despite the stunning setting, I slept fitfully – due, I suspect, to excitement about the coming day's 1,000m (3,281ft) ascent and my body adjusting to the altitude. It was almost a relief when the alarm went off at 04:00 and we crawled out of our beds. We strapped the crampons onto our boots to prevent sliding on the glacial ice and roped ourselves up together – just in case someone slipped into a crevasse. We set out over the glacier and, after an hour or so of hauling ourselves through a spiderweb of crevasses, cleared a ridge and trudged across the mountain bowl. Behind us, dawn clouds bubbled in the valleys and ahead stood the walls of 4,000m (13,123ft) peaks. Despite the drama of the Alpine scenery, this middle section of the hike was considerably easier than traversing the steep, ruptured and torn up glacier crossing. Before I knew it, we were starting the final haul up to the refuge. Although I've never suffered major ill effects from altitude, I do struggle with vertigo. As we zig-zagged sharply up the summit cone, teetering alongside a ridge that fell away into the haze, I began feeling the unmistakable dizzy sensation kicking in and, instead of taking in the view, concentrated on where I was placing my feet. But when I next raised my head, we had made it. The vertigo eased as I stepped out onto the snowy dome. Fold after fold of mountain peaks sparkling with icy crowns stretched out around me – and the refuge itself. I was exhausted. But would I be able to sleep in what was easily one of the most hair-raising buildings I had ever seen? The highest sleep in Europe Once inside, the refuge felt more like a safe cocoon, and it was easy to forget how precarious our situation was. A dining room took up almost the entirety of the ground floor while the upper two were filled with dormitory-style beds which, the night of my stay, were completely booked. I dropped my backpack onto one of the bunks and headed downstairs to order a frothy bowl of cioccolato caldo (hot chocolate) topped with a dollop of Chantilly cream. As I savoured the drink, I fell into conversation with Tommaso Bagnati, one of the refuge's four wardens, who told me how the weather conditions can bring the reality of living on the top of Europe into stark focus. "When there's a big storm the building shakes a bit and you can feel very small," he said. "If there's a thunderstorm it can feel like you're right in the middle of it. All our supplies are delivered by helicopter, so when the weather is very bad and the helicopters can't fly, you can feel a bit cut off from the world." As I sat down to dinner, a weather front rolled across the mountains. The refuge became blanketed in clouds and sleet splattered against the windows. Sitting next to me at the communal dining table was Chinese YouTuber Jianpeng Cui, who told me that despite the "end of the world" feel to the place, he was pleasantly surprised. "I thought there'd only be a bed," he said. "No toilet. No kitchen. But it's not at all like that. I can even buy pizza and juice up here!" I was relieved that altitude sickness had missed me this time. But not everyone was so lucky. Mikhail Morozov, whom I met on his way down from the summit, had suffered headaches and nausea. "Coping with the altitude was the hardest part," he said. "I wasn't acclimatised and you go up very fast. After a couple of hours, the altitude started to hit me hard." More like this: Life in the Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita – as with all mountain huts – is very communal. Sleeping at high altitude in a cramped dormitory with seven or eight strangers, sharing two toilets with no shower, means you get far cosier than you perhaps want. But the shared effort of reaching the refuge also creates an easy camaraderie. "The best part for me has been meeting people from all over the world who have come here to climb the mountain," said Craig Shaw, a New Zealander living in Switzerland. "Seeing all these different nationalities together in this refuge is just phenomenal". Perhaps the real magic of this mountain is not just its ability to support a crazily positioned refuge. It's an ability to bring people together. --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.46
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia. "Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. --

item.title: Why Swedes think standing out is embarrassing
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.14
'You're not to think you're anything special': Why Swedes hate standing out Swedes prize equality, dislike boasting and are famously reluctant to stand out – yet they're also fiercely individualistic and know how to celebrate. The century-old idea of Jantelagen helps explain these contradictions, and offers visitors a fascinating key to decoding Swedish culture. As an utlandssvensk – a Swede who grew up abroad – I've always been fascinated by the unwritten rules that shape Swedish social life. I once got to chatting with a fellow Swede at a party. It was 4 July, and we discussed why our country didn't celebrate its national day as fervently as Americans. No fireworks, no parades – how come? "Well, it would be fairly embarrassing wouldn't it?" she said. "All that self-celebration. It's a bit over-the-top," she added, lowering her voice, as if there was an American hovering inches away from our table. As she explained, setting off fireworks for your nation (and therefore yourself) smacks of back-patting and ostentatiousness – two things that are anathema to much of Scandinavia. When I complimented my companion on how well she'd outlined the issue, she looked askance and waved my praise away like a bad smell. "No, please. That's just my little opinion, of course." A modest code of conduct To understand this aversion to basking in even the smallest of spotlights, many Swedes point to Jantelagen, or the Law of Jante: an unwritten social code embedded across Scandinavia that prizes humility, equality and not placing yourself above others. The term comes from Danish-Norwegian author Aksel Sandemose's satirical 1933 novel A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, set in the fictional town of Jante. Sandemose used Jante to skewer the conformism of small-town Scandinavian life, laying out 10 "laws" designed to put anyone who considered themselves exceptional firmly back in their place. Rules such as "you're not to think you're anything special" and "you're not to think you're smarter than [anyone else]" leave the reader with a deliberately bruised ego – and that's the point. Nearly a century on, Sandemose's laws remain memorable and highly quotable, helping Jantelagen endure as cultural shorthand. How to connect with Swedes Be proactive: Small talk with strangers isn't the norm, so don't mistake reserve for unfriendliness. "Swedes tend to be very loyal and trustworthy once a friendship is established," says Gossner. "I often advise newcomers to take the initiative. Don't wait for Swedes to come to you, as they appreciate when others make the first move." Suggest fika: The Swedish ritual of cake and coffee offers a low-pressure way to socialise. Meet over coffee and a modest but delicious kanelbulle (cinnamon bun) rather than trying to force conversation in the street. Be punctual: Swedes place a high value on being on time, particularly when you're invited to someone's home. Stefan Dahlberg, a professor of political science at Mid Sweden University, has written a paper on Jantelagen's modern legacy. He sees the rules less as firm laws governing Swedish behaviour. Instead, he explains, "they are better understood as a cultural shorthand for a set of familiar norms […] that you can recognise in everyday Swedish interaction. Status differences tend to be played down, social relations are relatively informal and conspicuous self-promotion can be viewed negatively." Visitors to Sweden will likely see this in action when chatting to locals. Compliment a Swede on their English, for example, and they may quickly play it down – switching to Swedish and muttering, "Äsch, det är ju inte flytande…" (Shucks, it's not like it's fluent…). Sandemose would be proud. The qualities can also be seen in everyday Swedish rituals, from Fredagsmys – unpretentious "cosy Fridays" with friends or family – to Lördagsgodis ("Saturday-candy") that's practiced by parents as the one day that kids can unleash their sweet tooth after a week of modest abstention. That doesn't mean that Jantelagen functions as a literal rulebook – or identically across Scandinavia. Dahlberg's study of Jantelagen in Norway, a geographical and cultural neighbour, found the average respondent tended to disagree with the Jante statements. After all, Dahlberg explains, Sandemose invented the list as a scathing takedown of conformity. "So there are really two things mixed together in the concept: an egalitarian idea that nobody is inherently better than anyone else, and a more negative pressure not to distinguish yourself too much." Jante's mirror image Jantelagen has another, less obvious side. In a culture where seeking the limelight is usually frowned upon, Swedish reserve can disappear at parties when a tradition of snappsvisor (increasingly risqué songs belted out while drinking heroic amounts of aquavit) and performative speeches create safe social spaces to open up. So, while Jantelagen is often used as a reasoning for Swedish reserve and diffidence, it can also reveal the inverse. More like this: As Dahlberg notes, "'Don't think you are better than anyone else' can be read in the opposite direction: don't assume that somebody is better than you simply because they are richer, more successful or have a more prestigious title." With so much bubbling under the surface, Sweden can feel deceptively complex. Luckily, there are classes designed to help mystified foreigners. Yvonne Gossner runs Learn Swedish Culture AB – and business is booming. "I realised there was a big demand for practical insights into Swedish culture, especially for foreigners trying to navigate life here," she says. "Many felt lost or misunderstood in everyday settings, or even when trying to make Swedish friends." Case in point: a South American client once arrived at a Swedish woman's party an hour late, carrying a big dish of food as a surprise. The hostess "was not pleased" as the guests had already eaten, and the immodestly large, late-coming dish was left untouched in a bedroom. Swedes, Gossner says, place a high value on punctuality and politeness; if you're invited to a Swede's house, she suggests sending a post-party message of thanks. "There is even a Swedish joke: 'Don't forget to send a thank-you note for the thank-you note'," she adds. An unasked-for dish can risk looking like a statement that "my food is better than yours", while failing to acknowledge someone's politeness can jar the sense of social balance. Cracking the Swedish ice Lola Akinmade Åkerström, a Nigerian-American author, travel writer and photographer who moved to Sweden more than 15 years ago, was initially "a bit floored by the unspoken ethos" of Jantelagen, as well as the contradictory layers of national character. "Sweden is the most open society, run by the most private people," she says. If you want to deeply discomfit a Swede, she advises, just make eye contact on a quiet train, and hit them with "Hi! How you doing?" Yet they're not being cold, just respectful of the idea that no one should impose themselves on a stranger's space. That preference for understatement extends beyond social interactions. Travel through the countryside and you can see it reflected in the nation's beloved summer houses. "I think Swedes hold the world record in the number of summer houses per capita – around half the population has access to one," says Orvar Löfgren, professor emeritus of ethnology at Lund University. Yet these are rarely flashy second homes; instead, they reflect rustic, rural values, even among wealthy owners. (Don't think your cabin is better than other cabins, Sandemose might say.) While in Sweden, visitors might also notice small Swedish flags on birthday cakes, supermarket products and during student celebrations. "Swedes who love to see themselves as non-nationalistic are actually good at waving the flag," says Löfgren. And despite their quiet reputation, "Swedes are great at celebrating," he adds. Christmas, Easter, Midsummer, birthdays, and student exams are celebrated "with more intensity than in most European countries". You could say these occasions showcase Swedes at their best – not that they'd put it so boastfully, of course. --

item.title: A 2,500km road trip in search of wild lemurs
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.04
I drove 2,500km across Madagascar to find the world's last lemurs One epic road trip connects Madagascar's richest wildlife, most spectacular landscapes and the world's last lemurs. Sitting beneath a thick canopy of trees in Mitsinjo Reserve, I crane my neck skyward, straining beneath the weight of my camera. A flash of white and black fur leaps across my lens, much closer than anticipated. I drop the camera from my eye and the heavy jungle air erupts with the haunting, whale-like cries of the indri, the largest lemur species on Earth. Critically endangered, strictly arboreal and the origin of man, according to Malagasy lore, the indri is a wide-eyed, tuft-eared rarity known to few but the most exuberant wildlife enthusiasts. Madagascar's crown jewel of more than 150,000 endemic species is sitting just 3m (10ft) above my head. Madagascar is the only place on Earth where lemurs survive in the wild, and my husband and I had come here to see how much of that extraordinary wildlife we could encounter on an independent road trip. Over three weeks, our 2,500km (1,553-mile) route would take us from the capital, Antananarivo, through rainforest, rice paddies, prehistoric canyons and spiny desert to the island's west coast, linking eight national parks and reserves along the way. With a rented 4X4 and an ever-changing cast of park guides, the route offered a surprisingly achievable way to encounter species found nowhere else on the planet. The RN7: Madagascar's lemur highway We rented a 4x4 for the journey, and with the bustle of Antananarivo fading into our rear-view mirror, we rode the RN7's ribbon of freshly laid tarmac up into the central highlands where two-storey trano gasy homes made of red earthen bricks sat on the fringes of expansive rice paddies. Families watched from behind swinging wooden shutters as we passed by. Rolling green hills and terraced valleys grazed by long-horned zebu punctuated the winding roads between towns. Plan your trip: How to do it: Rent a 4x4 vehicle and camping gear from Roadtrip Africa. If you intend to depart the RN7, you can also organise a pisteur through them for a small fee. Best time to go: May to October, the island's dry season Don't-miss stops: Mitsinjo Reserve, Anja Reserve, Ranomafana and Isalo National Park offer the most diverse lemur sightings without venturing far from the tarmac. Our first wildlife stop was the dense jungle of Ranomafana National Park. Trudging through the rain, I followed a local guide – required in Madagascar's national parks and readily available at every park entrance – up the muddy trail. Walking with a slight limp, acquired while rescuing a traveller from a jungle waterfall years ago, he pointed out clumsy red-bellied lemurs, self-assured greater bamboo lemurs basking in the sun and ultra-rare golden bamboo lemurs. The latter survive largely on giant bamboo, consuming quantities of cyanide that would be lethal to most other mammals. The sheer variety is partly a product of Madagascar's fragmented habitats. "Lemurs are ultra-specialised creatures evolved to fill a single ecological niche," our guide explained. "Each forest in Madagascar hosts its own unique adapted species." More than 110 lemur species have been identified, many restricted to small pockets of forest. To see more of them, you have to keep moving. But the ease of the sightings has a darker explanation. Madagascar's forests are shrinking, our guide said, as communities cut down trees for fuel and agriculture, squeezing lemurs into ever-smaller fragments of habitat. Continuing south brought new species with each change in landscape. We sunned on chunky boulders surrounded by ring-tailed lemurs in Anja Community Reserve and searched for tree boas in the shadow of the Andringitra massif. Hiking within the ruiniform plateau and jagged canyons of Isalo National Park, the final stop on our voyage down the RN7, we stumbled through verdant foliage and went nearly nose-to-nose with Verreaux's sifaka, long-limbed lemurs famous for their sideways, dancing gait. Into Madagascar's wild west Reaching Tsingy required a four-day traverse across some of the roughest roads of the trip. For the most difficult stretch, between Manja and Morondava, we hired a local pisteur – a ride-along guide who knows every river crossing, mud pits and hidden routes through the maze of dirt tracks. More like this: We crossed rivers where the flow nearly crested the hood of our truck. Elsewhere, tall grass swallowed the track entirely. Without GPS or a reliable map, the pisteur became our eyes, picking a path through the endless web of sandy tracks and occasionally guiding us through isolated Sakalava communities. Careening around a particularly sandy corridor, we burst into a kianja, or village square, alive with a market and hundreds of shoppers. Thick ropes of tobacco, roasting cassava and an array of plastic trinkets were spread out on colorful lambahoany, the printed cotton wraps worn across Madagascar. It was a vibrant bazaar erected seemingly out of nowhere, surrounded by wooded savannah a day's drive in any direction. By the time we reached the town of Morondava in the dim evening light, after days of mud and river crossings, hitting tarmac again felt like a relief. We thanked our pisteur for his life-saving navigational services before setting up camp beneath the moonlit shade of a baobab, Madagascar's emblematic tree. Baobabs, fossa and Tsingy We woke at the edge of Avenue of the Baobabs – Madagascar's famous dirt road lined with towering baobab trees – in the soft pink light of dawn. For a few precious moments we had the country's most photographed landscape almost to ourselves before the tour groups arrived. Kirindy Reserve was a natural stop on our final stretch to Tsingy, and a welcome break before another gruelling day on the road. Kirindy is all about nocturnal wildlife. That night, our guide led us through the reserve, where in the glow of my headlamp, a Madame Berthe's mouse lemur scampered into the canopy while the wide, spectral eyes of a red-tailed sportive lemur reflected crimson in the beam. Back in camp, a particularly pudgy fossa – Madagascar's largest predator, with the long body of a mongoose and cat-like features – wandered from the treeline in the shadow of our tent. The next day, as we neared Tsingy, the hard dirt road devolved into a thick mud pit. Stranded vehicles littered both sides of the swampy mess and crowds from the nearby village gathered to haul drivers free. Before long, our 4X4 was bogged too. But Tsingy was worth every difficult kilometre. Its unique stone forests host many endemic lemurs, and we spent several days clipping into via ferrata lines and climbing through the Unesco-listed limestone pinnacles in search of aye-ayes, stump-tailed chameleons and tiny leaf chameleons. With our final park behind us, we turned the 4x4 back towards Antananarivo. After weeks of river crossing, mud and increasingly rough roads, the smooth tarmac through the central highlands felt strangely uneventful. We had succeeded in seeing Madagascar's extraordinary wildlife without joining a tour. But you never really travel "independently" here. Every national park guide who helped us track lemurs, the pisteurwho pointed the way andthe villagers who hauled us from the mud had made the journey possible. --

item.title: How to Boil Potatoes (and How Long to Boil Them)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.37
So many potato recipes start with the same instruction: “Boil the potatoes.” Simple enough—until you’re wondering whether to start them in cold or boiling water, how much salt to add, or how long the potatoes actually need to cook. The short version: Start potatoes in cold, well-salted water, bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer until tender. That’s it! Depending on their size and what you’re making, the actual cooking time could range from 8–40 minutes. A baby potato destined for smashing needs far less time than a big chunk of russet headed for mashed potatoes. Want to know more? Here’s how to get it right every time. How to boil potatoes The essential rule for boiling potatoes: Start them in cold water. When you drop potatoes into water that’s already boiling, the outsides overcook before the centers turn tender. Starting them cold lets the potatoes and water heat up together so they cook more evenly. Ingredients - 2 lb. potatoes, scrubbed, prepared as desired (more on that in a minute) - 1 cup Diamond Crystal or ½ cup Morton kosher salt - Place 2 lb. potatoes, scrubbed, in a large pot. Baby, small, and medium potatoes can stay whole; cut large potatoes into evenly sized pieces. Peel them first if your recipe calls for it. - Cover the potatoes with 3 qt. cold water and add 1 cup Diamond Crystal or ½ cup Morton kosher salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stirring occasionally. Reduce the heat to maintain a simmer and cook until the potatoes reach the desired tenderness (more on that below). - Drain in a colander and let cool for 10 minutes, or proceed as directed in your recipe. Potatoes are dense, so seasoning only the exterior after boiling won’t give you the same deeply seasoned result. For 3 quarts of cold water, we recommend 1 cup of Diamond Crystal or ½ cup of Morton kosher salt (Morton is denser than Diamond Crystal, so you need less). Most of that salt goes down the drain with the cooking water, but the concentrated salt bath gives the potatoes a chance to absorb the seasoning as they cook. The time it takes to boil potatoes depends primarily on their size and how you plan to use them. Small potatoes can be ready in less than 15 minutes; larger pieces destined for mashed potatoes, gnocchi, or dumplings may need 30 minutes or more. | How long to boil potatoes for: | Smashed Potatoes | Potato Salad | Mashed Potatoes | Gnocchi and Dumplings | |---|---|---|---|---| | Fingerling potatoes | 8–12 minutes | 15–20 minutes | n/a | n/a | | Baby potatoes | 8–12 minutes | 10–15 minutes | n/a | n/a | | Medium potatoes | 18–22 minutes | 20–25 minutes | 30–35 minutes | 30–35 minutes | | Large potatoes (cut into 2" cubes) | n/a | 15–20 min | 20–25 minutes | 35–40 minutes | Large potatoes should be cut before boiling so they cook evenly—a whole russet may still be firm in the center by the time its exterior is overcooked. The exact dimensions matter less than consistency: Cut the pieces roughly the same size, and they should finish cooking at about the same time. Baby and other small potatoes can generally be boiled whole. Consider these time ranges as guidelines rather than deadlines. Start checking your potatoes at the low end of the range and let their texture—not the timer—tell you when they’re ready. How to tell when boiled potatoes are done “Fork-tender” is the usual cue: A fork, cake tester, or paring knife should pierce the potato easily. Exactly how tender you want it depends on what you’re making. A knife or cake tester should slide easily into and out of the potato. You want the potatoes fully tender all the way through, without any firm or crunchy spots. A knife or tester should slide in easily but meet a little resistance on the way out. The potatoes should be tender without falling apart when you toss or dress them. The best potatoes for boiling You can boil just about any potato, but the best variety depends on what you plan to do with it afterward. Idaho, russet, and other high-starch potatoes cook up fluffy and readily break down with a ricer or food mill, making them a classic choice for mashed potatoes. They’re also more prone to becoming waterlogged if overcooked, so keep an eye on them. New potatoes, Red Bliss, fingerlings, and other waxy varieties have a dense texture and hold their shape particularly well after boiling. That makes them a good choice for potato salad, niçoise, and other dishes where you want distinct, intact pieces. Yukon Golds land somewhere between starchy and waxy potatoes, with enough starch to make a creamy mash but enough structure to hold their shape. They’re the Test Kitchen favorite for ultra-creamy, buttery mashed potatoes—and a reliable all-purpose choice. Boiled potato FAQs Do you need to peel potatoes before boiling? Not necessarily. Thin-skinned potatoes like Yukon Golds, red potatoes, fingerlings, and baby potatoes can be boiled with their skins on after a good scrub. Whether you peel thicker-skinned potatoes like russets depends on the dish you’re making; peel them when you want an especially smooth final texture. Can you boil potatoes whole? Yes. Baby, small, and medium potatoes can be boiled whole. Large potatoes should be cut into evenly sized pieces so their centers cook through before their exteriors become overdone. Can you overboil potatoes? Yes. Cook potatoes too long and they can become waterlogged or start falling apart. Starchy potatoes like russets are particularly prone to breaking down, while waxy varieties tend to hold their shape better. Start checking for doneness at the low end of the suggested cooking-time range. Editor’s note: This article was originally published online in June 2019. It has been expanded and updated for style with further reporting by Zoe Denenberg and Hannah Lee Leidy.

item.title: Lemon Bars With Shortbread Crust
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.10
These lemon bars have everything we want from the classic dessert: buttery shortbread crust, smooth, puckery lemon filling, and a snowy dusting of powdered sugar. The filling gets extra citrusy flavor from rubbing fresh lemon zest into the sugar before whisking in the eggs and lemon juice. Better yet, there’s no stovetop curd to make—the filling goes straight on the baked crust. That simplicity comes with one important rule: Pack the shortbread crust firmly and evenly into the pan before baking. A flat-bottomed measuring cup, drinking glass, or large offset spatula works well for this. Once baked, let the crust cool for just 5 minutes, then pour in the lemon filling while the crust is still hot. The heat helps set the filling on contact, keeping the liquid custard from seeping beneath the crust. Chill the baked lemon bars at least 4 hours before slicing so the filling has time to set completely. Dust with powdered sugar just before serving—it will gradually dissolve into the moist lemon topping if added too far in advance. Lemon bars FAQ Why did my lemon bars turn out upside down? If the lemon filling seeps underneath the shortbread, the crust can essentially float to the top as the bars bake. To prevent this, pack the crust firmly and evenly into the pan before baking, ensuring it reaches all the way to the corners. Once the crust comes out of the oven, set a timer for 5 minutes. As soon as it goes off, pour in the filling and return the pan to the oven promptly. The crust should still be hot when the filling goes in. How do I know when lemon bars are done? The lemon filling should look set around the edges but still jiggle slightly in the center when you gently shake the pan, which should take 20–25 minutes. The filling will continue to firm up as the bars cool and chill. Refrigerate them for at least 4 hours before slicing. Do lemon bars need to be refrigerated? Yes. Once cooled, refrigerate the lemon bars until cold and keep leftovers chilled. They can be baked up to 2 days ahead; wait to dust them with powdered sugar until just before serving. Can I make lemon bars with Meyer lemons? Yes. Meyer lemons will work, though their juice is typically sweeter and less sharply acidic than that of conventional lemons, so the finished bars will have a softer, more floral lemon flavor. Can I make lemon bars in a 9x9" pan? Yes. An 8x8" pan gives these lemon bars their thick layers, but a 9x9" pan also works. Because the crust and filling will be slightly thinner, start checking for doneness toward the early end of the suggested baking times. Read more: Watch Kendra make lemon bars: Recipe information - Total Time 70 minutes (plus cooling and chilling) - Yield Makes 16 Ingredients 1¼ ¼ 1¼ 7 2 1 2 3 ⅔ ¼ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Line an 8x8" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Pulse 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (28 g) powdered sugar, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a food processor to combine. Add 7 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and pulse until mixture is sandy with very small butter pieces. Add 1 large egg yolk and pulse until combined; mixture will be very dry looking and powdery but should hold together when squeezed in your hand. Step 2Transfer mixture to prepared pan and spread into an even layer to fill pan. Using a flat-bottomed measuring cup or glass, pack into a compressed layer (use your fingers to get into the corners). Bake crust until golden, 27–29 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes. (Set a timer; you don’t want to go longer. The crust needs to be warm when you add the lemon mixture.) Step 3While the crust is baking, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and 2 tsp. finely grated lemon zest in a medium bowl. Using your fingers, massage zest into sugar until fragrant and lightly tinted yellow, about 1 minute. Add 3 large eggs, remaining 1 large egg yolk, and remaining 3 Tbsp. (23 g) all-purpose flour and gently whisk just until combined. Add ⅔ cup fresh lemon juice, ¼ cup whole milk, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; stir to combine. Step 4As soon as the timer for the crust goes off, pour lemon mixture over (the hot crust will start to cook the filling and prevent the layers from inverting). Gently tap pan on counter to pop any air bubbles on surface and return pan to oven quickly. Bake until lemon mixture is set but still jiggles slightly when gently shaken, 20–25 minutes. Let lemon bar cool, then chill until cold, at least 4 hours. Step 5Using parchment paper overhang, lift lemon bar from pan and place on a cutting board. Cut into 16 squares. Step 6Dust lemon bars with powdered sugar just before serving. Do Ahead: Lemon bars (without powdered sugar topping) can be baked 2 days ahead. Cover and keep chilled. Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published on October 19, 2023. In response to reader feedback, we retested it in September 2026 and updated the instructions with additional guidance for keeping the shortbread crust and lemon filling in distinct layers. Head this way for more of our best lemon desserts →

item.title: 19 Margarita Recipes for Any Season
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.78
A great margarita is hard to beat: tequila, fresh lime juice, orange liqueur, and salt in sweet-tart harmony. But the classic margarita recipe is also an excellent starting point for experimentation. Small tweaks—swapping triple sec for agave syrup, say, or tequila for mezcal—can create a whole new drink. Perhaps even more compelling is the margarita’s ability to veer into maximalism. Blend yours with frozen mango, muddle in fresh blackberries, or infuse the tequila with chiles. Below you’ll find 19 of our best margarita recipes, including frozen margaritas, spicy margaritas, fruit-forward riffs, and a few less traditional variations. There’s a salted watermelon margarita for summer, a blood orange version for winter, and an avocado margarita that blends up remarkably creamy. Whether you like yours on the rocks, straight up, or frozen, there’s a margarita here for you.

item.title: Gochujang Yogurt Chicken
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.56
Don’t be surprised if this becomes your new go-to weeknight chicken dish. The marinade features a host of winning pantry ingredients you likely already have on hand: yogurt, gochujang, soy sauce, and maple syrup. A smack of freshly grated garlic joins in to make a delicious spicy-savory-sweet marinade you’ll find yourself using on everything. (Yes, in fact, you can reserve a small portion to thin out later to become a nice drizzling sauce over the cooked chicken. More on that below in the recipe instructions.) Yogurt is a powerful tenderizer, so even just 20 minutes of marinating time while you prep the rest of dinner is enough to imbue flavor into the meat. The yogurt also helps to temper the heat from smoky-spicy gochujang, the assertive and versatile Korean hot pepper paste. If you have the time, an overnight rest in the fridge is even better. Lean on my favorite go-to broiler for a quick cook with minimal cleanup. These chicken thighs take very well to batch-cooking at the start of the week and enjoying in the ensuing days. They are great with rice, over salad, in a wrap, or even just cold out of the fridge (who, me?). Save more weeknight dinner winners: Gorgeous Green Shrimp; Spicy Salmon Bowl; and Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry Recipe information - Total Time 30 minutes (plus marinating) - Yield 4–6 servings Ingredients 4–6 ½ ¼ 3 3 1 1½ ½ 2½–3 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 4–6 garlic cloves, finely grated (about 1 Tbsp.), ½ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt, ¼ cup gochujang (Korean hot pepper paste), 3 Tbsp. pure maple syrup, 3 Tbsp. soy sauce, 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a small bowl until salt is mostly dissolved. (If you’d like to reserve ¼ cup marinade for dressing, now is the time; chill until ready to use.) Step 2Pour marinade into a large resealable plastic bag and add 2½–3 lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs. Close bag and turn chicken to coat. Let sit at room temperature at least 20 minutes, or chill, turning occasionally, up to 12 hours. Step 3Heat broiler. Place a wire rack inside a foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Coat or brush rack with nonstick vegetable oil spray or vegetable oil. Remove chicken from marinade, letting excess drip back into bag, and arrange, smoother side up, on rack. Broil, turning halfway through, until golden brown with some edges getting a deeper char, 15–18 minutes. Let chicken rest about 5 minutes, then slice if desired. Step 4If using reserved marinade as a sauce, add 1–2 Tbsp. water to reserved marinade to thin to desired consistency. Serve chicken with sauce drizzled over.

item.title: How to Build a Knife Set
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.54
For years we’ve been convinced that the best knife sets are made, knife by knife, by considering what you cook, how you cook, and the size of your space. Knife sets have their place, but really, we think of them as a stopgap as you assemble your own personal knife roll. Building a knife collection is extremely personal—the look, feel, and utility of each knife will read differently from person to person. And after all my time testing knives, the blades that became my go-tos have surprised me. I never expected a nakiri knife to be one of my daily drivers, and I never expected myself to own different styles of chef’s knives for different tasks. Not everyone is going to keep a gyuto around just to slice meat, but I was able to perfectly cut the flatiron steak I grilled the other week into thin strips that almost melted in my mouth because I had one. So this guide walks you through all the different categories of knives we’ve tested and how necessary they’re likely to be in your kitchen. Even though there’s a case to be made that you only need three knives, I think you should give yourself the opportunity to be surprised by some of the incredibly useful blades out there, just like I was. The essential knife You’re going to need a chef’s knife. Full stop. Many people prefer the durability of a Western chef’s knife, but some people might want the precision and steel quality of a Japanese chef’s knife. Most people will pick one or the other, but it’s also common for many home cooks to have one of each. Chef’s Knife The chef’s knife is the do-it-all star of any professional or home kitchen. This versatile blade can chop, slice, dice, even peel and core if you’re in a pinch. Generally defined by its tall heel, curved belly, and fine point, a good chef’s knife should be one of the first purchases you make for your kitchen. But because they have some of the most varied designs in the knife world, my full review of chef’s knives breaks down a large variety of top picks to help you find exactly what type of chef’s knife works best for you. Western chef’s knives tend to be sturdy, heavy, and made with slightly softer and more forgiving steel; Japanese chef’s knives (known as a gyuto), on the other hand, are designed to be sharp, nimble, and excellent slicers. Gyutos have finer edges made from harder steel, which helps them stay sharper longer but also makes them more vulnerable to chipping. If you’re looking for more precision and don’t mind a bit more maintenance, you might snag a Japanese chef’s knife for your daily use. Important knives you’ll use constantly: No matter how good your chef’s knife is, it won’t cut bread as well as a serrated knife. It will also feel ungainly for peeling or coring. That’s work for a paring knife. Bread knife Serrated knives cut bread without squishing it, which chef’s knives really can’t pull off. The best serrated knives are sharp, long enough to tackle big loaves, and sturdy enough to cut through a defined crust. They’re also useful for delicate tasks, like slicing tomatoes, and their overall size can help with big tasks, like splitting or peeling a watermelon. Paring knife Paring knives are great for coring and peeling, and their short blades give the user more control over small movements than a full-size chef’s knife or even a mid-size utility knife. They’re also useful for ultra-small tasks like slicing and hulling berries. But not all paring knives are designed the same, some have longer handles, some have narrow blades, some really can’t be sharpened. We tested and reviewed a wide variety of shapes, sizes, and price points to help you snag the type of paring knife you’ll find most useful. Useful knives you may not own: Adding a mid-size specialized knife to your kit, like a santoku, nakiri, or petty knife, brings more versatility while taking some workload off your other knives (meaning they’ll stay sharper longer). Most home cooks won’t need all three; most knife enthusiasts couldn’t imagine their collection without them. Santoku knife Named after the “three virtues,” santoku knives are great at chopping, slicing, and dicing. Their shape takes inspiration from a trio of other knives: the straight edge of the nakiri, the overall length of a petty knife, and the slight curve of a gyuto. They also have extremely pronounced sheep’s foot tips for precision point work. Santoku knives are great for a large variety of tasks and are often prized for their daily use for things like slicing cheese, cutting an apple, breaking down an onion, or chopping herbs. Nakiri knife Nakiri knives are traditional Japanese vegetable cleavers that feature a sturdy spine and a straight edge. These knives are great for breaking down tough vegetables like sweet potatoes and hard-skinned squash, and the straight edge is ideal for matchsticking carrots and cucumbers because the entire edge cuts all the way through to the cutting board (unlike the curved edge of a chef’s knife). If you have a fine-edged gyuto for an everyday chef’s knife, you might want a nakiri with its sturdy spine and heftier weight to handle some tougher jobs. Petty knife Petty knives are small Japanese utility knives that are great for precision work and slicing. Shaped like a gyuto, but with blades just a smidge longer than a paring knife, a petty knife is great for tasks like breaking down a whole chicken because they can easily fit between joints. The length of the blade gives you more freedom to tackle everyday tasks, and while they’re ideal for small tasks like dicing a shallot or cutting hard cheese, their nimbleness also makes them adept at slicing a steak. Nice-to-have knives: You may not ever need a heavy-duty meat cleaver, but you might be surprised at how versatile a Chinese cleaver is. Neither is essential in a kitchen, but both are great to have on hand when you need one. Same goes for the boning knife: You might not always bring home an entire striped bass, but on the occasion you do, you’ll be glad you have a boning knife on hand. Meat cleavers and Chinese cleavers Heavy-duty cleavers tend to be blunter than most knives, but that’s on purpose. Their edges are designed to crack through bone, so don’t expect them to slice through a delicate steak easily. Chinese cleavers, on the other hand, are thin and sharp, designed for precision push cuts. Our review breaks down the difference between the two in detail, while also showcasing why you might need one or the other more than you think. Boning knife Many home cooks get by just fine asking their butcher counter to portion their meat and fish, but more intrepid folks might find that breaking down a whole chicken, filleting a fresh-caught sea bream, or portioning a T-bone gives them more control over the meal they want to cook. A good boning knife is nimble, sharp, and easy to maneuver—it may be a specialized knife, but it excels at the task it was designed for. And don't forget… You’ll probably want to pick up a knife sharpener and honing rod to keep your knives pristine.

item.title: 53 Thanksgiving Recipes We Turn to Year After Year
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.43
Preparing and hosting a literal feast is hard enough without scouring the internet for the best Thanksgiving recipes—so we’ve done the work for you. A traditional Thanksgiving dinner might include roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes and gravy, cranberry sauce, sweet potatoes, green beans or brussels sprouts, dinner rolls, and pumpkin, apple, or pecan pie. You’ll find some version of all of those here, alongside the recipes we’re especially excited to put on the table right now. If turkey is nonnegotiable, we’ve got roasted, grilled, and smoked options, plus guides to turkey cooking times and carving the bird. Prefer a vegetarian Thanksgiving? There are plenty of meatless mains and sides too. And if 53 choices sound like about 48 too many, our Classic Thanksgiving Menu maps out the whole meal for you. Of course, the turkey is only the beginning. Browse our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes, then round out the feast with appetizers, cocktails, pies, cakes, and other desserts. And when the day is done, our leftover turkey recipes ensure the feast keeps giving.

item.title: 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.99
This dead simple three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat. It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You’ll Fall For. Recipe information - Total Time 30 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 1 1 2 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

item.title: Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.80
For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format. Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth Recipe information - Total Time 15 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 2 1 3 1¾ 1 2 1 ½ 1 4 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes. Step 2Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes. Step 3Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

item.title: I've Tested 41 Rice Cookers and Swear By These 4 (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.23
In college, I was introduced to the world of rice cookers when my roommate bought one for our house. I didn't fully realize how spoiled I'd been until we graduated and she moved across the country, taking her rice cooker with her. I was left to make do with the finicky stovetop method that never turned out quite right. In the years since, I've never been without one. Having consistently fluffy, well-cooked rice means I can turn my attention to the other components of the meal, and that convenience is well worth the price tag and the extra storage space a rice cooker comes with. Besides, there's nothing as humbling as cooking a big pot of rice for company only to find it's turned into a pile of mush. Our top picks - Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker - The one that makes the best rice: Zojirushi 5.5-Cup Induction Rice Cooker (NP-HCC10) - Best small rice cooker (that's also PFAS-free): GreenPan Advanced 4-Cup Rice Cooker - A great stainless steel rice cooker: Tatung Electric 6-Cup Rice Cooker and Steamer The best rice cookers are like a kitchen cheat code, a helping hand that ensures at least one part of your meal goes off without a hitch. But they vary a lot in performance. I've tested 41 rice cookers and cooked over 120 cups of rice (and that's just in the Test Kitchen), so I'm here to give you the lowdown and help you choose the right one for your lifestyle, budget, and household size. I believe the best rice cooker for your money is the Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker. It's the right size for most people (making up to 14 cups of cooked rice), and at $70 it's a great price. But I also have picks for PFAS-free options, small cookers for tiny spaces, and the Zojirushi NP-HCC10 that makes the absolute best rice, as long as you're willing to pay for it. We think it's worth it. New in this update: I tested the GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup (Cooked) Rice Cooker and found it to be a good option for those looking for a small rice cooker with a ceramic, PFAS-free nonstick inner pot. I also tested the new KitchenAid Compact Grain and Rice Cooker, but didn't think its performance merited its price tag. Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker Pros and cons Pros: - Consistently good rice - Affordable - Handy features Cons: - Rice can get scorched on the bottom - Brown rice may be too al dente for some Specs Capacity: 7 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10.75" x 10.75" x 11" Weight: 4.8 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, whole grain, hot cereals, steam cook, heat/simmer You don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars to make great rice. The Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker has consistently impressed me throughout years of testing, and at under $70, I think it’s the best option for most home cooks. What I love: The Hamilton Beach ranked right behind the Zojirushi (our splurge pick below) in a side-by-side blind tasting of white rice. It excelled in the brown rice test, producing individual and intact grains that had a satisfying amount of bite to them (though if you prefer your brown rice on the softer side, I'd recommend adding a bit more water than the recommended amount). It also fared well with long-grain basmati, producing a pot of fluffy rice on par with (if not better than) some of the more expensive cookers I tested. It cooked each pot of rice significantly faster than the Zojirushi, too: 35 minutes for a pot of white rice as opposed to the Zojirushi’s 50, and an hour for brown rice as opposed to 90 minutes. But what I really loved about the Hamilton Beach is that despite its low price tag, it doesn't sacrifice some of the helpful features the more high-end cookers tend to have. Besides a standard Keep Warm function, there are also six presets to choose from (white rice, quick rice, whole grain, heat/simmer, steam cook, and hot cereals), a handy delayed start feature (great if you want to prep a pot of rice before work and have it ready by the time you get home in the evening), a cook time countdown, and an audible beep when the rice is done cooking—all things most other options at this price point lack. Its 7-cup (uncooked) capacity is also larger than that of many of the other rice cookers I tested, but the machine's footprint is comparably compact. It's also technically a multi-cooker thanks to the heat/simmer and steam cook settings, though I was primarily interested in its rice-making capabilities for this review and will not vouch for those other functions here. I named the Hamilton Beach our budget pick two years ago, but after continuing to test it against the previous overall winner and countless other new-to-me models over the past couple of years while watching the price of the Zojirushi climb closer to—and oftentimes above—$400, I can confidently say that it’s the best choice for most home cooks for its balance of performance, features, and affordability. What I'd leave: While I found the Hamilton Beach to be well-made for a $70-ish machine, it didn’t feel quite as sturdy as the higher-end models we tested. I also didn’t love the design of the lid: It requires you to press and hold a button while manually opening it, and it opens sideways rather than front to back. The inner pot is also relatively thin, which contributed to a scorched layer of rice at the bottom in some of my tests—something that wasn’t a deal-breaker for me in the end but is worth noting. And, unlike many other models we tested, there is no differentiation in the recommended amount of water for different types of rice. I didn’t find that this negatively impacted the resulting rice, though the brown rice, which had a nice bite to it, could be a tad al dente for some with the recommended amount of water. The one that makes the best rice: Zojirushi 5.5-Cup Induction Rice Cooker (NP-HCC10) Pros and cons Pros: - Consistent results - Wide range of capabilities Cons: - Expensive - Bulky cord is not retractable Specs Capacity: 5.5 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10" x 14" x 8" Weight: 9 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Micom technology, induction heating, delay cook, automatic keep warm function Menu settings: white rice (regular, softer or harder), jasmine rice, mixed rice, sushi rice, porridge/congee, sweet rice, brown rice, GABA brown rice and quick-cooking, rice paddle and measuring cup, nonstick pot. Zojirushi is to rice cookers what Vitamix is to blenders, and KitchenAid is to stand mixers. That is to say, it's the brand everyone knows to buy if you want the best. We've tested seven of Zojirushi's 19 models, and I've been most impressed by the NP-HCC10, which has won our blind taste tests every time. If you're serious about your rice and willing to invest in a perfectly fluffy pot, this is the model for you. What I love: BA staffers have crowned this machine the winner time and time again in blind taste tests, noting the way it produced grains that were not too soft, not too hard, and never mushy. In my own testing, it turned out evenly cooked, perfectly fluffy rice every time. That comes down to two technologies working together. Micom (short for microcomputerized) technology, found in many of Zojirushi's cookers, uses built-in sensors that adjust temperature and cook time according to real-time feedback, acting as a safeguard against imprecise water-to-rice ratios. Induction heating, more specific to this tier of Zojirushis, lets the cooker maintain a precise temperature and conduct heat evenly across the whole pot, rather than from the bottom only, as non-induction cookers do. Rice quality was my number one criterion in evaluating these cookers, but I also gave points for design and features. The NP-HCC10 has a 5.5-cup (uncooked) capacity, enough to feed six people. Its nonstick pot is a breeze to clean, and the interior is clearly marked in white with the water levels for various types of rice. I loved that this model counts down the total cook time, a surprising rarity among the rice cookers I've tested, though the Hamilton Beach does it too. Its extended Keep Warm setting, on top of the standard automatic one, prevents rice from yellowing or drying out when it's left to sit. A delayed start setting lets you set your rice to be done cooking at a certain time. And nine programmed settings cover several types of rice, including jasmine, brown, and sushi (the White Rice setting on a Zojirushi refers to short-grain white rice). For other grains like quinoa or oats, Zojirushi has a guide here. What I’d leave: The main downside to the NP-HCC10, and the reason it's no longer my top pick, is the price. This model has gotten steadily more expensive over the years and now sits around $400, which makes it a definite investment piece. Still, our testers could tell the difference in rice quality during every blind tasting, so if rice is something you care about, that's what you're paying for. Zojirushi also tends to fall short on brown rice across the board. I found the brown rice this model produced to be a touch soft for my liking, though using a bit less water than the recommended amount fixes it. There's also no retractable cord, which makes storage more of a hassle. Another thing to know if you’re new to the world of precision rice cookers, is that it takes a very long time to make a pot of rice. Depending on the volume, white rice can take up to an hour and brown rice up to two. That's not a shortcoming. It's part of the reason they work so well. Get in the habit of starting the cooker before you begin the rest of your cooking and you won't notice. On weeknights when you're tight on time, the timer function guarantees your rice will be done when you need it. For more information about Zojirushi’s line of rice cookers, read our guide. Instagram content The best small rice cooker: GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup Rice Cooker Pros and cons Pros: - Easy to use - Decent rice - PFAS-free ceramic nonstick inner pot Cons: - White rice was a touch unevenly cooked - Brown rice may be too al dente for some Specs Capacity: 4 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 9.8" x 7.5" x 8.7" Weight: 5.2 lb. Warranty: Lifetime limited warranty Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, brown rice This sleek little rice cooker makes a good pot of rice and takes up less counter space than the other models on this list—plus it's got a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated inner pot that makes cleanup a breeze. What I loved: This new rice cooker from GreenPan is lightweight, relatively compact, and quite sleek, with a straightforward interface that’s intuitive to use. It made serviceable white and basmati rice in testing and excelled in the brown rice test, producing extremely individualized grains with a satisfying amount of bite, similar in texture to the batch made in the Hamilton Beach. While the GreenPan doesn’t offer a ton of presets, it’s got everything you need if your main use case for it is cooking rice: dedicated white and brown rice settings, a Quick Cook setting, an automatic Keep Warm function, and a Delay Timer. The ceramic nonstick-coated inner pot cleaned up easily with a sponge during testing, but it’s also dishwasher-safe. What I’d leave: While the GreenPan made acceptable rice, it wasn’t perfect—the white rice was a bit unevenly cooked according to some blind taste testers, and the brown rice was too firm for some tasters’ preferences (though others disagreed). Unlike the Hamilton Beach and the Zojirushi, the GreenPan is limited when it comes to settings. I also wish it had a carrying handle, though it’s so lightweight that it’s relatively easy to move around anyway. The best PFAS-free rice cooker: Tatung Electric Rice Cooker and Steamer Pros and cons Pros: - PFAS-free - Makes great rice Cons: - Stainless-steel pot is hard to clean - Lid gets very hot - Lid rattles around when rice is cooking - Pricey given lack of features Specs Capacity: 6 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 12" x 9.8" x 9.8" Weight: 7.1 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Automatic keep warm function Menu settings: None Tatung has been a leading manufacturer of rice cookers and steamers in Taiwan for over 60 years. With its straightforward on/off switch and cook/warm lever, the company's signature rice cooker looks like some of the simpler Zojirushi models, but it features a unique inner and outer pot system that steams the rice as it cooks. What I loved: In my testing, the Tatung produced fluffy pots of rice that earned praise from blind taste testers. The white rice had a nice amount of bite to it and a pleasant, slightly sticky texture. The brown rice was a good middle ground, al dente but not as dry as the rice from the Hamilton Beach. And the basmati was fluffy, the delicate grains all relatively intact. One major plus? Each pot of rice was done in about half the amount of time as the Zojirushi NP-HCC10. The Tatung is all stainless steel, with an inner pot that fits inside the appliance like a nesting doll. That nesting design is what makes it work differently from most rice cookers. Rice and water go into the inner pot as usual, then you add more water to the outer pot, which heats up and steams the rice from the outside in. The Tatung features an all-stainless-steel construction, with an inner pot that fits inside the appliance like a nesting doll. To make a pot of rice, you'll add rice and water to the inner pot as per usual, and then add more water to the outer pot before covering with the lid and setting to cook. What I'd leave: Because it's made of stainless steel, the Tatung can get quite hot while cooking—especially the lid, which I burned my hands on a few times during testing. The lightweight lid and addition of water surrounding the inner pot also meant that this model rattled quite a bit as it cooked, and water occasionally bubbled up over the edge when making large batches of rice. The stainless-steel inner pot is, as expected, much harder to clean than a nonstick pot, and required some soaking and serious elbow grease in order to scrub clean. The other thing to note is that at $210 at the time of writing, this is not a cheap appliance, but it doesn't come with the kinds of features (like delayed start or multiple settings) you might expect from a rice cooker at this price. How we tested rice cookers Many rice cookers these days try to position themselves as do-it-all appliances (the Instant Pot-ification of the category), but we were here to see how each model performed at one all-important function: making rice. We’ve spent years testing over two dozen models and have held numerous taste tests among Bon Appétit staffers, abiding by the following testing process each time: Each rice cooker was first put through a white rice test. We used Nishiki Japanese medium-grain white rice, cooking two cups worth in each full-size cooker and one cup in the mini cookers (models with 4-cup uncooked capacities or less). Models that performed adequately in this test then moved onto short-grain brown rice, and finally to long-grain basmati rice. Our tasters were on the lookout for fluffy pots of rice made up of nicely individualized grains that had just enough bite and didn’t mush together. Cookers that fared well in our initial testing were then given to several different editors to use in their own homes. Those editors have and will continue to provide feedback on how these models perform in the long-term. What we looked for in the best rice cookers Let’s start with the obvious: How was the rice? While we evaluated rice cookers based on several factors, no amount of fancy features or high-tech claims mattered if the resulting rice wasn’t up to par. Our testers and tasters scored models on the quality of all three kinds of rice, and they were looking for evenly cooked grains that were neither over- nor undercooked, not too wet and not too dry, and fluffy rather than gummy or mushy. How’s the user experience? The whole point of having a rice cooker is to make your life easier, so we were looking for rice cookers that were straightforward and intuitive to use. We valued clear instructions on how to wash and measure rice, guidance on water ratios and selecting settings, and automatic Keep Warm functionality. A timer function was an added bonus that we appreciated in some of the more advanced models. We also looked at the accessories each model came with. Every rice cooker comes with a few necessities, which usually include a rice paddle and a measuring cup. Every model we tested, save for the Cuckoos, came with a built-in paddle holder, and many came with an additional steamer basket insert. While we didn’t test out steamer or synchro cooking functionality in our initial tests, our long-term testers were encouraged to report back on how such functions performed. How easy is it to clean? Nearly every model we tested had a nonstick coating on its inner pot, and the few that didn’t were a bit of a nightmare to clean. We wanted to be able to cleanly scoop rice out of the cooker without leaving any residue behind, and looked for pots that were easily washed with a soapy sponge and some warm water (if you are really trying to avoid PFAS coatings, note that most rice cooker pots are not dishwasher-safe). Some models have removable, cleanable lids, something we appreciated and noted where applicable. How easy is it to store? We took note of the footprint of each model, but found that most full-size options were around the same size. Is it worth the price? The rice cookers we tested ranged in price from $25–$750. While we think a great model like our winning Zojirushi is worth its $300 price tag, we awarded points to models like the Hamilton Beach that provide a great value, performing better than their cost might suggest. Other rice cookers we tested and liked Cuckoo 6-Cup Rice Cooker and Warmer CR-0655F This model from Cuckoo is a great rice cooker for the price. Tasters ranked the rice it made nearly as highly as our winning Zojirushi, which is a feat considering the Cuckoo is a third of the price.
