It’s also much faster than the Zojirushi, finishing in 15 minutes less, and a bit larger, with a 6-cup capacity. Why didn’t it take the top spot, you might ask? A couple of reasons: The lid jerks open with so much force that it can knock the whole appliance off the counter (as well as any objects surrounding it), and it doesn’t have a countdown for the total cook time. Tiger Micom Rice Cooker JBV-A10U This former best budget pick is made by Tiger, another Japan-based company with over 100 years of history making many of the same kinds of products Zojirushi does. It’s one of the most affordable Micom models out there, ringing in at $99 (at the time of writing). And while it doesn’t have all the fancy bells and whistles of our winning Zojirushi, it still makes consistently great rice. In our blind taste tests, staffers picked the Tiger over several more expensive models. We also loved this cooker’s generous 5.5-cup (uncooked) capacity, the fact that it’s easy to clean, and that it offers something a step above a simple one-button, non-Micom model. This is still a dead-simple, no-frills rice cooker though. You get what you pay for: There is no alarm, timer, or digital interface, and fewer settings than you’ll get on something like our winning Zojirushi or some of the fancier Tiger models. In our most recent round of testing, the Hamilton Beach model edged it out by producing slightly better rice and having more helpful features, all while ringing in at practically half the price. Zojirushi Pressure Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NW-JEC10 The Zojirushi NW-JEC10 is like if Apple made a rice cooker: It’s sleek, high-tech, and expensive. It’s the most expensive home rice cooker in the brand’s lineup, as a matter of fact. Of its host of features, the one that sets it apart from the other high-end models Zojirushi offers is the My Rice setting, which uses artificial intelligence to learn your preferred rice texture based on inputs you give it after cooking through each batch of rice. Commerce writer Wilder Davies has been testing the NW-JEC10 for over a year and has come around to the view that the My Rice functionality is no gimmick. He found that his batches of rice evolved for the better over time as he gave the machine more feedback (specifically, it will ask you to input whether the stickiness and firmness of the previous batch you made was “not enough,” “okay,” or “too much”). What’s more, this rice won its initial taste test with our staffers. But the difference in rice quality was not enough to merit the $750 price tag, hence our recommendation for the average rice eater remains the (nearly $450 cheaper) NP-HCC10. Zojirushi Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer NS-TSC10A This model is similar to our top pick in design and functionality, but rings in at about $100 cheaper. The main reason for that is likely that it lacks the induction heating capabilities of the NP-HCC10. While it produced good rice across all of our tests, it never quite achieved as perfectly textured results as our winner. Our testers found the rice to be a bit too soft across the board (though this could be remedied by adding a bit less water than the recommended amount). We did, however, appreciate the retractable cord—plus the silver-and-light gray design is rather chic. Toshiba TRCS01 Rice Cooker This model performed exceedingly well in our initial blind taste test, producing fluffy grains that won over our testers. We also loved its suite of programmable features, the way it gave us a timer countdown from the start of cooking as well as the option to delay cooking until later, its audible alarm, and its use of fuzzy logic to make minute temperature and time adjustments according to real time sensor feedback (something more typically seen in higher priced models). We found it easy to use, with helpful presets for a range of rice types and a Quick Rice function that worked well for grains like quinoa, farro, and polenta, and an included steamer basket. But our long-term testing of this product revealed a major flaw: We found that the timer would repeatedly freeze (sometimes for 20 minutes or longer) while the machine continued to cook. This issue was particularly prevalent when using the Mixed Rice and Quick Rice settings. It’s worth noting that the timer function on a rice cooker is typically more of an approximation, and it’s not uncommon for it to change or stall momentarily—but not to this extent. It resulted in overcooked or even burned rice. It was not a consistent problem, but a problem nonetheless, and a big enough one to give us pause about recommending this model as our top budget pick. Zojirushi Neuro Fuzzy Rice Cooker and Warmer NS-ZCC10 The Zojirushi NS-ZCC10 didn’t make as nicely textured and fluffy rice as our winning pick. It does include many of the features we loved in our winner at a lower price point, like the intuitive interface, sturdy inner pot, Keep Warm function, and array of presets. It also had some additional features our winner lacked, like a retractable cord and handles on the sides of the pot that allow you to lift it out from the cooker while it’s still hot. However, at over $240 at the time of publication, we just don’t think this cooker produced rice that merited the still-high price tag. Toshiba TRSH01 Low-Carb Digital Programmable Multi-Functional Rice Cooker This sleek model from Toshiba has an intuitive digital interface and eight different settings, including one for “low-carb” rice that uses a colander-like insert to drain away starchy water as the rice cooks (which Toshiba claims “can remove unhealthy digestive starch by up to 37% and increase healthy resistant starch by up to 34%”). We aren't going to vouch for the low-carb claims, but we can tell you that this model fared relatively well in testing. We found the white and jasmine rice to be a tad soft for our liking, which ultimately kept it out of our top picks (though this could be remedied by using a touch less water than recommended). It excelled in the brown rice test, producing rice with just enough bite—the Goldilocks of brown rice, as one of our taste testers put it. If you’re a brown rice fiend, this may be the model for you. Tiger 5.5-Cup IH Rice Cooker JKT-D10U This model performed similarly to our winning pick from Zojirushi, scoring just a few points below it in our taste test. It has a 5.5-cup uncooked capacity, a sturdy nonstick inner pot with handles for safely lifting it out of the machine while hot, and all the other features we’d expect from a rice cooker with its price tag: A bevy of settings (12 to be exact), automatic logic technology, an audible chime, and an automatic Keep Warm functionality. It produced beautifully cooked white rice that was nearly on par with the Zojirushi NP-HCC10, but fell a bit short in the brown rice test, where the grains were on the mushier side. All in all, it’s a great rice cooker that any home cook would be happy to use, but for just a few dollars more, we’d recommend you go with our winning pick from Zojirushi. Zojirushi Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NW-QAC10 This model is part of Zojirushi’s newest line of rice cookers, and it looks similar to the pricey NW-JEC10 model we mentioned above. It is similar to our winner in terms of functionality, but it couldn’t match up to the NP-HCC10’s results in the white rice test. Our tasters found the rice this model produced to be soft and less intact than they’d have liked. That said, the NW-QAC10 features quinoa and oatmeal settings, which makes it a good rice cooker for anyone with a particular affinity for either of those grains. Zojirushi Pressure Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NP-NWC10 With Micom technology and induction heating, this model is very similar to our top pick. If you’re wondering why it’s over $100 more expensive, that’s because, unlike our winner, it uses pressure when cooking rice. While intended to produce a more tender grain, our testers preferred the rice the NP-HCC10 churned out, deeming the NP-NWC10’s rice a bit soft for their liking when cooked on a standard setting. It’s worth noting that this model allows you to adjust texture and consistency with relative ease, which worked well in our long-term testing, but we cannot recommend you shell out an additional $100-plus for it based on its overall performance. Rice cookers we don’t recommend Whether because of how they fared in our taste test or because of their design, these are the rice cookers that we don't recommend buying. - Aroma Digital Rice Cooker ARC-914SBD: This affordable 4-cup model performed well in the white rice test, but failed with brown rice. It leaked starchy water onto the lid that would have spilled everywhere had we not mopped it up. The rice itself was wet and oh-so-mushy. - Aroma 2.5-Cup Rice Cooker ARC-753SG: This model from Aroma has a stainless-steel inner pot that we found difficult to clean. It made white rice in near record time (20 minutes or so), but it tended to be a bit underdone. The same can be said for the brown rice test—the rice was good, but certainly not great. This model also exhibited some leakage through the steam vent even when just cooking one cup of rice, which we imagine would only get worse if you filled it to capacity. - Beautiful by Drew Barrymore 14-Cup Rice and Grain Cooker: I’ve generally been impressed by Drew Barrymore’s line of appliances, but this rice cooker was disappointing. It produced mushy, gummy white rice and didn't make it past the first round of testing. - Cosori 5-Cup Rice Cooker: Standard settings on this model produced rice that was a bit undercooked, according to most of our testers. This machine does have a whopping 18 settings, including a range of different grains, so it could be a decent option for anyone who frequently cooks steel-cut oats, barley, farro, and the like. - Cuckoo 6-Cup Heating Pressure Rice Cooker CRP-P0609S: The rice this Cuckoo made was incredibly sticky. It also suffered some design flaws: the lid snaps open aggressively, the control panel is unintuitive, and there's no countdown timer. - Cuckoo 6-Cup Micom Rice Cooker CR-0675F: This model made great rice. However, unresponsive buttons, a confusing interface, and a poorly translated manual made it frustrating to use. So while this cooker checks the "Makes Great Rice" box, the same cannot be said for the "Is a Joy to Use" box. - Cuckoo 6-Cup HP Twin Pressure Rice Cooker CRP-ST0609F: Like the other Cuckoos, this model made decent rice. However, its control panel was irritatingly unresponsive. It also talks, and in a voice that can only be described as Barbie DreamHouse-core—which may be amusing to some, but aggravating to others. - Cuisinart 4-Cup Rice Cooker: This mini model didn't move past the white rice test–the rice it produced looked very wet and undercooked at the time it finished cooking and switched to the Keep Warm function, and it tasted too firm in the middle. - Dash Mini Rice Cooker: This one-button model has a lid that is too light to stay sealed, allowing steam and heat to escape during cooking. - Imusa GAU-00011 Electric Nonstick Rice Cooker: This is one of the cheapest rice cookers you can get these days. Was the rice edible? Totally. But we found the white rice to be undercooked, and the brown rice it made was sort of wet, as if not enough water had been cooked off. - Instant Pot Duo: The beloved Instant Pot Duo is a multi-cooker that claims to do it all—including make rice. It was one of the fastest models to do so, but the grains it produced were gummy and decidedly un-fluffable. - KitchenAid Rice and Grain Cooker: This model from KitchenAid has a unique design that comprises an integrated scale and attached water tank. It uses that scale and whichever of the 21 preset functions you've chosen to determine how much water to add, eliminating the need to futz around with measuring cups and ratios. While it's an interesting concept, we weren't impressed enough by this model's performance to recommend it. The first batch of white rice we made was painfully dry, though the second batch we made using the Softer setting was an improvement. The brown rice was serviceable, nicely textured if still a touch dry. We spent time in 2025 testing its other capabilities as well and found them hit or miss. You can check out our complete KitchenAid rice cooker review here. - KitchenAid Compact Rice and Grain Cooker: This new version of the KitchenAid model above eliminates the attached water tank for a more compact footprint. While it made decent rice, we found the workflow of pouring water into the inner pot while it was attached to its base (rather than filling it to a designated line at the sink) somewhat annoying, and ultimately weren't impressed enough by the quality of the rice to justify the somewhat steep price tag. - Nutribullet EveryGrain Cooker: This cooker has settings for specific grains like white rice, quinoa, and oats, plus other nice-to-have features like a Delay Start button and Steam option. While we can't comment on how this cooker performs with other grains, we can say that it did not fare well with rice. The white rice we made was wildly inconsistent, even within the same batch. - Our Place Rice Cooker: This rice cooker is cute as can be. It's intuitive to use and looks nice on a countertop—an attribute most rice cookers lack; however, the appliance is bulky and pricey considering the small, 3-cup uncooked capacity. After some long-term testing, we found that the rice cooked inconsistently, either too mushy one time or too dry another, despite the fuzzy logic, so ultimately we don't think it's worth the price tag. - Tiger Microcomputer Controlled Rice Cooker JAX-T10U: Despite its promising features, this model produced white rice that was a bit wet and soft for our testers' liking. The brown rice had a nice bite to it, but its exterior was a tad mushy. We found that the less expensive Tiger JBV-A10U outperformed this pricier model. - Tiger 10-Cup (Uncooked) Rice Cooker JNP-1800-FL: This is a straightforward, single-button rice cooker that makes enough rice for the whole family (and a large one at that). Unfortunately, the rice it produced proved some of the softest of the bunch. With few features and lackluster performance, it's hard to recommend. - Toshiba TRCS02: This 3-cup model from Toshiba fared relatively well in the white rice portion of our taste test, but produced overcooked brown rice that kept it from earning a top spot. - Yum Asia Panda: This cooker is a bestseller on Amazon, so we wanted to see what all the fuss was about. It remained a promising contender through the first round of taste testing, in which it produced excellent white rice. However, the brown rice this model made was overcooked and mushy. But if brown rice isn't your thing, you might still consider this model. - Zojirushi 3-Cup Rice Cooker: This dead-simple mini model from Zojirushi uses a single button to start cooking. Unlike some competitors we tested, it didn't leak starchy water, but it produced inconsistent results. It also lacks a Keep Warm function, and we found it didn't handle brown rice well. - Zojirushi Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer NS-LGC05: This 3-cup version of one of Zojirushi's micom models ultimately failed to impress us—especially compared to the other mini models we tested, which performed much better even despite being lower tech. The white rice made in this model was quite sticky and mushy, as was the brown rice. Because of that micom technology, it also took longer to cook than the other small models. - Zojirushi NL-EAC10: This newest model in Zojirushi's lineup is cute, but it lacked the helpful carrying handle that most other Zojirushis have, took longer to cook rice than our winner, and produced white rice that was overcooked and a touch mushy. FAQs Should you rinse your rice? To make a long story short, you probably should. Washing rice strips the grains of their starchy coating and keeps them from sticking together and becoming a gummy mess when cooked—something you want for most types of rice (exceptions to this rule include arborio rice used for risotto, where the excess starch is necessary to create that creamy texture). In testing these cookers, we followed each model’s instructions with regard to rinsing rice. In general, you’ll want to swish your measured rice around in some water, pour that water out, and repeat until the water runs clear. Do you need a rice cooker? What about stovetop rice? You don’t need a rice cooker, but there’s no denying that having one makes getting weeknight dinners on the table or cooking rice for a crowd infinitely easier. That said, making great stovetop rice is a skill worth mastering—and the food editors in our test kitchen can help you with that. How much rice can a rice cooker make? You’ll notice that many of the rice cookers on this list have cup capacities in their names. That number refers to the amount of uncooked rice a given cooker can make at a time, measured in 180-ml rice cooker cups rather than standard US cups (which are 237 ml). Rice approximately doubles in size after cooking, so a 5.5-cup rice cooker like the winning Zojirushi will make a maximum of about 11 cups of cooked rice (which is enough to feed around 5–6 people). If you’re cooking for just yourself, note that the minimum amount of rice most rice cookers can make is one rice cooker cup’s worth. This will likely be more rice that you need for a single serving meal, but we’d advise against trying to make less rice than the cooker is designed for. And besides, the leftovers will make for excellent fried rice the next day.

item.title: The Great Date Boom is Here
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.22
There's nothing the internet loves more than a trendy ingredient. A few years ago, tinned fish became the It girl of the proverbial pantry, inspiring folks to swap their cheese boards for brinier, braver "seacuteries." Then cottage cheese blew up. Creators on TikTok and Reels proved that the creamy breakfast staple could be whipped, baked, blended, braised, and even frozen and churned for a delicious, protein-packed snack. Now, in 2026, we've seemingly reached peak pickle, with pickle-flavored everything from lip balms to (yes, even) lube. But the newest snack darling is one of the oldest ingredients in the world: the date. We saw it firsthand during Pantry Awards judging, when date-based products started landing in our submissions pile in numbers we hadn't seen before. These fiber-filled fruits are having a moment, in new and unexpected ways. Sour date snacks, date-sweetened boxed cakes, date-based candies and syrups, even the world's first soft drink made from dates—the primordial fruit is being reimagined for modern times, and people love it. "Consumers are starting to see dates as more than just a traditional dried fruit," says Amanda Sains-Harris, vice president of marketing for the date-based snack brand Joolies. Sains-Harris explains that the date boom has been a long time coming: Dates have been gaining popularity on social media and at industry trade shows for years. Now the fruits are flying off shelves. The category is up 24.1 percent in conventional grocery channels through June 2026, she says, citing point-of-sale data from the market-intelligence platform SPINS. As with cottage-cheese ice cream and tinned-fish cheese boards, folks seem to be looking for a healthy snack that still tastes good. Cardboard protein bars and chemical-tasting sodas are a thing of the past. "[Dates] check a lot of boxes without feeling overly engineered," Sains-Harris says. "Consumers also don't necessarily want to choose between better-for-you and indulgent anymore. They want both. Dates naturally live in that sweet spot." Grace Finerman founded Date Smarter!, which makes decadent chocolate-covered date caramels (and won one of our 2026 Pantry Awards, BTW). She agrees that consumers are seeking out healthier alternatives to sugary snacks—but they don't want zero-sugar, either. "Five years ago people were really turning to stevia," Finerman says. "I think the pendulum has kind of switched to people now wanting not cane sugar, but something sweet that's not processed." Despite their sticky sweetness, she says, dates are naturally low-glycemic. They're also high in fiber (6.7 to 8 grams per 100 grams), which is a tempting proposition in the age of GLP-1s and fiber-maxxing. And they make great fuel, especially when filled with protein-packed nut butters. "We actually have a large customer base of endurance athletes, professional and collegiate athletes, and overall fitness enthusiasts," says Sophia Karbowski, co-founder of Realsy, which specializes in date snacks stuffed with different nut butters. "The natural combination of carbs, sugar, and fiber in dates—plus a bit of added protein and fat from the natural nut butter filling—is the perfect source of clean energy athletes are looking for." Dates are also incredibly versatile, which makes them attractive to brands, too. On their own, the dried fruits are indulgent. But wrap 'em in bacon or stuff 'em with something sweet, and they're practically heaven. Since they're so sticky, they make excellent binders. Mashed together à la the viral peanut butter date bark that's taken over TikTok, or blended into a paste, they hold nuts, fruits, and other ingredients together. And when they're dried and powdered, they make an excellent refined-sugar substitute in baking mixes, syrups, and more. "We [Date Smarter!] use date powder, which is when you take a date that's dehydrated and run it through a processor," says Finerman. "We make all our caramel with that." Food trends come and go, but these brands are all betting that dates are here to stay (and given that they've been around since literally Mesopotamia, we think so, too). Karbowski expects to see dates on labels across the whole grocery store, from beverages to baking mixes. Sains-Harris wants to push the boundaries of where the fruits can go, and she's already getting creative: In May 2026, Joolies launched Date Sours, which swap the traditional buttery fillings for flavors like sour blue raspberry and cherry cola. "We always say dates are 'the original palm tree candy,'" says Sains-Harris. "And I think they're finally getting the spotlight they deserve." Whatever happens, we're here for it.

item.title: What Are Budget-Friendly Recipes I Can Make for My 60-Person Wedding?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.70
There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here. My 60-person wedding is going to be a DIY affair at a small inn-turned-Airbnb. The big meals are going to be handled by professionals, but there’s a couple meals—Friday breakfast and lunch, Saturday breakfast—that we’re hoping to cobble together ourselves in the inn’s commercial kitchen. While we regularly host groups of 20ish at our apartment, 60 people feels like an entirely different beast. How can we (simply! not-too-expensively!) scale up and make sure everyone is well-fed? We’re nominating some friends to help prep and serve food for each meal, but where do we start with the menu? How do you think about how much food you need? —I Do Congrats are in order! Thanks for writing in about your big day—I’m honored. This is a great size for a guest list. My husband and I invited a similar range (scandalous in pre-pandemic times) and the room was overflowing, bountiful, raucous at times. The funny thing about a small wedding is…it’s still a lot of people. And you’re right, it’s an entirely different beast than your everyday dinner party. I applaud you for tapping in friends. Delegation is—begging my editor to let me keep italics here—of the utmost importance. Not just because, unless you are a Top Chef contestant, feeding 60 people should not be a one-person endeavor. But also because, ahem, you’re the one getting married! As corny as it sounds, I hope that the top item on your to-do list is: Have fun. Everything else can wait, or should be someone else’s problem. Okay, speech over, taking a sip of pét-nat, onto the recipes! Breakfasts Not actually a recipe: My family has a reunion at the Shore every summer and our foolproof feed-a-crowd breakfast is bagels plus fixings. Can’t be beat. BA Bake Club has a wonderful homemade bagel recipe, which you should save for later and not use for this occasion. Now is the time to buy and assemble: bagels (if they’re fresh, skip toasting; if not, broil on a sheet pan); a few flavors of whipped cream cheese; smoked salmon (skip if this breaks the budget); sliced tomatoes and onion; capers; pickles. Optional fruit alongside. The math: - 1¼ bagels per person = 75 bagels - 1½ oz. cream cheese per person = 90 oz. (12 eight-oz. containers) - 2 oz. lox per person = 7½ lb. (Costco is your friend) - ⅓ tomato per person = 20 tomatoes - ⅙ onion per person = 10 onions - 1 tsp. capers per person = 1 giant jar - Who can say how many cornichons per person = 4 jars Ham-and-Cheese Croissant Bake. A charming, crowd-pleasing dish that you can assemble in advance, then bake the next day. Serve with some store-bought prewashed mixed greens splashed with Three-Minute Vinaigrette. Simple and chic. Mix the custard in two batches, each in a humongous bowl. (I have one of these and, honestly, can’t recommend it enough. Sure, it only comes in handy two-ish times a year, and my family makes fun of me for it, but when you need it, nothing else will do.) Bake in disposable aluminum pans. The math (recipe times eight for 64 servings): - 80 croissants (cheap supermarket ones! Lidl is known for them) - 3 lb. Gruyère (could do cheddar for a cheaper alt) - 3 lb. ham - 40 eggs - 8 pints heavy cream - 1 cup Dijon mustard - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt* - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2 tsp. freshly grated nutmeg - 2 handfuls thinly sliced chives *Please get Diamond Crystal for this measurement or adjust the quantity for another brand. The type of salt always matters, but especially so in large batches. Lunches Olive Bar Pasta Salad. As my colleague Rebecca Firkser writes, “The beauty of this pasta salad is its flexibility.” In your case, I would actually avoid the supermarket olive bar; it can get pricey in large quantities. Instead, find a Trader Joe’s or Costco and make the most of their shelf-stable antipasti offerings: marinated artichokes, roasted peppers, pitted olives, white beans, etc. More cost effective and just as yum. If you have an ambitious pal who wants to grill or sear chicken for a crowd, that would be a nice addition, estimating ½ breast per serving, or 30 breasts total. But not needed by any means! The math (recipe times 10 for 60 servings): - 20 garlic cloves - 5 cups finely chopped oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes - 2½ cups sun-dried tomato oil (cut with olive oil if you don’t have enough) - 3 cups plus 2 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (optional) - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt - 10 (1-lb.) boxes short pasta - 5 lb. small mozzarella balls or torn mozzarella - 10 quarts (40 cups) mixed antipasti (see above) Marinated Mixed Beans. I can hear someone scoffing in the distance at the audacity of the suggestion that you serve your beloved guests canned beans. But hear me out. They are delicious and cheap, can be assembled days in advance, and can confidently anchor an unfussy menu. Serve the beans in the same bowl linked above (see? Already coming in handy again), along with: crusty sliced bread; one to three cheeses (burrata, Brie, whatever strikes your fancy); soft-boiled eggs; olives and pickles; maybe some charcuterie. Nosh-y and fun. The math (recipe times 15—gasp—for 1 cup per person): - 15 shallots, finely chopped (use a food processor if you have one) - 2¾ cups plus 1 Tbsp. white wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 7½ cups finely chopped tender herbs (again with the food processor) - 5 cups olive oil - 30 (15.5-oz.) cans beans (bride’s pick!) - 5 Tbsp. Aleppo-style pepper or gochugaru - Kosher salt, to taste Drinks For breakfast, get some travel boxes of joe from a nearby coffee shop and call it a day. For either lunch: If one of your friends (read: not you) wants to go the extra mile, set up a vermouth-spritz bar with: bottles of rogue and blanc vermouth; cans of seltzer; lots of ice; lemon and lime wedges. Celebratory but won’t have everyone sloshed in the middle of the day. Readers, what’s the best wedding food you’ve ever had? (Yes, sure, it can be from your own wedding. But only if you’re telling the truth!) Share in the comments. Warmly, Emma Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

item.title: 43 Easy 30-Minute Dinner Ideas for Busy Nights
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.59
When you need dinner on the table fast, these 30-minute dinner ideas deliver. They’re the recipes Bon Appétit editors turn to when it’s 7 p.m., we’re already hungry, and we haven’t even made it home yet. But quick doesn’t have to mean boring. These easy 30-minute meals include spicy chicken lettuce wraps, sizzling shrimp fajitas, creamy carbonara, crispy tofu with peanut sauce, and plenty of one-pan dinners that minimize cleanup. Some lean on smart shortcuts like rotisserie chicken, canned tuna, or store-bought dumplings; others take advantage of naturally quick-cooking ingredients like shrimp, ground meat, tofu, and eggs. Every recipe here can be made in 30 minutes or less, start to finish. Really pressed for time? Our 15-minute meals round-up includes even speedier options. More easy dinner ideas:

item.title: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You'll Fall For
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.46
It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Each fall the first crimson-hued leaf drops to the ground, declaring the start of Pumpkin Season. And suddenly the perennial darling is everywhere. Pumpkin bread, pumpkin spice lattes, babies in pumpkin costumes, the list goes on. This year we’re declaring our favorite: a comforting curry pumpkin soup that comes together with just three ingredients. A three-ingredient soup may sound like a hack job, but think again. Each element—pumpkin purée, curry paste, and coconut milk—brings its own strength, creating a flavor that’s as cozy as a vintage sweater. Start by heating oil in a pot. Any type works, but I like to use unrefined coconut oil for a tropical fruitiness. From there, add a dollop of red curry paste. For a gentle warmth, turn to a jar of Thai Kitchen. To level up the spice, grab a can of Maesri, our Test Kitchen’s go-to brand. Cook the paste until it deepens to a sun-baked terra-cotta hue and is fragrant enough to tickle your nose. This step unleashes the nuances so you can taste every ingredient, like chiles, shallots, and lemongrass—none of which you had to prep yourself. Next, dump in cans of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, add some water, and let it all simmer. Taste and add salt if needed. That’s it. You’ve just made soup in 15 minutes. And a really good one at that! Feel free to gussy it up. I like to reserve a few spoonfuls of coconut milk from the can to swirl on top. (Once a food stylist, always a food stylist.) You could stir in baby spinach or top with cilantro or mint. For a hit of protein, poach a handful of shrimp in the simmering pot. However you serve it, this soup is bound to be an annual favorite, a nourishing bowl you can pull off even on the busiest fall night.

item.title: The Most Remote Places on Earth You Can Actually Visit
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.99
Reaching the most remote places on Earth takes more than just a plane ticket—it takes patience, endurance, and often a string of connections that make the arrival feel like an achievement in itself. These are places where airports are rare, ships arrive only a handful of times a year, and the communities you meet are outnumbered by wildlife. What they offer in return is a kind of distance that feels almost impossible in the modern world—skies free of light pollution, landscapes shaped by extremes, and the rare quiet that comes from being far beyond the usual travel circuit. Why do we seek remoteness? Journeys to places like these are rarely simple, but that difficulty is part of the allure. They remind us what travel feels like when the destination is hard-won, when the act of arriving carries its own reward. In the Kerguelen Islands, there are no hotels or tour buses, only wind, sea, and wildlife. In Russia's Oymyakon, for example, just stepping outside is an act of endurance. And on South Georgia, hundreds of thousands of penguins gather on beaches once scarred by whaling. In a world where so much feels accessible, true remoteness has become rare. These are the most remote places on Earth that shift our sense of scale and remind us that there are still corners of this planet where distance is intact. Kerguelen Islands, Southern Indian Ocean Nicknamed the “Desolation Islands,” this French territory sits marooned in the southern Indian Ocean, approximately 1,865 miles from Madagascar. Few places feel so utterly cut off. Volcanic cliffs plunge into storm-lashed seas, while king penguins and elephant seals crowd the beaches in their thousands. Nobody lives here permanently—only rotating teams of scientists, engineers, and unconventional travelers. What surrounds you is a world sculpted by wind, sea, and stone, where humanity has left little mark. How to get there: The French supply vessel Marion Dufresne II sails from Réunion Island several times a year. The voyage takes around six days. Quttinirpaaq National Park, Canada On the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, just shy of 500 miles from the North Pole, Quttinirpaaq lives up to its Inuktitut name: “top of the world.” It is a place of extremes—glaciers stretch for miles, jagged peaks rise from polar deserts, and the summer sun never sets. Muskoxen graze the tundra, Arctic wolves hunt in silence, and traces of ancient Inuit encampments remind you how long people have endured at this latitude. Few visitors make it here, but those who do find a landscape that feels infinite. How to get there: Travel first to Resolute Bay in Nunavut, then connect by charter plane to Tanquary Fiord, open only in the summer months. Ittoqqortoormiit, Greenland Few places capture the human will to survive like Ittoqqortoormiit, a settlement of around 450 people perched at the edge of Scoresby Sound, the world's largest fjord system. Wooden houses painted red, blue, and yellow dot the snowy cliffs, while rhythms of life here still follow the seasons: hunting and fishing sustain families, sled dogs line the streets, and in winter the sea ice seals the town off from the outside world completely. The surrounding waters carry drifting icebergs, and it's not unusual to see polar bears wandering the coast. How to get there: Reachable by helicopter from Nerlerit Inaat Airport, itself connected by small aircraft from Reykjavik, Iceland. Longyearbyen, Norway Longyearbyen, in the Svalbard archipelago, is the northernmost town of its size in the world. Despite its isolation, it's surprisingly lived-in, with cafés, a craft brewery, and even a fine-dining restaurant. Beyond town, reindeer roam freely, glaciers carve the landscape, and the Global Seed Vault safeguards the world's crops in a frozen hillside. Here, summers pass in endless daylight; winters in an unbroken stretch of night. How to get there: Daily flights connect Oslo and Tromsø to Svalbard Airport, making it one of the more accessible remote places. South Georgia, South Atlantic Ocean A remote island once known for whaling, South Georgia is now a sanctuary where wildlife has reclaimed the land. More than half a million king penguins gather on its beaches, while elephant seals occupy the shore in extraordinary numbers. Rusting relics of abandoned whaling stations remain, and the grave of polar explorer Ernest Shackleton—the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic—lies at Grytviken, a pilgrimage for history enthusiasts. After decades of ecological strain, including the introduction of reindeer by whalers, conservation projects are now restoring the island’s native habitats and protecting its fragile ecosystem. How to get there: No airports exist—visitors arrive by expedition ship, usually as part of cruises departing from Ushuaia, Argentina. McMurdo Station, Antarctica On Ross Island, McMurdo Station is the largest research base on the continent, supporting around 1,000 people each summer. It has been the launch point for many of Antarctica’s most important expeditions, from early 20th-century journeys led by Scott and Shackleton to modern scientific studies on climate change and glaciology. The surrounding landscape—glaciers, volcanic peaks, and the vast Ross Ice Shelf—has shaped much of what we know about the polar world. Travelers can’t stay at McMurdo, but expedition cruises to the Ross Sea sometimes include landings nearby, offering the rare chance to stand at the centre of Antarctic exploration. How to get there: Expedition cruises to the Ross Sea depart from New Zealand or Australia, with limited charter flights from Christchurch supporting specialist itineraries. Pitcairn Islands, South Pacific Ocean Home to just under 50 people, the Pitcairn Islands are one of the world’s least populated territories. Settled by the HMS Bounty mutineers in 1790, the community is still made up of their descendants. Life moves at a slow rhythm, shaped by the island’s rugged volcanic terrain and the surrounding Pacific waters. For visitors, the appeal lies in the intimacy: hiking to hidden caves, diving into crystalline waters, and being welcomed by almost every resident. How to get there: Fly to Tahiti, then on to Mangareva in French Polynesia. From there, a supply ship makes the 32-hour crossing to Pitcairn several times a year. Changthang, Ladakh, India High on the Tibetan Plateau, Changthang is a high-altitude desert where the air is thin and the landscape seems endless. Nomadic Changpa herders graze yak and goats across sweeping plains, while saltwater lakes like Tso Moriri and Pangong Tso shimmer beneath snow-capped peaks. Black-necked cranes, wild asses, and even snow leopards are spotted here, adding to its sense of undisturbed isolation. How to get there: Flights run from Delhi to Leh, followed by an overland journey across rugged mountain passes into the plateau. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: Everyone Seems to Be Taking a “Fallcation” This Year—What Does That Mean for Travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.67
Fall was always my favorite time to travel. It’s when the crowds have loosened their grip on Paris, the weather is better in Italy, and the hotel rates are lower in Marrakech. But over the last few years, I’ve noticed more and more travelers at airports near and far in September, October, and November. Indicating demand, plane tickets haven’t been dipping in the same way that they used to when the leaves turned. Open any news app, and you’ll see the headlines shouting from the rooftops: We are in the era of the “fallcation.” “Savvy travelers are establishing autumn as the new peak season for global trips,” says John Clifford, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and founder of International Travel Management. He attributes this to the fact that more people are traveling than ever in the summertime, leading to crowded destinations. On top of that, summers are only getting hotter. All this, Clifford says, leads to people looking to take their big annual vacation outside of the summer season. The data backs it up: According to Virtuoso, the global network of luxury travel agencies and advisors, bookings for fall travel this year have increased by 59% compared to last year; the network’s agents report a 77% increase in September sales, making it a peak month for travel. October and November sales are up 54% and 71%, respectively. Fall travel is increasing even to destinations in Asia, where the window between September and November is already the peak season. Catherine Heald, another CNT Top Travel Specialist and founder of Asia-focused Remote Lands, says her company has been seeing around 15% more fall bookings in the last few years. But nowhere is it more pronounced than in universally loved Italy, where September and October have become the height of the season, when it’s still “summer-like” in Southern Europe, says Gary Portuesi, a CNT Top Travel Specialist and a co-managing partner of Authentic Explorations. To Portuesi, fall in Italy now means November and December—and yes, they’re seeing a surge in bookings for those months too, when temperatures are cooler, crowds have dwindled, and hotel rates tend to drop. As he puts it, “It’s the new shoulder season.” To learn more about the rise of the fallcation, I tapped a host of Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists to weigh in: Who’s actually traveling in the fall? Where are people going? And will we eventually have to avoid traveling in the fall, too? In a few years, will we be craving “summercations”? Here’s what the experts had to say. What is leading to more “fallcations”? At this point, it’s conventional wisdom that September, October, and November are more comfortable times to travel because, in most destinations, you get more temperate weather and fewer crowds in the fall. “Autumn has outperformed summer for at least the past two years,” says Tom Barber of UK-based Original Travel. For Barber, September and October departures are up by 53% and 45%, respectively, compared to August departures. He explains, “People still want the classic summer destinations—Greece, Italy, Spain, Egypt, Morocco—but they increasingly want to experience them without the intense heat.” September is now one of the busiest months for travel company Red Savannah, says Camilla Davidson, its head of destination management for the UK, France, and Ireland. The relentless summer news cycle is also playing a part in this behavioral shift. “It’s all dominated by headlines around European wildfires, unlivable temperatures, endless lines on arrival at airports, overtourism, and elevated prices,” Davidson says. “Many savvy travelers are looking to shoulder seasons to avoid these pitfalls, with the fall seen as a more ‘reliable option’ than the spring.” On the other hand, Cari Gray of Gray & Co., which focuses on private active trips, says that fall has always been her clients’ preferred travel period over the summer season. “So many folks have well-established summer routines like going to their cabins and annual visits to favorite lodges,” Gray says. “They break free in the fall when kids are in school—both in grade school and college—and the weather is perfect for outdoor activities.” Who are the people actually taking “fallcations”? Travelers with kids in school are often tied to the academic calendar—back to school in the autumn, big vacation periods in the summer. So fall travel has historically been the domain of empty-nesters, young couples without dependents, parents bringing along adult children (or vice versa), friend groups, and solo adventurers. This has largely remained the case in our current era of the fallcation. “Couples and adults traveling without children have the most flexibility,” says Jonathan Alder of Jonathan’s Travels. But he notes that a good chunk of parents aren’t opposed to their kids missing class for the right family trip. “It really depends on the age. Pulling a child out of kindergarten for a week is very different from pulling an older child out during an important academic period,” Alder says. Rather than simply recreating a summer itinerary at a different time of year, fallcation travelers are looking for activities and experiences that are better suited to the autumn season, says Mark Bonte of France-based French Side Travel. Foodies in particular love to travel in September and October to catch various harvests, Bonte says: “Wine aficionados enjoy the mid-October fête des vendanges in Bordeaux’s Saint-Émilion. Champagne is another popular fall destination. Although the exact date varies annually, harvest typically begins in late summer and lasts several weeks.” More broadly speaking, Bonte says travelers who choose the fall tend to be keen on moving “more deeply” through a destination, “whether that means focusing on wine, gastronomy, culture, or a specific region rather than trying to see all of a country in one trip.” Are travelers swapping out summer for fall? The rise of the fallcation doesn’t necessarily spell the doom of the summercation. “Rather than give up the traditional summer vacation, travelers are adding a second vacation later in the year,” says Julie Durso, a private travel manager at Scott Dunn. “We’re seeing an increase in both summer and fall travel,” says Red Savannah’s managing director for villas Nick Westwood. The company’s villa bookings in June this year were up 24%, compared to the same month in 2025; July and August were up by 65%. Other travel advisors agree that summer travel is not going extinct, but have indeed noticed shifts in terms of where—and when—people are going. “There’s definitely some substitution happening,” says Barber of Original Travel. He observes that the UK market is increasingly staying closer to home during the summer, and their big international trips are instead happening in October or even the Easter season. Alder of Jonathan’s Travels says clients from the United States are saving places like Europe for later in the year: “Europe is fading as a summer destination for our clients, as it should be. When you have the flexibility, there’s little reason to fight the extreme heat and enormous summer crowds when you can experience many of the same destinations beautifully in September or October.” Authentic Explorations is seeing the same trend, says Portuesi; a wine tour in late October was sold out quickly, and past summer trips were more difficult to fill up with travelers who were largely staying in the US. Where are people going for “fallcations”? The short answer: People are going everywhere. Some fall trips, though, are certainly trending among the travel specialists I consulted. Going to Japan for the autumn is big right now, where the fall colors are just as spectacular as the cherry blossoms in spring. Of course Italy and Greece are big, especially for non-beach trips: the Peloponnese and Tuscany in the fall, Athens and Venice in winter. But for travelers insisting on jumping into the Mediterranean, October is still a good time to go. Overall the conventional wisdom holds: weather is better, crowds are fewer, and costs are more manageable outside of the summer season. Whether that pattern will hold as more people eye autumn remains to be seen. As for domestic travel, Clifford of International Travel Management says his clients are “focused on places where you can easily escape the crowds: the historic coastal estates of Newport, Rhode Island, the open spaces and private ranches of Big Sky, Montana, and the high-desert mountains of Santa Fe, New Mexico.” How is the travel industry meeting the moment? Now that September is squarely part of the summer travel schedule, “shoulder season” and “off season” are being pushed later into the year. This means some seasonal destinations and hotels are staying open longer. Gray of Gray & Co. name checks popular destinations that used to shutter at summer’s close, like the Amalfi Coast in Italy, where hotels like Palazzo Avino in Ravello welcome guests until late October, and Le Sirenuse in Positano until November 1. Gray says that the task of hoteliers and restaurateurs extending their seasons is to keep up the level of service and energy as one would expect in the summertime. The cruise industry, too, is investing in fall and winter travel. Cruise lines like Regent Seven Seas and Explora Journeys are operating their first full winter seasons in the Mediterranean this year. Cruises expert Mary Jean Tully of Tully Luxury Travel sailed with Explora in November last year and says, “It was fabulous. No crowds. The weather was fresh but not cold. It’s a great time to go.” Additionally, airlines are making moves for the fall and even the winter, extending seasonal flight routes beyond their usual September cutoffs. For example, United Airlines will operate its thrice-weekly flight between Newark International Airport and Palermo, Sicily, until mid-December this year. Delta is operating flights from New York-JFK to Catania in Sicily and Porto in Portugal through January 2027. What are the potential repercussions of the “fallcation”? The fallcation began as an escape from the heat and crowds of high summer, but its longer-term effect may be to redraw the entire travel calendar. Barber expects that seasons will shift: “September and October will stop being the ‘shoulder season.’ In the most popular parts of southern Europe, they’ll increasingly become part of the main season, with higher hotel rates, tighter availability, and fuller flights. Destinations will stay open longer. Hotels, beach clubs, restaurants, guides, and seasonal flight routes have a commercial reason to extend their seasons.” We’re already seeing this happening, though the adjustments currently seem like temporary novelties. There’s a world in which fall becomes a high-traffic season too. “That could be hugely positive for local employment, making tourism less dependent on an eight-week summer bonanza,” Barber says. “If fall travel continues to grow, certain destinations could eventually face some of the same pressures we're seeing in peak summer,” says Bonte of French Side Travel. He makes the case for cultivating travel programming that does not simply repeat its old mistakes—“reshuffling by destination” rather than the creation of “a single new peak season.” Regions could start reverting to the seasons that actually suit them, Bonte says, rather than times of year into which they’ve been pigeonholed. As opposed to a summer spree, the French Riviera could become hot for winter again, as it historically had been; the Alps could pick up as a summer destination. “Each region in France has a season where it truly shines, and the opportunity is to match travelers to that, rather than pushing everyone into the same few months,” he says. It’s work that falls on travel specialists to accomplish as well, to spread the travel traffic around—to bring it not only to the destinations that need it, but the parts of the calendar that do too. Is there still an off season in the age of the “fallcation”? Every part of the calendar is largely claimed by a good reason—and a good place—to travel. Put another way, one place’s “off season” may be another destination’s perfect window. Portuesi says the dead-of-winter months of January and February are still considered the low season in Europe, save for ski destinations like the Dolomites. Meanwhile, that’s one of the best times to go to the Caribbean because hurricane season is usually over by Christmas. For other places, what we might traditionally assume to be peak season is actually low season. Take Asia, for example. “Rainy periods in Southeast Asia and Japan also generally coincide with the summer months,” says Heald of Remote Lands. “But even then, some travelers will visit because it is the only time their schedules allow. In Japan, summers can be extremely hot and humid, yet travelers continue to go.” “I really don't think there is such a thing as an off-season anymore,” Alder says, adamant that the idea of everyone going to the same place at the same time of year is not sustainable or desirable. Besides, there’s a whole world out there and an entire calendar to consider. As Alder puts it, “There's almost always a great place to go, and increasingly we're helping clients identify when a destination is at its best for them, rather than simply when it's traditionally considered peak season.”

item.title: Newport, Rhode Island, Is New England’s Gilded Jewel—Here’s Where to Eat, Stay, and Play
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.24
Newport, Rhode Island, has certainly been having a moment as of late. You can attribute it to the Gilded Age dramas taking over small screens, the old-money aesthetic taking over TikTok, the Real Housewives of Rhode Island taking over Bravo, or just the fact that it’s beyond beautiful all year long. Either way, it’s undeniable that this compact coastal city has become a mecca of sorts for travelers eager to live out their East Coast fantasies—seafood, seersucker, sailboats, and all. But truth be told, Newport has never been a bad idea. The charming city has been a popular summer destination since the early 19th century, first as a playground for America’s elite, with families like the Vanderbilts and Astors building massive mansions along the water to serve as vacation homes (more on those later). Today, it’s a little less exclusive and a hot spot year-round, with New Englanders and international visitors alike spending sunny days becoming one with the sand at Easton’s Beach, breezy afternoons hiking the Cliff Walk, and chilly nights imbibing their way through Bowen’s Wharf before retreating to shingled cottages and luxurious hotels across town. If all that sounds like your kind of bliss, keep reading for a guide to seeing Newport in all its glory, as compiled by two New Yorkers who have been returning over and over again for the past decade. Here’s where to eat, stay, and play in the City by the Sea. Where to eat We’d argue the food and drink scene in Newport is reason enough to come to town, boasting old favorites and newer hubs that have given the city’s dining scene some fresh energy. Early birds, hit up Cru Cafe for a cozy bistro vibe and elevated comfort dishes like smoked salmon avocado toast. If you’re willing to wait in line, The Nitro Bar is a newer favorite (especially among influencers) with coffee and pastries that just might be worth the hype. Or, head to locally loved Franklin Spa, a legendary diner that hasn't changed its retro greasy-spoon energy in decades, and still serves one of the best lunches in town. Speaking of lunch, if the weather calls for it, take yours alfresco. Use Bowen’s Wharf as your hub: Belly up at 22 Bowen’s outdoor bar-restaurant area, have a casual seafood lunch at The Mooring, or get your clam chowder fix at The Black Pearl, with its lively dockside setting. You'll also find Clarke Cooke House, one of Newport's most popular restaurants, at the wharf. Its ship-like setting is one for the books, and the bistro offers a big menu spanning summer sushi to burgers, native cod, and even steak frites. For something less serious, Wally’s Weiners is another classic, and the kind of place you'll want to work into a day of wandering around Thames Street, known for being the center of the city. For harbor views and a Mediterranean-inspired menu, head to Flora, one of the newer names in town housed within the Gardiner House hotel. White Horse Tavern, on the other hand, offers classic Americana, with upscale farm-to-table dining (and stellar rum drinks) inside a building dating back to 1673. Crossing the bridge into Jamestown? Head to Beech if you want dinner to be the main event, with tasty, seasonal American fare headed up by locals. Where to stay Newport has no shortage of gorgeous hotels scattered from busy Thames Street to breezy Castle Hill Cove. Most guest rooms fall on the smaller side—this is a compact city, after all—but the best properties go big on glamour, offering gobsmacking views, old-world interiors, and exceptional in-house eateries and wellness facilities. Those looking for a taste of the Gilded Age should opt for spots like The Vanderbilt, an Auberge property built by a member of the Vanderbilt family in 1908, or Francis Malbone House, a Georgian-style mansion that dates back to 1760. If you’re all about location, location, location, book The Chanler at Cliff Walk for easy access to the popular waterfront hiking trail, Hammetts Hotel if you want to be steps from some of the city’s best bars and restaurants, or Forty 1º North Hotel Marina Resort to be so close to the water you’re basically swimming. Whether you’re staying there or not, you don't skip a stop inside Castle Hill Inn, a landmark Victorian mansion and one of the most iconic hotels in town. With an incredible location atop rocky bluffs that overlook the sailboat-studded ocean, the property’s Lawn Terrace is where you’ll want to grab a glass of Sauv Blanc and pretend you’re an Astor. Of course, hotels in Newport can be pricey, so if you’re on a budget or traveling with a group, an Airbnb might be a better bet—especially if the sound of a kitchen or common hangout space tickles your fancy. You can find smaller homes and apartments in Newport proper, like this four-bedroom with harbor views right downtown or this minimalist waterfront condo in the Historic District, but many visitors look to Middletown, Rhode Island—a town right outside Newport—for bigger, more affordable rentals. This adorable three-bedroom cottage with a shingled façade, for example, is technically in Middletown, but just five minutes from downtown Newport. Where to play The soul of Newport is rooted in the very concept of play. It’s a family-friendly destination and a romantic coastal escape; a place where sweet boutiques meet cool bars and Gilded Age history meets a working harbor. In the warmer months, chase the sea: Easton’s Beach is the most convenient option near town, Gooseberry Beach is tucked along Ocean Drive, and Second (or Sachuest) Beach offers a long stretch of sand and Atlantic surf. Post up at Second for a lobster roll and fries (sold from a beachside concession stand, the best), then grab an icy, refreshing Del’s Lemonade served from its iconic truck before heading home. Oh, and before you go, buy your next beach read at Commonwealth Books of Newport in the Historic Hill neighborhood. If you time it right, you can hit Newport's renowned Jazz Festival and the Newport Folk Festival, both hosted annually at the end of July (and sometimes running through early August). Plan in advance to secure tickets, as they can go quickly. For a more last-minute excursion that's completely free to the public, walk the Cliff Walk on the southeastern shoreline. The scenic coastal path threads between the Atlantic and the Newport Mansions, which, of course, you'll want to go inside and tour. If you’d rather be on the water than beside it, Sail Newport offers a Try Sailing experience, as well as afternoon-to-sunset sails. For something further from the coast, the International Tennis Hall of Fame is a great rainy day pit stop for exploring the history of the beloved sport and sniffing your way through the gardens surrounding the iconic grass courts. The Preserve in Blackstone Valley offers guided horseback tours, carriage rides, and sunset strolls, while Shephard’s Run Winery is a dreamy estate that gives you an excuse to head inland in South Kingstown for a tasting. As for a great Irish pub, The Fastnet has frosty beers on tap, while O’Brien’s is ever-abuzz and makes a mean house mudslide. If you want to make a night of it, have a drink and bites at Hotel Viking’s French-inspired Pescadou restaurant, then dance to the live DJ at its rooftop bar, Cap Club. Midtown Oyster Bar is perfect for a nightcap.

item.title: TSA’s New PreCheck Perk Allows Non-Ticketed Visitors to Accompany Friends and Family at the Gate
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.06
TSA’s newest PreCheck perk is intended for people who aren’t flying at all. Gateside by TSA PreCheck, which began rolling out this month at 13 US airports, allows eligible non-ticketed visitors to pass through security after receiving advance approval. That means they can accompany someone to a departure gate, meet an arriving traveler airside, visit a friend or relative during a layover, or access the restaurants and shops beyond the checkpoint. The program marks an expansion of an idea that several individual airports have experimented with in recent years: allowing some people without boarding passes back into the secure side of the terminal. But Gateside also raises a more practical question—who actually wants to go through airport security on their own volition when they don’t have a flight to catch? Jennifer Yellin, managing editor at travel rewards platform Points Path, expects the answer to be mostly people helping or meeting someone they know. “I think families will be the ones to use this the most,” Yellin says “I foresee this being the most beneficial for parents accompanying their child for an outbound flight as well as welcoming home family members.” She also sees potential for older travelers, nervous or infrequent fliers, and people navigating unfamiliar airports with the help of a friend or relative. In those cases, Gateside could make it possible for someone to stay alongside a traveler all the way to the gate, rather than saying goodbye before security. “If you have a child, parent, spouse, or even friend who is a nervous flier, being able to walk them to their gate and see them off could help put their nerves to ease,” Yellin says. “It can also be useful to help the same younger or older family member navigate an airport, which might otherwise be challenging. For some travelers, having someone there with you to the very end can put them at ease.” That doesn’t mean Gateside will replace existing assistance available to travelers who need it. Airlines already issue escort or gate passes in certain circumstances, including unaccompanied minors, and airports and airlines offer assistance for travelers with disabilities. Gateside is broader: A visitor doesn’t need to be escorting someone who qualifies for one of those services. Instead, access is based primarily on the visitor’s eligibility for TSA PreCheck screening and approval for Gateside. How Gateside by TSA PreCheck works Gateside is currently being offered as an “operational assessment” at 13 airports, including major hubs such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, and Salt Lake City International Airport. To use it, visitors need to be eligible for TSA PreCheck screening and have a Known Traveler Number. That includes TSA PreCheck members as well as eligible members of trusted traveler programs such as Global Entry, NEXUS, and SENTRI. The pass itself is free, but visitors have to apply online one to three days before their intended airport visit and select the participating airport they plan to enter. Those who are approved bring an acceptable form of identification to the airport and go through a TSA PreCheck checkpoint; they are still subject to normal security screening and restrictions. An approval is valid for the designated calendar day and allows the visitor to leave and re-enter the secure area that day. Gateside isn’t the first way for a non-ticketed visitor to get beyond airport security. Airports including Seattle, New Orleans, Orlando, Tampa, Palm Springs, and Tulsa already operate their own visitor-pass programs, each with its own rules. Detroit and San Diego have existing visitor programs in addition to being among the first Gateside airports. The distinction with the new TSA program is that Gateside is tied to PreCheck eligibility and gives approved visitors access through the PreCheck screening lane. For the average traveler, Yellin says, the program is still likely to remain fairly niche. “While it's a meaningful change, it's only beneficial for a small group of travelers,” she says. “For the average traveler, it won't change the airport experience since this is limited to a very small subset of airports and advance approval is required.” Seeing off a family member is perhaps the most obvious use for the program, but Gateside could also make it easier to spend time with someone who isn’t beginning or ending their trip in your city. “If you have a friend or family member traveling with a long layover in your home airport, meeting them during their connection is the perfect situation,” Yellin says. “This allows the traveler to stay near their gate without having to leave security.” Currently, meeting a connecting passenger generally requires the traveler to leave the secure area of the airport, then go through security again before continuing their trip. That may not be practical on a shorter connection, particularly at a large airport where getting between the gate and terminal exit can itself take time. With Gateside, the local visitor goes through security instead. Still, Yellin doesn’t expect non-ticketed visitors to start heading to airports simply because they now can. “The airport experience today is tiring for many and extremely different than what it once was,” she says. “Because of that, I do not believe too many people are going to choose to park their car and navigate their way through security, without actually traveling that day, unless they have a very real reason.” The program’s arrival also comes 25 years after the September 11 attacks transformed who could access US airport gate areas. Before 9/11, people without tickets could generally accompany passengers through security; afterward, access to the secure side of terminals became largely limited to ticketed passengers and those with specific authorization. However, Yellin doesn't believe Gateside is a signal that TSA is returning to the old airport model. “Now that it's been 25 years, TSA is experimenting to see how the overall experience can be better for travelers, while still keeping safety in mind,” she says.
