item.title: These US Airlines Have Mishandled the Most Bags in 2026, According to New Data
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.99
Most travelers have experienced that sinking feeling at baggage claim when the carousel stops and their checked luggage is still nowhere to be seen. While lost or delayed bags are sometimes just an unfortunate part of air travel, there are some airlines that statistically mishandle checked bags more often than others. The situation can be extra frustrating in 2026, as most carriers have significantly raised the cost of checking luggage on domestic and short-haul international routes to an average of $45 for the first bag. Despite the elevated fee, US airlines have collectively mishandled 1,120,760 checked bags in the first six months of 2026, according to new data from the Department of Transportation (DOT). That’s an average of about 0.5 bags mishandled per 100 bags enplaned. Although those numbers can seem shocking, they’re similar to mishandled baggage rates for the same stretch in 2025, which saw an average of 0.52 bags mishandled for every 100 loaded into planes’ cargo holds. If you’d like to avoid your carefully packed luggage being on the wrong side of those statistics, it’s a good idea to know which airlines routinely have the highest rates of mishandled bags. The DOT’s monthly air travel consumer reports compare the 13 largest US airlines and how many bags each carrier mishandles per 100 loaded onto planes. A mishandled bag includes baggage that is lost, delayed, damaged, or stolen. In the first half of 2026, American Airlines had the highest rate of mishandled bags, with an average rate of 0.73 mishandled bags per 100 enplaned, the DOT data shows. Closely following is American’s wholly owned regional subsidiary Envoy Air, which mishandled an average of 0.72 bags per 100 enplaned. United Airlines was next, with a mishandled baggage rate of 0.66 bags per 100 enplaned from January to June 2026. On the flip side, low-cost carrier Allegiant Air had the best baggage handling rate, with just 0.12 bags mishandled per 100 enplaned. Travelers who want to keep close tabs on their checked luggage can put devices like Apple Air Tags into their bags and track them during each stage of the flight. Many airlines now integrate Air Tag data into their baggage tracking process, allowing travelers to share the device location with customer service representatives through their mobile apps. Here’s a look at the DOT’s full US airline rankings for the most mishandled bags per 100 enplaned for the first half of 2026: - American Airlines: 0.73 bags - Envoy Air: 0.72 bags - United Airlines: 0.66 bags - Skywest: 0.55 bags - Republic Airways: 0.53 bags - Alaska Airlines/Hawaiian Airlines: 0.53 bags - Frontier Airlines: 0.51 bags - Spirit Airlines: 0.47 bags - PSA Airlines: 0.44 bags - Delta Air Lines: 0.38 bags - Southwest Airlines: 0.32 bags - JetBlue Airways: 0.31 bags - Allegiant Air: 0.12 bags

item.title: The Best Beaches in Italy, From Sicily to Puglia
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.89
You’d be hard-pressed to find a more quintessential Italian pastime than spending a summer day at the beach—and the best beaches in Italy lend themselves to precisely that kind of leisurely indulgence. The country has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, so you can bet there’s a piece of waterfront for everyone. Some are long, wide strips of sand dotted by neat rows of lounge chairs and umbrellas, while others are rocky inlets or hidden coves reachable only by boat or hike. The list below culls our picks for the best beaches all along the peninsula and on the islands, from Liguria in the north to Sicily in the south, along with tips on where to stay near each. Some are accessible by train or public ferry, while others require a car (road trip, anyone?). Keep in mind that summer (especially July and August) is the high season, so expect beaches to be more crowded than at other times of the year. For fewer crowds, consider shoulder season months like May, early June, and September. Tips for visiting the best beaches in Italy For some expert advice on planning a beach-oriented itinerary in Italy, we tapped Georgia Yuill, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and Butterfield & Robinson’s region director for Italy. Though the best time to visit Italy can vary depending on the type of trip you want to have, a beach vacation warrants some summer vibes—and strategy. “The best time to go to the beaches of Italy are on the weekdays of June, early July, and September,” Yuill says. “Waterfronts in Sardinia and Sicily are particularly lovely in September with the water warmed up over the previous months and visitor numbers low, leaving you with a tranquil and gorgeous setting.” Yuill says the beaches can get crowded on the weekends in June, July, and August, when you’re competing not only with fellow tourists for spots on the sand but also with Italians who are on their own vacations as well. “That said, experiencing the coastline or islands such as Sardinia by gulet or catamaran is an excellent solution to finding quiet inlets and harder-to-reach beaches,” says Yuill. This list features beaches that are free to access, but if you can swing it, private strips of sand at beach clubs are a great option as well. “Not only are they perfect for people-watching, but they provide all the things travelers may not have packed, like umbrellas and lounge chairs,” Yuill says. Plus, families traveling to Italy with kids will especially appreciate the lifeguards on duty. And who can say no to the convenience of showers, changing areas, and eateries? Finally, Yuill suggests choosing an area designated as a Blue Flag Beach, which indicates that it is clean and well cared for from an environmental perspective. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Kris Fordham and Caitlin Morton.

item.title: An Ode to Gander Airport, 25 Years After 9/11
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.44
Twenty-five years ago, the remote Newfoundland town of Gander found itself becoming an unlikely haven at the edge of the North Atlantic. In the wake of 9/11, more than 4,000 airborne flights were forced to divert when the Federal Aviation Administration closed American airspace—and 38 of those aircraft landed in Gander, bringing nearly 7,000 passengers and crew to a town of just 10,000 people. Brian Mosher, a Gander resident and TV reporter, filmed practically non-stop in the days following September 11, in an attempt to share what was happening on the ground with the world. “There were 7,000 different reasons why people had to get home,” says Mosher. “We were their shoulders to cry on.” The “come from aways,” the Newfoundland term for out-of-towners, were welcomed into the community with warmth, love, food, and anything else their hosts could provide. Buffet tables were set up to feed the new arrivals, and accommodation arranged in homes, schools, and churches. “We thought we’d give them a bite to eat before we put them back on their planes, not realizing they were going to have to stay here five days,” he says. The events of these confusing, confounding days went on to inspire a hit Broadway musical, Come From Away, with Ganderites immortalized in song. Today, Gander International Airport feels smaller and sleepier than its reputation might suggest. Most travelers who find themselves here are on brief stopovers en route to or from other destinations in Newfoundland and Labrador. Others have made a special visit, drawn by the extraordinary architecture and design of the former International Departures Terminal, a Modernist time capsule dating back to 1959. Gander Airport’s legacy actually far predates the events of 9/11–in fact, going all the way back to a time when global aviation was, literally, just taking off. It was the late 1930s, just three decades after Orville and Wilbur Wright’s first flight took off from Kitty Hawk beach in North Carolina. With long-haul air travel underway, and Newfoundland’s location on the Great Circle Route—930 miles closer to Europe than anywhere else in North America—positioned Gander as the perfect staging point for refueling, maintenance, and emergencies at a time when flying was far more unpredictable and potentially unreliable than we know it to be today The first plane to land in Gander touched down on a snow-packed runway in 1938. By 1940, it was already the world’s largest airport, and in World War II served as the main maintenance point for Allied aircraft flying to Europe. Eventually, Gander would go on to welcome commercial flights from Europe and the Soviet Union for refueling stops, but it couldn’t throw off its military past. Until 1959, arriving travelers still found themselves disembarking into a hangar designed for WWII. The opening of the Gander Airport International Departures Terminal by Queen Elizabeth II in June that year changed everything. The new terminal was a showcase for an ambitious, modernizing, young nation featuring Canadian Modernist art and design, as well as stylish furniture by some of the design world’s greatest names like Charles and Ray Eames and Arne Jacobsen. Gander was now ready to welcome world leaders, celebrities, royalty, and rock stars to this little outpost in remote eastern Newfoundland, and was determined to put on a show. Major stars of the day passed through—Marilyn Monroe, Albert Einstein, and Elizabeth Taylor—and could be seen drinking martinis at the Big Dipper, Newfoundland’s only 24-hour bar. As the Jet Age advanced and aircraft became more powerful with increased ranges, trans-Atlantic flights no longer needed to make refueling stops. Arrivals into what was once the “crossroads of the world” began to slow, and Gander’s fortunes declined. The glamorous international terminal and lounge, no longer a necessity, was at risk of being lost to a newer, smaller, more economical option. Eventually, an outpouring of support led to its rescue, and in 2022 it reopened as a museum space with a small movie theater, gastropub, and souvenir shop. Today, it is preserved largely as it was in its heyday. The Mondrian-esque terrazzo floor in shades of salmon, slate, and jade still carries the sheen of 1950s glamour. Clocks on the wall still tell the time in London, Montreal, New York, and Moscow. Stylized bird sculptures by Arthur Price welcoming arriving passengers to Canada still gather in a flock. But the most dramatic feature is the 72-foot Flight and Its Allegories mural by Canadian artist Kenneth Lochhead, featuring a dynamic scene of activity and abundance. A matronly figure stands with arms outstretched. A bearded man feeds airplane-shaped bluebirds. A boy peers through binoculars. Stylized birds burst into the air, some Concorde-like in form, predating the iconic supersonic aircraft by over a decade. Gander-born Todd Saunders, the celebrated architect behind Newfoundland modern icon Fogo Island Inn, credits the International Departure Terminal as being his first exposure to contemporary architecture. “The Canadian government invested in architecture because this was the first face of Canada, and that first impression was really important,” he says. But the airport’s pull went beyond architecture alone. Saunders still recalls the smell of Cuban cigars that lingered after flights stopped in en route between Havana and Moscow. “In a way, it was like Penn Station in New York, but for the world,” he says. The international terminal used to be open to the public at the time, and in doing so, held a cosmopolitan allure for the people of Gander. “My dad worked there as an airplane mechanic and he would call me and say, ‘The [Rolling] Stones are here’, and I’d get on my BMX and head down. You’d be looking at Mick Jagger because they’d had to stop for gas," he recalls. For local textile artist and designer Janet Langdon, whose father worked as an aircraft refueler in Gander in the 1950s and 60s, the airport offered an opportunity to see the world come to town. “I was making my own clothes at the time, and through my young eyes it was super exciting to see worldly fashions.” As a teenager, she would hitchhike to the airport to see the exotic arrivals, including off the many Aeroflot flights that touched down in the early 1970s. “A passenger once gave me a small container of yoghurt,” Langdon says. “It was my first time enjoying it.” Today, flights use the more modern, but less romantic, building next door to the original, but for aviation geeks and history lovers, the museum space is still worth the flight to Gander, not least of all for the history it documents. One display highlights all the most unusual cargo to have moved through the airport, including an aircraft load of ping-pong balls en route to Moscow, a Boeing 747 full of toothpicks, and a shipment of live alligators. Another features episodes like the rescue of George Bush Sr. when he got stuck in a local bog, and Frank Sinatra being admonished for jumping the bar queue and being told to wait his turn. My favorite display is the photo of Fidel Castro sledding in Gander in December 1976: a cadre of heavy-coated officials looking on with concern as a giddy Castro is about to topple off into a heap of snow. But it’s not all about the history. The airport is still a vital part of the Gander community. “An economic impact study concluded last year shows that one in five jobs in the town of Gander are associated with the airport,” Reg Wright, President and CEO of Gander International Airport, says. “It’s nice to see Gander and its guests gather in the lounge again.” For Langdon, the airport is synonymous with what it means to be from this small aviation town in Newfoundland. “Originally it brought people together from all over for employment, and during 9/11 it brought the world to our town,” she says. “Today, people come for the history, some because of Come From Away, and of course the aviation geeks. I just met a retired Lufthansa flight dispatcher who was going to spend time at the lounge before heading back to Luxembourg.” Langdon is hopeful that the airport and departures lounge will remain thriving community spaces. “To quote Reg Wright, we as Ganderites have jet fuel in our veins.” For the town and its people, the airport will never be just a place people pass through; it is woven into their identity and history—and, despite the changing tides of aviation, will remain part of their future. And if there is ever another time when they must heed the call of the world's travelers again, the airport and the community will no doubt stand ready.

item.title: Where Was 'Practical Magic 2' Filmed? Coastal Massachusetts Moves Over for Southern England
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.14
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Practical Magic 2. In 1998, Hollywood starlets Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock played Gillian and Sally Owens, two sisters in possession of special powers in Practical Magic, a film adapted from the eponymous Alice Hoffman novel. Set in the witch-rich state of Massachusetts, the outcasted siblings attempt to lift their ancestral curse, which strikes dead any man who falls in love with an Owens woman. As they embark on this harrowing journey, spells are cast, midnight margaritas are made, and matriarchy reigns supreme. At the time, the film’s reception was middling at best—with a New York Times review describing it as “Barbie Joins a Coven”—and its performance at the box office not much better. With a little room to breathe and bask in nostalgia’s rose-colored glow, the movie has transformed into a feminist cult classic with Gen X and Gen Z fans alike. From 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple to The Devil Wears Prada 2, the past year has been a boon for follow-up films. In that same vein, Kidman and Bullock have reunited in Practical Magic 2, a sequel directed by Susanne Bier that promises to delight fans and take us across the pond to a whole new continent of spooky locales. Another generation of the coven-loving lives on in Practical Magic 2, which picks up after a sizable time jump but with more of the same kooky hijinks. A generous interpretation of time—and a little movie magic—lands Sally’s daughters Antonia (Maisie Williams) and Kylie (Joey King) in their early 20s. Up until now, they have lived their lives ignorant to their powers, which their mother has deliberately shielded them from. Medical student Antonia most closely resembles her mother, while Kylie, now a Harvard student, is a bit more of a free spirit. When Kylie falls for sweet Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) and then he falls into a coma, she follows her mother’s path of attempting to right things. Counseled by the recently uncovered Book of the Raven, Kylie sets off to her family’s ancestral home of England, bringing much of the story to English territory. While the original movie used Washington State's Whidbey Island as a stand-in for New England, production for the sequel moved to the United Kingdom. Here are all the places where Practical Magic 2 was filmed. Leavesden Studios – Hertfordshire, England The Owens women remain the main characters in this film, and fans of the original film will recall the outstanding Victorian-style Owens family home. The house itself has reached a cult status with its cutesy cottage core aesthetic, and its recreation was crucial to the making of the sequel. Practical Magic 2’s production notes explain the importance of the revival of the house. Producer Denise De Novi felt that bringing the house back to life was one of the most rewarding components of making this movie. “The house in this movie is just a phenomenon,” she noted. In the first film, the exterior of the house was built on San Juan Island in Washington state, and the interiors were created on a soundstage in Los Angeles. Those structures no longer exist so this time around, production designer Tom Burton determined that the most economical option was to build the house from scratch on the back lot at Leavesden Studios. Great care was taken to ensure that the replica was consistent with the original home, including establishing the same positioning to the sun so that the sun would set in the same position as it did in the original film. Once the house’s construction was almost complete, the greens team descended upon the set to bring the renowned garden to life, with over 4,000 plants brought in. While about half of the 55 shooting days were spent at Leavesden Studios, the remainder were shot at several notable locations in and around the London area. Village of Hambleden The quaint village of Hambleden, just west of London, served as the town Thornfield. The center of the village is filled with old, picturesque brick and flint cottages, all with the signature dormer windows. The Royal Standard of England, Beaconsfield British viewers might take notice of this historic pub, which serves at the exterior of the fictional Thornfield Inn just northwest of London. The Royal Standard, which has been around for over 900 years, claims to be the oldest pub in Great Britain. Located in the Chiltern Hills, the scenic old pub is filled with charm and has been featured in numerous films and television shows, including The Theory of Everything, Hot Fuzz, and Too Much. Oysters, fish and chips, and a robust beer list are on offer, and Quiz Night is every Tuesday. Langleybury Mansion in Hertfordshire Langlebury is a vacant 18th-century period house that has served as a backdrop for several notable productions including Downton Abbey, The Crown, and Paddington. The crew utilized this mansion to stand in for rooms at Harvard University as well as some of the UK lodgings. Wormsley Estate in Buckinghamshire The private 2,700-acre estate boasting an opera pavilion, cricket grounds, and a walled garden served as the backdrop for the cottage of Tom Lockland (Solly McLeod), a longtime magic student at Thornfield. Black Park Country Park Practical Magic 2 features sweeping views of the British rolling hills and conifer forests. Black Park, a large park with woodland trails, horse riding, and a lake, was filmed as the forest surrounding Thornfield. The Royal Chelsea Hospital The historic Royal Hospital Chelsea in London is a retirement and nursing home for British Army veterans who have reached the state pension age. The hospital was founded by Charles II in 1692, and it has maintained its grand property while modernizing to fit the present-day needs of its inhabitants. The impressive grounds with brick buildings and Roman columns were used in the film for a flower market and shots meant to be Harvard University exteriors. The Victorian flats of Cromwell Buildings The tattoo-covered Professor Ian Wright (Lee Pace), who quickly becomes Sally’s love interest, is one of the more charming updates in this sequel. His apartment was shot in these flats.

item.title: When Is Prime Big Deal Days? Here's Everything Travelers Need to Know About the Fall Sale
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.01
Another Amazon Prime Day is just around the corner, and I already have a shopping cart full of wish-listed items I'm hoping to save on. I usually wait for Prime Big Deal Days to stock up on my favorite home and beauty essentials—and this year, I might even try to get a head start on some holiday gifts before all the chaos of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. After all, Amazon tends to offer its steepest discounts during its twice-a-year mega sale. In years past, I've scored on trending shoes, hard-shell luggage, and electronics for up to 50% off. And since Amazon just announced the dates for this year's highly anticipated Prime Day, let this be your sign to start thinking about what you need to restock and which big-ticket items it might be time to buy (hello, Ōura Ring 5). Prime members are guaranteed to find deals across all major categories, including clothing and shoes, luggage, tech, premium beauty and skincare, outdoor gear, and home goods. Below, I'm breaking down everything there is to know so far about Prime Big Deal Days 2026. Plus, I've listed out some deals running on Amazon right now, so you can start shopping—and saving—early. What is Prime Day? In case you're not familiar with Amazon's best sale of the year, let's get you up to speed: Prime Day is an annual savings event where thousands of products are marked down for a limited time. Prime members will have the chance to save up to 60% off best-selling gear, trending apparel, and so much more. Historically, Prime Day runs in July—but for the past few years, Amazon has been offering a similar sale in October, giving eager shoppers yet another chance to save big. Electronics and home goods tend to be the most popular—and most heavily discounted—items during these Prime Day events, but we typically also see great deals on clothing and shoes, luggage, beauty products, outdoor gear, and travel essentials. When is Prime Day? Amazon finally announced the dates for its fall sale. This year, Prime Big Deal Days will run from Tuesday, October 6, through Wednesday, October 7, 2026. This makes right now a great time to start thinking about which items you hope to see on sale and start building your wish list. Do I have to be an Amazon Prime member to shop the sales? Yes, to take advantage of the limited-time mega sale, you must be a Prime member. Not only do members get access to Prime Day deals, but they also earn free two-day shipping all year long. A Prime membership costs $139 annually or $15 per month. If you're on the fence about joining, sign up for a free 30-day trial. What did our readers buy most last Prime Day? Need some inspo on what to add to your shopping cart ahead of Prime Day 2026? Say no more—check below to see what CN Traveler readers bought most during Amazon's July sale. First and foremost, Away luggage was very popular—and for good reason. The brand's lightweight suitcases are some of our editors' all-time favorite carry-ons and checked bags to travel with. Our readers also picked up a bunch of in-flight essentials, from comfy eye masks to neck pillows (these must-haves can make even the longest flights in economy a little bit more bearable!). In addition, comfortable sneakers, trendy jelly flats, Levi's jeans, portable steamers, and the viral Ōura Ring were big hits among our readers. What early sales can I shop now? We're still a few weeks away from Prime Big Deal Days, but Amazon has plenty of great deals running right now worth checking out. From Bagsmart's top-selling toiletry bag to noise-canceling headphones from Beats, there are already plenty of discounted travel essentials marked down. Also on sale: expandable carry-ons and luggage sets from Samsonite, as well as some travel backpacks and duffel bags. Discounted sneakers, Chelsea boots, and workout sets are all up for grabs too. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: The Quiet Magic of Greece in the Off Season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.62
Few eras of Greek history compare to the ancient times that the country has become so synonymous with—the cinematic fables of Odysseus, comic-book lore of Leonidas, and philosophic creeds of Socrates are ever-present in pop culture. But anyone who’s been to Hellas in the past few years can tell you that something new is brewing here—current-day Greece is coming close to a similar precipice, one that could be nearly as definitive as the Bronze Age, as visitors arrive in droves higher than ever before. Arrivals to the nation of 10 million people were up by 38% in the first few months of 2026, the highest increase on the continent for that period by far (Italy was second, with a 21% rise). Now, more than ever, it feels like everyone is planning a seafaring escape or mountain adventure to Athens and the islands—or, if you’re in-the-know, to the serene coastal towns of the Peloponnese peninsula or the northern Aegean’s sparkling Thermaic Gulf. One decade after the country’s financial crisis peaked, and a half decade since the pandemic-era halt in tourism that had so many here pleading for the long-despised cruise ships to return, you would think this is good news for a state as tourism-dependent as Greece. And you could be right—but the unfortunate reality, according to the Bank of Greece, is that the crescendo coincides with mounting climate disasters that threaten the infrastructure of a nation still in the throes of recovery; a particularly harrowing warning ahead of this year’s El Niño; not to mention during their Mediterranean neighbors' unprecedented fire seasons. The seasonal pressure has become a balancing act. The good news, though, is that summer is far from the only time to visit. Outside the grip of sweltering summer heat lies some of Greece’s most delicious adventures: tasting early spring’s olive oils straight from the groves right after harvest; fall parties with small-island locals celebrating another season of panigiria wrapped; perusing the treasures of Athens’ open-air ruins in the soft, pre-winter light. There is so much more to Greece than the postcard islands—and the packed ferries to get to them—and with the mainland about to have its moment in the sun (we’re looking at you, Christopher Nolan), there’s no better time than the off-season to uncover every corner’s most spectacular self—the one without the heaving crowds. To prove it, we’ve tapped the best local creators to share how they do it, and how you can, too, siga siga (more slowly). —Shannon McMahon, senior destinations editor Over the last 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has made Ammos Hotel (and its beloved on-site Red Jane Bakery) one of Crete’s most talked-about hotels. Born and raised in Chania, the owner’s joyful, design-led approach to hospitality is rooted in his hometown, with 80% of his staff also locals. From its high-quality cuisine to its warm, home-away-from-home atmosphere, Ammos reflects Tsepetis’s deep connection to Chania. Here, he shares why spring is his favorite time to experience the city. For Dutch artist Christiane Smit, a vacation on Paros in 2008 changed the course of her life. Drawn instinctively to the Cycladic island, she stayed and has lived in villages across Paros ever since. Today, she runs a ceramics atelier in Lefkes and owns minimalist clifftop villa Moonhouse, while restoring a century-old stone house in Kostos. Here, Smit shares the shoulder-season pleasures that keep her on the island year-round, and where to eat and stay. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, moving to Santorini from Greece's mainland 11 years ago was an easy choice: “It is the mecca of Greek white wine.” Since then, he has worked across the island’s wineries before launching Orycton, a small-batch Assyrtiko made with grapes from old vines. Now based in quiet Monolithos, Kouloglou has lived throughout Santorini, gaining an intimate understanding of its villages, landscapes, and rhythms. Here, he shares why autumn is his favorite season to explore the island. Greek family recipes are often passed down by instinct rather than instruction—a pinch here, a glug there, learned at the kitchen table. Food writer Anastasia Miari has spent nearly a decade documenting these dishes and the older generations and remote villages that have kept them alive. Her cooking celebrates Greece’s culinary traditions, while her latest book, Mediterranea, expands the journey across the region, from Moroccan tagines and Turkish breakfasts to Sicilian pasta. “Alive. That’s how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. Having lived in the capital since she was 18, Sbokou has watched the city continually evolve, while retaining its irresistible energy. For her, the joy of visiting somewhere lies in understanding its local rhythm. Here, she shares why autumn is so magical in Athens, alongside some of her favorite places to explore in the city. Lead editors: Sarah Allard, Shannon McMahon, Arati Menon, Lisa Riehl Writers: Shannon McMahon, Chadner Navarro, Noo Saro-Wiwa, Olivia Morelli Visuals and social media: Sophie Knight, Mercedes Bleth, Lucy Bruton Syndication editors: Kat Chen, Skyli Alvarez This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Shoulder Season on Paros: Ceramicist Christiane Smit Finds Inspiration at a Slower Pace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.55
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision, it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her unplanned move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse—both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round as well as her favorite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery, and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbors greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most. It changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colors, textures, and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colors of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea—those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travelers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer vacation, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship—from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming, and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favorite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged—a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine—dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages—Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos—that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures; crisp, sunny days; and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both! This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: The Best Rentals and Airbnbs Near Disney World Have Private Pools, Themed Bunk Rooms, and More Fun Amenities
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.31
I've been visiting Walt Disney World my entire life. I've snacked my way around EPCOT, waited out afternoon storms in Magic Kingdom, and celebrated more special occasions at the parks than I can count. But some of my favorite Disney trips happened once I committed to leaving “the bubble” and chose to book a rental property just outside the gates. Staying in a vacation home or Airbnb near Disney World means access to a full kitchen to cut down on pricey park meals, more room to spread out after a long day, and a home base within easy reach of other attractions like Universal Studios, SeaWorld, and Central Florida’s freshwater springs and lakes. Whether you're traveling with a big group, crave a private pool to wind down in post-park, or just want more space than a standard hotel suite allows for, these are the best rentals near Disney World to book for families, friend groups, and solo travelers alike. We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. FAQ: Is it cheaper to stay off-property at Disney World? It is usually cheaper to stay off-property when visiting Disney World. For big groups or families that require additional space and amenities outside of park access, booking a vacation rental is a great option. Before you book though, there are a few extra costs to keep in mind, including rental cars and Disney World parking. You also won't have access to some of the special perks that on-property hotels receive, like early entry to the parks, free park and resort parking, and priority access to booking Lightning Lanes skip-the-line services. How do you get to Disney World? Walt Disney World is about a 30-minute drive from Orlando International Airport. If you're staying at a vacation rental, you'll likely also need access to a car to get to and from the parks. There are a few rentals above, however, that partner with resorts to give you free shuttle access to the parks, which can come in handy if you're an out-of-towner. You can also book ride-shares to and from the park if necessary, but that can add up depending on how far away you're staying. Plus, wait times can be long, especially if you're staying further away or trying to leave at peak times, like after the fireworks show. Once on property, you'll be able to take advantage of Disney's free internal shuttle transportation to get around.

item.title: How to Make the Most of Greece’s Shoulder Season, According to Condé Nast Traveler Specialists
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.23
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Condé Nast Traveler's Top Travel Specialists about how to decide which off-season destination in Greece for you. As we continue to spread the good word of traveling outside of summer—peak season for most destinations, but most of all European—let us convince you that this advice is especially prescient for Greece, which is also magical in late fall, winter (skiing, anyone?), and early spring. But you might ask, how do you even travel to Greece in the off season? This country of many island groups, from Aegean to Ionian, is not just to be experienced at its peak in the summer, when ferries are run to and fro, and your social feed becomes awash with selfies from white-plastered Mykonos. Nay—Όχι! For reasons climate- and crowd-related, certain sides of Greece shine brighter when the brutal Grecian sun lets up and Zeus’s calming clouds roll in, when you actually have breathing room at the Parthenon and can even potentially commune with Athena herself in the soft winter light of Athens. Or, hey, why not just take advantage of the cheaper hotel rates and airfare while most families are wrapped up at school? For these reasons and more, locals and in-the-know visitors know that, in Hellas, “off season” truly means “game on.” To learn what it takes to make the most out of the off season, we tapped some of our favorite Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists who are experts on visiting Greece: Julie Durso of Scott Dunn, Lisa Kusak of Kusak & Co., Emily Rister of Original Travel, and Laura Plansky of Audley Travel. Here they tell us the pros of visiting outside of summer, where to take a city break, and what to pack so that you’re prepared for your own off-season odyssey to Greece. Why you should visit Greece in the off season After an entirely too-hot Eurosummer this year (every year now, it seems), the pros of visiting Greece in the cooler off season have never been more evident. “Visiting off season is perfect for avoiding crowds and the heat,” says Rister of Original Travel. “Generally, Greece can be quite mild, even in winter, so it’s still pleasant to visit and be out and about exploring. Cultural sites are much quieter and you don’t have to book restaurants weeks in advance.” Rister also says that hotel rates massively drop at this time of year, outside of the peak summer travel months, so the off season is a chance to experience luxurious properties for a fraction of the cost. Beyond the weather and value-for-money factor, Kusak of Kusak & Co. says there’s a human element too: “In the off season you find a certain authenticity. With fewer people present, you can get a real connection with the local community—the pace is gentler for everyone.” To top it off, the off season is perhaps the best time for foodie travelers, given the bounty of the winter harvest. “The olive harvest runs from November into December, and some estates will welcome visitors to watch or take part,” Kusak explains. “Citrus season follows in the Peloponnese and Crete, when the orange and lemon groves are at their most vibrant." Of course, no rose is without its thorns: many establishments in Greece do close for the winter, and it’s not exactly prime time for beachgoers—so be sure to calibrate your expectations to cultural and culinary adventures. “It's not the peak season for swimming and boating, if guests have that as a priority,” says Durso of Scott Dunn. While there are locales where restaurants remain open year-round thanks to universities and locals (Athens, Corfu, and Crete among them) it depends where you are: “Many restaurants will also begin closing for the season, so I tend to recommend resorts with restaurants on property, so guests don't feel like they're missing out” if the small tavernas, cafés, and bakeries are shuttered until the spring. The cultural and culinary prowess of Greece in the off season First, the culture and history buffs will greatly appreciate Greece in the off season, Planksy says, because fewer people crowd the main tourist sites and the sun isn’t beating down on travelers as aggressively. Lines are shorter, and there’s more room to breathe in museums and at archaeological locations like the Acropolis or the Agora in Athens. Plus you’ll be able to relish the hike up to the Parthenon without melting in the heat. Of course don’t just waltz in anywhere without tickets or reservations—traveling in the off season still requires the usual due diligence as a traveler. You’ll just have less competition for tables at the best restaurants in Athens. “This time of year is also great for guests who are excited to interact more with locals in the small towns,” Durso says, “those who prefer a relaxed pace rather than enduring crowded tourist areas during high season.” Whether you go to romantic Nafplio in the Peloponnese with its neoclassical mansions or seaside Galaxidi with its cobblestoned alleys, locals will be pleasantly surprised to see out-of-towners passing through, happy for your business and company in the off-season. As Kusak puts it, the off season in Greece is for “someone who wants authenticity and a genuine connection to the place, rather than just boat days and beaches.” There’s no shame in wanting boat days and beaches, of course—we at Traveler love partying and seaside time when we go to Greece too. But just know that if that’s what you’re looking for, summer really is your best bet, Durso says, when all the restaurants and beach clubs are open. How to do it: practical tips When visiting Greece in the off season, one of the first things we need to talk about is the climate. “As the weather starts to shift, you get more wind and cooler evenings,” says Durso. “So it’s important to pack layers,” like lightweight sweaters, linen that you can wear on top of each other, a rain jacket, maybe a little bit of cashmere while you’re at it. Take it from me: Even in May of this year on Corfu, I found myself reaching for my denim jacket more than once, even on a beach day. The next thing to be mindful of is the country’s schedule, from the timetables for ferries to the opening hours of restaurants, tourist and archaeological sites, and even whole islands. “Ferry schedules are reduced in the off season and the weather is more likely to impact those journeys,” says Plansky. Don’t go to Greece in the off-season hoping for the typical island-hopping style vacation, because many of the smaller islands close between November to April. “So it’s better to explore the mainland of Greece and some of the bigger islands like Crete, Corfu, and Santorini during that time,” she says. And double check with your hotel if they’ll be open during your visit. Chances are that a hotel won’t accept your booking if they see that you’re in town when they’re not, but it never hurts to be sure. “It is worth planning around what is genuinely open rather than where you want to go on the map,” Kusak says. “This is where I lean on my team in Greece. They know which properties are running, which restaurants stay open through the winter, and where a January afternoon is best spent. It isn't information you can always find online, and it changes from year to year.” Are you, conveniently enough, hoping to spend a January afternoon in Greece? “A January afternoon in Athens is best spent on foot,” Kusak asserts. “I’d wander a few of the neighborhoods—Plaka, Monastiraki, Thisio, Kolonaki—just to get a feel for how the city lives, pausing at a small shop for a warm koulouri or a slice of spanakopita along the way. Then the Acropolis, which in the off-season is blissfully unhurried. With the crowds thinned, there's room to take it in properly.” Where (else) to go in Greece in the off season In the off season, while many places in some smaller islands and destinations may “shut down,” Greece does not close uniformly. Athens, the rest of the mainland, and many of the larger islands carry on much as usual. In addition to Athens, Corfu, Crete, Santorini, and Paros—as recommended by locals we admire and trust—our Top Travel Specialists also gave their own additional recommendations for where to go in Greece in the off season: Thessaloniki and the Peloponnese. Thessaloniki: Culinary heritage on the Thermaic Gulf Waterfront Thessaloniki is designated a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, with a dining scene informed by a long history as a crossroads of ancient and modern trade. Given its position in Northern Greece, Thessaloniki has played host to Greeks, Ottoman Turks, Sephardic Jews, Armenians, and Slavs for centuries, resulting in meals and dishes that pull influences from all over the continent. And because Thessaliniki is also the second largest city in Greece, it has more in common with Athens schedule-wise and stays open even after the summer is over. Kusak has two restaurant recommendations: “For something traditional, I suggest The Rouga. It’s a good place to share meze and a few Greek classics. For a quieter, more polished evening, there’s Olympos Naoussa inside the ON Residence, a Small Luxury Hotels of the World hotel. It sits in a restored heritage building overlooking the Thermaic Gulf, and suits a special occasion or a last-night-before-we-go-home dinner.” As for where to stay, Rister often books clients at The Modernist Thessaloniki set in a 1920s heritage building; The Excelsior, just a block away from the harbor; and Electra Palace Thessaloniki, a grande dame on Aristotelous Square. When it comes to cultural excursions, Rister recommends a walking tour of the city with a private guide—“Great for fans of Alexander the Great.” and a day trip to Vergina, home to the tomb of Philip II of Macedon, Alexander the Great’s father. Rister at Original Travel can help put these offerings together for those who are keen. The Peloponnese: Homeric outdoor adventure In lieu of the typical Greek islands vacay, a road trip that traces the coast of the rugged and mountainous Peloponnese peninsula could scratch that itch to be near some water, as long as you’re okay with the fact that it may be too cold to go in. Kusak recommends a few seaside towns in the Peloponnese: “On a rocky islet just off the coast, Monemvasia is a medieval town you reach almost by surprise, where you can wander the cobbled streets and stay in one of the restored stone houses,” she says. “And Pylos gathers around a waterfront square and an old natural harbor. It’s the way into the Costa Navarino resort area, with its beaches, golf, and resorts, though Pylos holds its own quiet history and lends itself to a slower coastal stay.” Kusak also recommends Nafplio for its proximity to Athens—under two hours apart by car—and the beautiful Venetian architecture in the area, souvenirs from when Venice held trading posts in Greece. Plansky also loves to send travelers to Nafplio: “It has a little bit of everything—history, culture, coastal beauty, plenty of food and wine. And there are some fantastic sites nearby including Mycenae, Epidavros, Ancient Corinth, and the Nemea wineries that are easy day trips.” Where to stay If you’re a fiend for a good hotel, Durso recommends Amanzoe, considered by Aman junkies to be one of the brand’s very best properties. “Plus it stays open through the second week of November, offering a luxurious option at sometimes less than half its peak-season rates,” Durso says. Conveniently it’s also close to villages like Nafplio and historic sites like Mycenae. “Another lovely property is Kinsterna in Monemvasia, a boutique hotel with fantastic farm-to-table cuisine,” Durso says. And for those seeking quiet, Rister suggests an easy-going stay in some of the most relaxing spa hotels in the Peloponnese for some true rest—Euphoria Retreat in Mystras and Manna Arcadia. The former is a wellness retreat located near epic Sparta and the UNESCO-listed Archaeological Site of Mystras, or castro (fortress), for those who like their relaxation with a side of historic adventure; the latter is surrounded by moody fir forests ideal for hiking, giving it the feel of a remote getaway. “They can be easily combined with a city break in Athens at any time of the year,” Rister says.

item.title: I Spent Four Days Touring Scotland’s Whisky Island—and It Was Better Than I Expected
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.15
My dad’s 60th birthday was coming up, and as an avid whisky drinker with a particularly sharp nose, his dream trip has always been to explore the coastline of Islay, a Scottish island famed worldwide for its smoky, peated single malt whiskies. I often travel solo and am fond of organized tours, so when I came across Rabbie’s four-day Islay and whisky tour—with pickup from Edinburgh, a selection of historic stops, a maximum group size of 16 people, and plenty of opportunities for drams—it sounded ideal for us both. Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, with a landscape of rugged beaches and peat bogs, and traveling through it usually involves many small logistics. I was thrilled to see that this tour handles all of the planning for you—including transportation, accommodations, attractions, and providing a local guide for the four-day trip. It starts at just $609 per adult without accommodations or distillery tours, or around $1,464 all-in, which seemed like a great deal. I was convinced, so I booked it! Our trip began with an evening in Edinburgh to recover from jet lag. The next morning, we made our way to the Edinburgh bus station to meet our driver and group. A 16-seat Mercedes mini coach pulled up, and we all piled in as our guide’s Celtic music played and we said goodbye to the city. Our first stop was the historic town of Falkirk, just 25 miles from Edinburgh, where we saw the iconic towering Kelpies sculptures and grabbed a coffee. I knew I was going to like our Glaswegian guide, Peter McShane, from the excitement in his voice as he told us about Scottish folklore. We then rode through the Lowlands and mountainous regions surrounding Loch Lomond and Trossachs National Park en route to the town of Oban, known as the “Gateway to the Isles.” There, we browsed local shops and grabbed some fresh seafood. Bellies full and a dram or two later at Oban Distillery, we hopped back on the coach and drove to Kennacraig to make our evening ferry to Islay. For two hours, we sailed along the glass-like Sound of Jura before the Paps of Jura mountains came into view, signaling that the island was just ahead. Arriving in Islay was like nothing I’d experienced before. At just 240 square miles, the island felt entirely remote yet surprisingly homey. We settled in for the evening in the town of Bowmore. We didn’t know what to expect when our itinerary said accommodations would be shared, but we were pleasantly surprised by the setup we were met with at Bowmore Distillery Cottages. There were four bedrooms, and my dad and I each had our own room, while two others from our group took over the other two rooms and shared the communal kitchen and living spaces with us. Our first full day on whisky island started with a short two-minute walk to the distillery that would kick off our tour: Bowmore Distillery. We learned about the distillery’s 240-year history on the island, which was a great starting point for the days ahead. Then came a tasting (straight from the cask!) in the cellar, and another tasting upstairs to end the tour, this time with whisky, chocolate, and views of the sea. Since Islay is a very small island with a population of a little over 3,000 people, it’s important to be flexible on these types of trips and just roll with the punches. Depending on the days of your tour, some distilleries may be closed or not open to full tours. Our itinerary said we’d be visiting Kilchoman on day one, but instead, we diverted to Ardnahoe for a lively tour and quick tasting before driving through the countryside to Bunnahabhain. With sweeping views of the clear blue waters, we explored the facilities and sampled four drams at Islay’s most remote distillery. While it's always great to meet new people and travel around with them, I appreciated that lunches and evenings were free for us to explore at leisure. After full days of sampling whiskies, it was a nice respite to just enjoy some quality time with my dad. That said, by day two, our group was buzzing as we became more comfortable with each other—and this second day was the big one for most of us as we took on the villages of Ardbeg, Lagavulin, and Laphroaig, each with their own distilleries. Though the island is small, the differences between the West Coast and Southern Coast became evident as we left Bowmore toward Ardbeg. Because it was a Saturday, our itinerary mentioned our visit to Ardbeg would not include a tour—but, as I said, roll with the punches. We did, in fact, get to see some of the facilities and end with a five-dram tasting. This experience was probably one of the most memorable moments of the trip for me—sitting around a table in the sunshine with people I’d just met, laughing, and sampling some of the finest whiskies in the world. We made a quick stop at Kildalton Church, home to an eighth-century cross and one of Scotland’s finest early Christian monuments, before continuing toward Port Ellen, a tiny town built around Loch Leòdamais, for a lunch break. Again, these parts of the tour are not organized, so if you have a restaurant or attraction in mind you want to visit, make an early reservation or chance your luck at walking in. At Lagavulin Distillery, our visit didn’t include a tour or tasting, but we chatted around the bar with our new friends and strolled down to the coast. In under five minutes, we made it to Laphroaig—our last whisky tasting of the trip. Here, we enjoyed an immersive tour of the peat kilns, stills, and warehouses before sampling a few more of their whiskies, our Glencairn glasses conveniently attached to lanyards around our necks. On day four, we had an early start and set sail again for a two-hour journey from Islay to Kennacraig. We treated ourselves to a full Scottish breakfast and explored the ferry, this time passing strangers-turned-friends. After an hour’s drive, we stopped in the castle town of Inveraray for lunch before making our way through the rugged Arrochar Alps to the “Rest and Be Thankful” mountain pass viewpoint. Our final stop was the quintessential village of Luss, where we, of course, found yet another distillery to visit. There was something heavy yet appreciative in the air during our last stop—we were sad it was our last day, but incredibly thankful for the new connections, laughs, and memories we’d made along the way. I’ve done Rabbie’s day tours in the past, but this one was particularly immersive because we were with the same people for the entirety of the trip—and we lucked out with our guide. All in all, this experience came at just the right time for my dad and me, and it was amazing learning more about his passions. According to him, a man with a collection of over 200 whiskies, “it was well worth the money.” How to book Rabbie’s Islay & the Whisky Coast tour Founded in Edinburgh in 1993, Rabbie’s specializes in small-group tours throughout Scotland, the UK, Ireland, and Europe. The four-day Islay & the Whisky Coast tour departs from Edinburgh and includes transportation, ferry crossings, entrance fees, and three nights in Bowmore (some distillery tours and tastings are available for an additional fee). You can book the tour on Rabbie's website, Viator, or GetYourGuide.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: To Avoid the Crowds on Crete, Hike and Ski in Early Spring
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’s improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning, year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city." Yet, 80 percent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience, because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity." Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favorite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favorite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains]—you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation, so spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here—not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favorite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern, it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous Restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages, because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs, and liver. We normally eat it at home—it’s not so much a restaurant dish—but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens—we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes—and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini, and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called dakos, a barley rusk with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in village Maza, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring, the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski, and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased, but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2:00 p.m., I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane, and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays, it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighborhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favorite open-air theater is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there, you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path—not for the faint-hearted—to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 13 Best Hotels in Key West, From Historic Inns to Private Islands
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.93
Long known for its free-spirited vibe and its identity as the iconoclastic “Conch Republic,” Key West welcomes you to come as you are, whether that means strolling past street-roaming roosters in your finest cowboy hat and Daisy Dukes, joining the revelers on Duval Street à la Mardi Gras, enjoying family time on the beach, or just staying put around your hotel pool “wasting away again in Margaritaville.” (Jimmy Buffett actually wrote the final verses of the song circa 1977 while stuck in traffic on the Seven Mile Bridge heading back to the Florida Keys, then debuted it on Duval Street shortly thereafter.) It’s definitely a place that caters to hedonistic tendencies at land’s end, especially during Fantasy Fest and other wild celebrations throughout the year, but it’s equally suited to soaking up the sun and embracing an IDGAF attitude. Beneath the more recent commercialization of Key West lies a deeper charm, reflected in its eclectic mix of resorts. The most sought-after stays are in Old Town, which occupies the island’s western edge, touching both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. Old Town is remarkably walkable, with fabulous restaurants, historic sites, and kitschy dive bars never more than a short stroll away. True, there are plenty of places to stay in New Town, often at lower rates. But why rely on an hourly shuttle to Old Town or stare at a chain mall parking lot from your room when so much of the fun of Key West is crawling back to your hotel through picturesque neighborhoods and lush gardens after a night of debauchery? There’s also something to be said for actually sleeping in one of the historic cottages and buildings that speak to Key West's earlier days, recalling the words of Hemingway and lyrics of Buffett. Whether you’re after a romantic retreat, a fun weekend with your besties, a gay nudist escape, or a laid-back family vacation, you’ll find it among our picks for the best hotels in Key West.
