Fun fact: there’s a schoolroom on the grounds that Ford had transplanted here, and which he believed had been the original inspiration for the nursery rhyme ‘Mary Had A Little Lamb’.

item.title: 19 best hotels in Sri Lanka including design-led boltholes and beachside resorts
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.34
Sri Lanka has had a rough ride at times, but this teardrop island is now thriving — and easier to reach than ever, with British Airways launching new direct flights from the UK in October 2026. And where better to enjoy this sublime sunny destination than at one of the best hotels in Sri Lanka? The country is as dynamic as it is diverse with gorgeous beaches, serene hill country and ancient ruins. There are also splendid national parks teeming with elephants, leopards and a dazzling array of birds. However, it’s not just about the places. Then there are the people, who are warm, generous and quick to make you feel at home. The delicious spice-laden food, accompanied by a cup of famous Ceylon tea, rounds off the appeal. When it comes to places to stay, there are myriad options. Heritage homes and hotels, often sporting a tropical modernist look spearheaded by star Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa, have long set the tone. But things are changing and the past decade has seen new design-led hotels crop up, pushing the boundaries of hospitality and bringing fresh energy to the country. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Sri Lanka - For honeymoon: Kahanda Kanda, Galle Fort - For families: Cape Weligama, Weligama - For beach: Amanwella, Tangalle - For a south coast location: Kayaam House, Rekawa What is the best part of Sri Lanka to stay in? Cosmopolitan capital Colombo is a quietly rising scene of stylish coffee shops, dynamic art galleries and independent boutiques. But really you want to spend your time on the southwest coast, with its idyllic beaches. There is a brilliant selection of oceanfront hotels around Galle, bringing in fresh seafood, laid-back cafes and toes-in-the-sand luxury. There are equally good properties a short tuk-tuk ride inland for more peace and quiet. While it's tempting to stick to the coast, Yala National Park has excellent lodges, with superb game viewing to go with it. If you have the time, continue up the country to one of the charming, restored colonial properties in the Hill Country, particularly around Ella and Hatton. Then there's the Cultural Triangle, which includes both Kandy, home to the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, one of Buddhism's most sacred shrines, and the extraordinary Sigiriya Rock. What area of Sri Lanka is best for first-time visitors? Sri Lanka is compact enough to explore in two or three weeks. Begin in Sri Lanka’s Cultural Triangle, with its ancient cities and temples, before boarding the famous scenic train from Kandy into the island’s lush hill country. Wind through emerald tea plantations to Nuwara Eliya or Ella, then head south for a safari in Yala National Park where elephants and leopards roam wild. Finish on the laid-back south coast, with golden beaches, palm-fringed shores and sparkling ocean views. If you're short on time, then focus on the southwest coast around Galle, particularly if you have family in tow. It's accessible from Colombo airport (two to three hours) and you can experience much of Sri Lanka's best in one fell swoop: glorious beaches, Bawa architecture and colonial history. Just save a night or two for wildlife spotting in Yala National Park. Which part of Sri Lanka is best for beaches? The southwest coast is lined with fantastic beaches, from lively surf hubs to quiet, palm-dotted bays. Highlights include Mirissa for whale-watching and the turquoise waters of horseshoe-shaped Hiriketiya Beach with its trendy cafes and surf vibes. Beginner surfers should head to Weligama Beach, known for its gentle, consistent waves. For simple beach bliss, choose the quiet coastline near Tangalle or the buzzier Unawatuna and Dalawella, with sea turtles wallowing near the shore. When the south coast is out of season (March to December), turn your attention to the beaches on the east coast such as Trincomalee for its deep natural harbours, historic sites and rich underwater biodiversity. Further south is Passikuda, with its shallow, calm coastline, and flourishing Arugam Bay, ‘A-Bay’, Sri Lanka’s surf capital. Where should I stay in Sri Lanka for wildlife? Yala National Park is Sri Lanka’s big hitter, with sightings of elephants near guaranteed, alongside sloth bears, water buffalo and deer. Leopards are also a possibility, though harder to spot. For less crowds, choose under-the-radar Gal Oya National Park, just east of the Hill Country. One of the country’s most unspoilt parks, swimming elephants are the main attraction plus it’s a paradise for bird lovers. How we choose the best hotels in Sri Lanka Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: Flying long haul but can't swing business class? These 16 premium economy seats are the next best thing
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.26
There’s a happy medium between the ultra-luxe business class cabin and the cramped claustrophobia of coach class: premium economy. With record-high airfares, splashing out on business class isn’t possible for every flight. Premium economy is designed for travellers who want a bit more pampering but on a tighter budget. The cabin usually offers comfier seats, more personal space, enhanced amenities, and upgraded meal and beverage selections compared to standard economy class. But not all premium economy products are worth the more expensive airfare. The best premium economy cabins are usually found on long-haul aircraft that operate lengthy international routes. These fare classes offer an elevated experience both on the ground and in the sky, with well-designed seats located in a separate, comparatively spacious cabin. During the booking process, it can be difficult to discern all the perks – or lack thereof – included in a premium economy fare. So we’ve rounded up a list of our favourite premium economy products from airlines across the globe. If you spend your precious airline miles or hard-earned cash on an upgrade to any of these seats, you’ll arrive at your destination well rested and ready to go. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Emirates One of the most popular premium economy cabins in the sky, Emirates debuted its version of the offering in 2021. The seats have continued to roll out to more aircraft, specifically on Emirates' double-decker Airbus A380 planes and on select retrofitted Boeing 777 aircraft. The cabin is at the front of the first deck. The seats are now available on more than 30 routes to and from Dubai, including US cities like New York, Los Angeles, Boston, Chicago, Miami, Dallas, San Francisco, Seattle, and Houston. For premium economy travellers, the perks start in the airport, with a separate check-in desk, larger carry-on bag allowance, and free seat selection. Inside the cabin, Emirates uses the same design elements as its iconic business-class cabin, such as cream leather with stitching details and wood accents. Passengers also get a large throw pillow, six-way adjustable headrest, calf-and-foot rests, and an in-flight entertainment screen measuring 13.3 inches wide, as well as a dining table with a side cocktail table and charging ports. As for in-flight dining, expect three-course dinners served on Royal Doulton china tableware with stainless steel cutlery. Emirates always includes a dish from the flight's destination on the premium economy menu – such as Thai pepper beef with jasmine rice and pak choi. Top it all off with a complimentary glass of wine or something sparkly like the vintage 2012 Chandon – one of the array of drink selections from the business-class wine list not available in regular economy. Qantas Australian carrier Qantas's premium economy cabin – available on the airline's Boeing 787 Dreamliners and Airbus A380s – is completely separate from regular economy with 32 to 40 seats in a two-three-two layout. Seats are wider and offer more legroom than coach seats, but they also feature wider armrests with storage compartments, two USB outlets, an ergonomic headrest, and a footrest. One of the most thoughtful aspects is the seat’s “unique recline motion,” designed to “provide a class-leading level of comfort,” Qantas says on its website. Instead of simply reclining backwards, the seat moves forward and up, so your legs and back are slightly elevated in a more comfortable position. Premium passengers are greeted with a complimentary sparkling wine or water upon boarding. Meals are served on custom-designed tableware by David Caan. Other in-flight amenities include noise-cancelling headphones, a large pillow, a 100 per cent wool blanket, and an amenity kit. Passengers in the cabin also have access to a dedicated check-in counter and priority boarding. The cabin class is available out of at least 13 airports, including US hubs like Dallas-Fort Worth, New York JFK, Honolulu, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. All Nippon Airways Premium economy on Japanese carrier ANA is truly a premium experience, starting in the terminal. On international flights, premium economy passengers are afforded access to the airline’s lounges at its major hubs, including Tokyo Haneda, Tokyo Narita, Osaka's Kansai airport, and Honolulu airport. ANA is also launching new premium economy seats on its fleet of fresh Boeing 787-9 aircraft, the first of which will be received in November 2026, that operate long-haul international flights. The overhauled seats offer 40 inches of pitch and nine inches of recline, an improvement of two additional inches for both dimensions. When it’s time to relax, a leg rest pops up that supports the entire calf. A 15.6-inch entertainment screen comes with Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C charging ports. Once in the air, premium economy fliers are treated to refreshments from ANA’s business-class drink menu, which includes curated selections of Champagne, sake, red and white wine, Umeshu plum wine, and shochu. Mealtime offers a selection of Asian-Western fusion cuisine, including the carrier’s homemade bread served in business class. Throughout the flight, premium economy passengers have access to substantial snacks, such as petit fours or cup-style noodles, usually reserved for business class. Upon landing, priority baggage handling means you won’t have to wring your hands at baggage claim, wondering if your checked luggage arrived safely. Virgin Atlantic On board Virgin Atlantic's sleekly designed planes, there's a lot to celebrate – like the revamped Upper Class cabin on the airline's Airbus A350S, featuring The Loft lounge. Not least among them is Virgin's premium economy cabin, simply called Premium, which is available on the carrier's A330-220 and A330-300 planes, its A350-1000s, and Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. Seats in Premium are roomy: They're up to 21 inches wide (four inches wider than economy), have seven to eight inches of recline, and up to 38 inches of pitch. Each one also has a footrest. Premium fliers get a dedicated check-in and bag drop line, plus priority boarding. Once aboard, passengers are handed a complimentary welcome glass of bubbly. Dinner includes a starter and main course served on china and paired with white or red wine. Select flights also include Virgin's signature afternoon tea service, featuring sandwiches, tea cakes, and warm scones with jam and clotted cream. Singapore Airlines Singapore, known for its over-the-top first-class suites, also offers a solid premium economy product on its A350, A380, and Boeing 777 aircraft. Seats are spacious, with up to 19.5 inches of width, an eight-inch recline, and calf and footrests. Each spot also has two USB ports and a 13.3-inch screen that comes with noise-cancelling headphones. There are also individual stowage areas specially designed for a water bottle, laptop, and headphones. While most of the seats are in a two-four-two layout, the airline's A350-900ULR planes have six single seats available, which would give the experience more of a business class feel. Premium economy passengers have access to additional meal and beverage choices, including Singapore's famous “book the cook” service, available on premium economy flights from 27 cities. This service allows customers to choose from in-flight meals created by the airline's International Culinary Panel and reserve them up to 24 hours in advance. Customers also receive priority check-in, boarding, and baggage handling. Cathay Pacific When it debuted a trio of overhauled cabins in 2025, Hong Kong-based carrier Cathay Pacific received numerous accolades for its new Aria business class suites. But its refreshed premium economy concept also offers a strong dose of luxury. The dedicated cabin has a total of 48 seats in a 2-4-2 layout. It’s easy to get cosy on Cathay’s long-haul routes, thanks to the generous dimensions of the premium economy seats. Expect a roomy 39-inch pitch, a seat width of 19.5 inches, and eight inches of recline, plus a calf rest and a footrest. The 15.6-inch entertainment screen has Bluetooth audio pairing, plus USB-A and USB-C ports, and fliers are provided with noise-cancelling headphones. Upon boarding, premium economy passengers are offered a welcome drink, as well as a menu of gourmet Cantonese cuisine and other international dishes. The cabin also has its own premium economy lavatory with touchless features. On the ground, fliers receive perks like priority boarding, dedicated check-in at select airports, and two free checked bags. Air France In the fall of 2024, Air France renamed its premium economy cabin to simply “Premium” and began installing larger seats in the cabin across its fleet. The new seats recline to a generous 124 degrees, offer 37 to 38 inches of legroom pitch and an adjustable footrest, and have been “widened for extra comfort,” the airline says. As an additional upgrade, Air France redesigned the seat foam and topped it with herringbone fabric for a softer, more cosy finish. The new seat is available on select Boeing 777 planes and Airbus A350 jets, and by the end of 2025, Air France expects them to be installed on 80 per cent of its fleet. Aside from the seat specifications, the Premium cabin offers a priority check-in counter and baggage drop at the airport, as well as priority boarding. Extra in-flight perks include 13.3-inch entertainment screens with Bluetooth connectivity, USB charging ports, noise-cancelling headphones, and an amenity kit designed specifically for the cabin class. And, as France’s national flag carrier, mealtime is its own momentous event. Premium passengers can expect to receive a glass of Champagne upon arrival, followed by a “full ‘French-style’ meal service, comprising snacks, a starter, a choice of two hot dishes, cheese and dessert, served in eco-designed tableware with stainless steel cutlery,” according to the airline’s site. Expect to top it all off with impressive French patisserie, like Paris-Brest and chocolate fondant. Lufthansa In Lufthansa’s new Allegris cabin concept, each seat in the cabin features a hard-shell backing that will allow fliers to recline without encroaching on the passenger behind them. Each seat has 39 inches of pitch, and, on average, Lufthansa’s premium economy seats offer 50 per cent more space than regular economy. The cabin’s 24 seats are laid out in a 2-3-2 configuration and also come with a 15.6-inch 4K monitor, wireless charging stations, leg rests, noise-cancelling headphones, a separate cocktail table, a personal reading light, a coat hook, and a water bottle holder. You’ll also get two free checked bags and, once on board, a welcome drink to sip as you settle in. The new Allegris cabin class is now available on nine of Lufthansa’s Airbus A350-900s, which are flying between Munich and San Francisco, Shanghai, Bengaluru, Mumbai, Chicago, Beijing, and New York-JFK. British Airways When flying in a premium economy seat on British Airways – called World Traveller Plus by the carrier – you’ll find a separate cabin with seats laid out in a two-four-two arrangement, for a total of about 40 seats on most transatlantic-operating aircraft. In terms of dimensions, seats offer 38 inches of pitch and eight inches of recline, and a footrest (but no leg support). The airline also notes that the seats are wider than in regular economy. Once you complete your priority boarding, you’ll be offered a welcome drink of sparkling wine or juice in real glassware. Meals are also served on ceramic tableware. Other amenities include over-ear headphones for your in-flight entertainment, plus a plusher blanket, pillow, and toiletry kit than those offered in coach. Two free checked bags round out the benefits in this comfortable fare class. Japan Airlines Although Japan Airlines has long offered a stellar premium economy product, the newest version of the cabin that’s rolling out on the carrier’s Airbus A350-1000 planes is on a different level. The 24 seats arranged in a 2-4-2 layout have hardshell seat backs so reclining passengers don’t steal away your elbow room. There are also divider walls between seats for extra privacy, and business-class features like motorised recline and leg rest functions that operate at the push of a button. The seat specifications are impressive, too: Leg rests rise to a comfy 90 degrees, and when that feature isn’t in use, a pitch of 42 inches means there’s plenty of room to stretch out. You’ll also find a massive, 16-inch 4K monitor for in-flight entertainment, an AC power outlet, USB type A and C charging ports. At the airport, premium economy passengers can expect priority check-in at a dedicated cabin counter, priority baggage handling, and access to the airline’s Sakura lounges in Japan. As of spring 2025, the airline was flying nine of the 13 total A350-1000 planes it had ordered. The nine planes currently operate on the airline’s routes between Tokyo Haneda and New York JFK, Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), London Heathrow (LHR), and Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG). In summer 2025, JAL will begin operating the new aircraft between Los Angeles (LAX) and Tokyo, as well. Air New Zealand Passengers on all of Air New Zealand’s long-haul routes operated by its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and 777 jets have the option of upgrading to its premium economy cabin. You’ll breeze through the airport with premium check-in and a luggage allowance of two checked bags. Inside the separate premium economy cabin, where 28 seats are arranged in a two-three-two layout, expect seat features like a legrest, extendable footrest, and 50 per cent more recline than regular economy for a total of nine inches. Seat pitch measures a roomy 41 inches. Come mealtime, you’ll have an upgraded menu to choose from, with dishes like slow-roasted lamb or New Zealand hāpuka fish, accompanied by a selection of award-winning New Zealand wines. What’s more: the airline unveiled the first of its redesigned 787-9 Dreamliners in May 2025, featuring an upgraded premium economy product with more storage options, side wings for added privacy, and fixed outer shells so reclining passengers don’t encroach on your personal space. That initial aircraft – tail number ZK-NZH – will operate flights between San Francisco (SFO) and Auckland (AKL). Seven of the new aircraft variant are expected to be in service by the end of 2025. EVA Air The airline that invented premium economy back in the 90s is still bringing new innovations to the fare class decades later. The Taiwan-based carrier has launched a completely reimagined version of its premium economy cabin on its new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner jets, and it’s well worth the splurge. For starters, the refreshed concept offers an industry-leading 42-inch pitch at every seat, making the seat’s specifications alone worth the price of an upgrade. Passengers can stretch out and use the seat’s ingenious recline function, which has hard-shell backing and offers a cradling motion that slides the seat forward and up for eight inches of recline without disturbing the flier behind. Footrests and privacy panels add even more comfort, and a 15.6-inch entertainment screen and personal device holder will hold your attention for the long-haul journey. The carrier is continually rolling out more of the 787-9 planes with its latest premium economy cabin and plans to deploy a total of nine of the widebody planes by 2029. Delta’s version of international premium economy – Delta Premium Select – underwent an extensive overhaul in 2022. The result: an even plusher cabin with more comfortable seats, cosier bedding, and food and beverage perks. The latter point may be what charms passengers most. After take-off, Premium Select fliers are now offered a “bubbles and bites” service with complimentary sparkling wine or sparkling water and savoury snacks such as mixed nuts. Other business-class-level touches, like printed menus and an oshibori towel, make meal service an event worth savouring. Seats offer 38 inches of pitch with a leg and footrest, 19 inches of width, and seven inches of recline – each dimension several inches larger than in regular economy. Other upgrades include two free checked bags, priority check-in and boarding, noise-cancelling headphones, and a plush memory foam pillow. Swiss Air If you’re flying to Zurich or Geneva from the US, consider upgrading from coach to Swiss Air’s new “Swiss Senses” premium economy cabin. The separate premium economy cabin features 38 seats in a two-three-two layout, offering an exclusive environment. Each seat is 19 inches wide with 39 inches of pitch, with thoughtful features like a hard shell for easy reclining without disturbing surrounding fliers and privacy dividers attached to the headrest. You’ll also find a leg and calf rest and a 15.6-inch entertainment screen with Bluetooth capability, so you can stretch out and watch a new movie. There’s even a wireless charging pad in the armrest (along with USB-A and USB-C ports) to keep your devices juiced up. Premium economy passengers are allowed two free checked bags, and upon boarding, they get a taste of Switzerland’s famous apéro culture with a welcome aperitif and a Sbrinz cheese snack, along with Swiss wines to complement their in-flight meal. Finnair For a sense of Nordic style in the skies, look no further than Finnair’s premium economy product. The Helsinki-based carrier’s upgraded cabin can be found on long-haul flights aboard its Airbus A350 and A330 aircraft and features collaborations with Finnish designers, including Marimekko amenity kits and Iittala tableware, which is used to serve three-course meals. Aside from its focus on style, the cabin offers substance, too, including spacious seats with 38 inches of pitch and a leg rest that cradles the entire leg. Each spot is also outfitted with a 13-inch entertainment screen, power outlets, and USB-A ports. When it’s time to rest, passengers will notice that the separate cabin, with just 26 seats in a two-four-two layout, fosters a quiet, calm atmosphere conducive to relaxation. ITA Airways Book a seat in ITA Airways’ premium economy class and bring a bit of “la dolce vita” lifestyle to your next flight without busting your budget. The dedicated cabin is outfitted with 24 seats in a spacious two-three-two layout. Every seat is upholstered in stylish beige and cream-colored textiles and offers seven inches of recline, 40 inches of pitch, and 19 inches of width. A leg and footrest, plus privacy wings on the headrest, make falling asleep easy, while perks like a 15.6-inch entertainment screen, noise-cancelling headphones, and USB-A and USB-C ports ensure quality in-flight entertainment. Each seat even has a separate cocktail table that can hold passengers’ welcome drink of prosecco, or maybe a glass of Italian wine, limoncello, or a freshly made espresso from Illy coffee. Meal time means Italian dishes served on porcelain tableware. The benefits extend to the airport experience, too: premium economy fliers are granted priority check-in, boarding, and baggage claim, as well as two free checked bags.

item.title: UK cities could soon be allowed to implement a tourist tax – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.07
Regions and cities across the country are set to benefit from extra funds following the latest announcements regarding the UK tourist tax – officially known as the overnight visitor levy. In a statement published by the UK Government on 10 September, it was announced that mayors and local leaders would soon be handed the power to introduce the overnight visitor levy to maximise the benefits of tourism to the country. The new fee on overnight stays may then be invested to boost tourism and drive growth, supporting local communities. Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said: “Our amazing towns and cities, and our picturesque rural and coastal communities welcome millions of visitors every year – local leaders should have the power to make the most of that popularity.” “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most. It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.” While early reports suggested that the UK tourist tax, as it has since been dubbed, would be uncapped, the statement released on 10 September made it clear that budget staycations would be protected. Rather than a flat fee or rate, the levy will be charged as a percentage of the cost of the accommodation – but UK citizens won’t be exempt from paying the fee in other UK regions or cities. This is just the latest in a growing number of fiscal devolution reforms that see local authorities have more power over their areas following the appointment of Andy Burnham as Prime Minister. Steve Rotheram, Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, said, “This is something I’ve been calling for over many years, so I’m really pleased the government is taking forward plans to give Mayors the power to introduce a visitor levy locally. “Our visitor economy is already worth more than £6.8bn a year and supports more than 55,000 jobs across the Liverpool City Region. A modest levy on overnight stays could potentially raise up to £18m a year – money that would stay here and be reinvested directly into the events, culture, experiences and infrastructure that bring millions of visitors to our region. “Visitor levy mechanisms are often used in many great cities across the globe to improve the visitor offer and attract even more people to enjoy the experience. It would give us more money to support the things that make our visitor economy such a success, while helping our businesses and communities to benefit from its continued growth.” Will there be a London tourist tax? While plans are yet to be confirmed, including how much visitors will need to pay on arrival in the capital, it’s expected that there will be some form of London tourist tax. In the 10 September statement, the Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I strongly welcome the Government giving London the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. This needs to happen sooner rather than later. London’s visitor economy is a huge success story, supporting jobs, businesses and investment across the capital and the wider country, and I have long argued that London should have the same flexibility as other major global cities to raise and invest funding locally. “A well-designed, modest levy has the potential to provide an important additional source of funding to support growth, strengthen London’s offer to visitors and help us remain globally competitive. It would allow us to reinvest in the places, infrastructure, culture and experiences that make London one of the world’s greatest cities to visit, while helping manage the pressures that come with welcoming tens of millions of visitors every year. “I will work closely with London’s boroughs, accommodation providers, hospitality and tourism businesses and other partners, before final decisions are taken.”

item.title: 17 best places to see autumn leaves in the UK
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.95
As another glorious summer comes to an end, the arrival of autumn leaves season transforms national parks, commons, and secret gardens across the British Isles. The lush greenery and beds of wildflowers wilt, turning popular picnic spots into kaleidoscopic paintings. Wild ponies navigate the changing landscapes of the Brecon Beacons, amblers take to the New Forest for bracing strolls before hiding out in cosy pubs, and Londoners wrap up for weekend markets and strolls around historic parks. As they change from bright green to a spectrum of red, orange and yellow, these are the most beautiful places in the UK to take in the spectacle. When can you see autumn leaves in the UK? Depending on how long the summer sunshine sticks around, autumn leaves can be found falling across the UK from mid-September. That said, for guaranteed colours – and spectacular photos – the best time to explore is between mid-October and mid-November. Where are the best places to see autumn leaves in the UK? London's parks put on pretty fabulous displays of colour, but the footfall through the capital's central green spaces means the combination of rain- and leaf-fall can make things a little slushy. Head a little further out for undisturbed scenes, such as the nooks and crannies of Richmond Park and beyond into the rolling Surrey Hills, where there are many attractions and towns to stop off at. The Peak District and Lake District are wonderful places in the autumn. Cosy fires roar in pub corners, hot chocolates keep amblers toasty on hiking trails, and pretty villages offer holiday cottages and bed and breakfast spots to get a good night's sleep. Further north, over the Scottish Border, you'll find some of the UK's last true wildernesses. Glide through the lochs and look to the hills, where auburn autumn leaves drift onto dewy grass, and keen walkers reconnect with nature.

item.title: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.44
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (18 - 20 September) 1. Shuck and slurp at the Oyster Championships 18 September Bentley’s Oyster Bar and Grill’s annual London Oyster Championships return this Friday, celebrating the start of the native oyster season. Swing by for bucket loads of Champagne, oysters and entertainment as two competition categories – the ‘Speed Shucking Oyster Open’ and ‘Best Dressed Oyster’ – get foodies going from afternoon into the evening. VIP tickets include exclusive access to an Oyster Masterclass hosted by Tristan Hugh Jones, the grower of the Rossmore oysters used in the competition. Address: Bentley's Oyster Bar and Grill, 11-15 Swallow Street, Piccadilly, London W1B 4DG Website: londonoysterchampionships.com 2. Honour the life of a music legend Until 15 October Mark 20 years of one of the most iconic albums of the century as a free outdoor photography exhibition in King’s Cross celebrates the life, music and legacy of Amy Winehouse. King’s Cross Group, in partnership with Universal Music and the Amy Winehouse Estate, has transformed 30 of King’s Cross' signature art benches in Granary Square and King’s Boulevard, creating an open-air gallery for all to enjoy. Address: King’s Cross, London Website: kingscross.co.uk 3. Secure a spot at a hot new opening Open now The exciting openings keep opening their doors in London. Among the hottest new dining spots is Le Café LPM at The Lanesborough – the new Riviera-inspired café concept from La Petite Maison. The exclusive year-long residency captures the joie de vivre of the Côte d'Azur through an all-day menu packed with favourite dishes, from indulgent classics such as croque-monsieur and veal milanese through to seafood delights like grilled octopus and prawns in herby butter. Elsewhere, Gordon Ramsay has added yet another address to his portfolio with the launch of Gordon Ramsay at Sea Containers. Slurp oysters and work through a menu celebrating British produce, seafood and the grill – on the open-air riverside terrace, should you choose to soak up the final run of summer. Address: Le Café LPM at The Lanesborough, Park Corner, Hyde, London SW1X 7TA; Gordon Ramsay at Sea Containers, 20 Upper Ground, London SE1 9PD Website: oetkerhotels.com; gordonramsayseacontainers.com 4. Indulge in one of London's best burgers With queues that stretch down Bethnal Green Road and plenty of virality, it was inevitable that Dumbo Shoreditch would soon have a sister site. Now, lovers of the smash patty can get their burger fix in Soho, as the brand-new site has opened its doors at 37 Berwick Street. Charles Ganem and Samuel Nataf’s Paris-born concept, credited by many foodies for bringing the smashburger concept to Europe, is the ultimate grab-and-go indulgence. Choose from a cheeseburger with onion, pickles, ketchup and mustard, an earth burger with ‘special sauce’, nuggets and French fries, and tuck in. Address: Dumbo Soho, 37 Berwick Street, London W1F 8RS Website: dumboparis.com 5. Enjoy a moment of reflection 19 - 20 September The Water Lantern Festival transforms Clapham Common into a tranquil haven this weekend, with live music, food and drink and activities for all the family, offering time to pause and reflect. Enjoy all the action throughout the afternoon before wrapping up warm for the evening’s spectacular, as hundreds of lanterns illuminate the water. Address: Clapham Common, Windmill Drive, London SW4 9DE Website: waterlanternfestival.com 6. Feast on Asian flavours along Brick Lane's curry festival 20 September The Brick Lane Curry Festival returns this Sunday, spicier and livelier than ever before following its triumphant 2025 comeback. The celebration of Bangladeshi and South Asian food, culture and community sees Brick Lane transform into a lively street festival as restaurants and vendors spill onto the iconic street. Expect traditional lion dancing, puppet shows and plenty of DJ shows between endless al fresco feasting. Address: Brick Lane, Tower Hamlets, London Website: eventbrite.co.uk 7. Get cultured across Chelsea 16 - 20 September Chelsea Arts Festival brings five days of film, literature, visual art, theatre, music and performance to venues across one of London’s glitziest neighbourhoods this week. Highlights include an exclusive Sense and Sensibility conversation at Cadogan Hall, with Fiona Shaw, Bodhi Rae Breathnach and screenwriter Diana Reid discussing the new adaptation ahead of its UK cinema release. Literature lovers can hear from Bernardine Evaristo, Katherine Rundell and Asa Butterfield, while Gavin Turk explores the role of rubbish in art at Saatchi Gallery. On Sunday, Duke of York Square becomes an open-air market home to artists, live music and workshops. Address: Across Chelsea Website: chelseaartsfestival.com 8. Savour a Sunday feast with a difference Sundays from 6 September If things still feel a little too balmy for a Sunday roast, make your way to Manteca, where Chris Leach’s team are serving special spreads sure to banish the dreaded scaries. The new, regularly changing menus are inspired by the family feasts Chris devoured during his journeys through Rome and Naples, designed to be enjoyed by groups. Think starters such as olives stuffed with Italian sausage and seafood fritto miso, followed by a large centrepiece such as a hearty tray of lasagne or spaghetti and meatballs, to be passed around. It’s great news for oenophiles, too, as head of wine Emily Acha Derrington is uncorking different magnums each weekend and pouring glasses all afternoon long. Address: Manteca, 49-51 Curtain Road, London EC2A 3PT Website: mantecarestaurant.co.uk 9. Check out the city’s new adults’ playground Open now Looking for a buzzy new hangout in the city? Look no further than Roxy Ballroom Holborn, which, following its official opening, promises flowing cocktails with a side of competitive chaos. Crazy pool, high-tech darts, basketball hoops, ping pong tables and karaoke booths are just a few of the activities on offer across the 12,000 square foot site, while the bar serves an array of tangy concoctions and American-style bites. Address: Roxy Ballroom Holborn, 246 High Holborn, London WC1V 7BN Website: roxyleisure.co.uk 10. Savour BBQ flavours at The Ned 4 September - 4 October Swanky London hotel The Ned welcomes two Michelin-starred barbecue chefs for a month of flame-kissed flavours from this Saturday. John Bates from InterStellar BBQ and Ali Clem from la Barbecue transform The Ned’s Electric Bar and Diner with Texan scents and flavours, serving a menu showcasing the craftsmanship, provenance and bold flavours that have made Austin one of the world's tastiest destinations. Think sharing trays uniting highlights from each restaurant’s menu, packed with treats such as peach tea-glazed pork belly, tender pulled lamb shoulder, chimichurri beef short rib and chopped cheese sausage. Address: Electric Bar & Diner, The Ned London, 27 Poultry, City of London Website: thened.com

item.title: Behind the scenes with Condé Nast Traveller on its latest fashion shoot in Salzburg, Austria
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.37
A team from the UK, France, Italy, the Czech Republic and Germany travelled to the beautiful lakes, soaring Alpine peaks and historical towns of the Salzkammergut region in Austria to shoot the new Fall/Winter collections. The varied weather, where you can experience all seasons in one day, inspired a rich palette of outfits from faux furs to gossamer silk. Soft leather and chunky knitwear, paired with diamonds and pearls, fit in perfectly with the elegant Salzburg crowd, who didn’t seem surprised to see our model, Ustyna, treat the cobbled street as her catwalk in a full look from Maria Grazia Chiuri’s first collection for Fendi. Here we share a behind-the-scenes peek at the locations and looks. Traunkirchen, Lake Traunsee The village of Traunkirchen lies on the western edge of Lake Traunsee in the Salzkammergut, directly across from Traunstein, an imposing peak that rises dramatically above the water. The dramatic scene is unsurprisingly a favourite spot among Instagrammers and was a shoo-in for the UK cover and a bright Chanel coat. The best view of the mountain is from the dock at Das Traunsee – Das Hotel zum See, whose owner Wolfgang Gröller has a considered collection of vintage boats. From time to time, he enjoys taking lucky guests out onto the water – our model Ustyna being one of them! First on the traditional boat in a national-inspired denim look and then again on the more modern motor boat wearing a very smart Stella McCartney Moire silk suit. Along with its charming shops and old boathouses, Traunkirchen’s town centre draws people with its stone walls and boathouses set amid green meadows. Other attractions include the Belétage restaurant and bar at the Hotel Post am See, a second property from the Gröller family. We recommended the basil cocktail for a refreshing start to an evening of traditional Austrian food. Feuerkogel Not far from Traunkirchen, the Feuerkogel is a must-hike mountain (if you’d rather, you can opt to take a cable car to the top). When there is still snow on the ground at the 5,200-foot summit, conditions can shift within minutes from crystal-clear sunlight to thick fog, a dynamic shoot location to say the least. If the visibility is good, stay on the northern side of the crest where several terraces offer the best views of the region, and a hot drink. If clouds roll in, a short hike takes you to Alberfeldkogel mountain less than a mile west of the Feuerkogel. Fir trees, cliffs and a mist-shrouded icy terrain create a mystical atmosphere like something out of a fantasy film. This was the perfect place to re-enact that twirling scene from The Sound of Music and to Yodel into the void. Our hairdresser Paulo was inspired by Heidi’s twin plaits, and they looked so chic against the snowy vista in a Louis Vuitton jumper dress complete with hood. Konditorei Zauner, Bad Ischl In the spa town of Bad Ischl, around 30 minutes by car from Traunkirchen, you’ll find the Konditorei Zauner, a patisserie with a glorious display case filled with exquisitely decorated cakes. Zauner has been in business since 1832, and to this day lovingly preserves traditional Austrian coffee culture, serving drinks from a milky melange to an indulgent double mocha. Ustyna, dressed exquisitely in Prada, fit right in. They also offer the country’s largest selection of cakes with some 250 creations as well as about 60 varieties of truffles, pralines and chocolates. The Zaunerstollen, a hazelnut and chocolate wafer, and the Ischler Törtchen, a fruity shortbread, are not to be missed. Lake Fuschl Located on the shores of Lake Fuschl, the Rosewood Schloss Fuschl Hotel is truly straight out of a movie… scenes from the famous Sissi trilogy of films starring Austrian-born Romy Schneider were shot here, and there is a small museum on-site. Today it is the hotel, inside and out, that is the star. The bar is one of the most beautiful in the country with dark wood panelling and hand-painted murals, while the clear lake is strikingly blue. It’s also decidedly more peaceful than other nearby lakes as motorboats are strictly prohibited. Every swim (or paddle) in its waters and every stroll through the nearby green meadows and forests feels like a meditative moment. When the weather might tempt you indoors, the oil paintings on display, whisky menu and board games on offer are extensive. Salzburg The most important city in this part of Austria, Salzburg is famous for its cultural highlights – it’s a destination for everyone who loves art, music and cuisine. The Hotel Goldener Hirsch, a Luxury Collection Hotel, is the place to enjoy a morning coffee with the dailies in a gemütlich historic setting – the hotel was first mentioned in a document from 1407. Or head straight to dinner, where backhendl, a traditional Austrian breaded fried chicken, is a delicious treat. A must on every Salzburg itinerary is a visit to the Kirchtag factory in the old Getreidegasse lane where Mozart was born. There you can watch craftsmen make umbrellas by hand. If you ask nicely, you may be able to take in the city views from the rooftop terrace, wearing Burberry, optional of course. It could be one of the most memorable moments of your Austrian holiday.

item.title: Craft x Tech: Shining a light on Japan’s Tokai region at London Design Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.20
What happens when centuries-old Japanese craft techniques meet the imagination of some of the world’s most experimental designers? At this year’s London Design Festival, the answer can be found inside the V&A in South Kensington, where six artisans from Japan’s Tokai region have joined forces with internationally acclaimed designers and artists to create a new generation of objects. The resulting works span ceramics, washi paper, textiles, cloisonné enamel, and braided cord, but share a common starting point: a desire to view tradition as something alive rather than fixed. For Craft x Tech Tokai Project, founded by designer and engineer Dr Hideki Yoshimoto of design studio Tangent, each designer was paired with a specialist maker from one of the region’s long-established craft communities, bringing contemporary perspectives to techniques passed down through generations. It forms one of the key shows at this year’s festival. “Japan has accumulated an extraordinary amount of knowledge through craft – knowledge about materials, processes, nature and making – much of it developed over hundreds of years,” says Yoshimoto. “I wanted to take that knowledge outside the context in which it is normally understood, and see what new relevance it might have when it encounters very different minds.” Tokai, which encompasses the prefectures of Aichi, Gifu, Mie and Shizuoka, has a rich history of making. Its abundant water, natural resources, high-quality clay and position along historic trade routes have fostered a diverse craft culture, while traditional knowledge and industrial innovation have developed alongside one another. Speaking of visitors to the show, Yoshimoto says: “I hope they see that Japanese craft is not one homogeneous culture, but an accumulation of very specific knowledge developed in different places over a very long time. Tokai is particularly rich in this respect, and if the project can bring some of that knowledge into a wider contemporary context, I think that is more important than simply introducing Japanese craft to a new audience.” Here, we speak to the designers behind the collaborations about the makers they worked with, the techniques they encountered, and what happened when their own creative languages met centuries of Japanese craft knowledge. Fushi: David Caon × Yohei Ito For Fushi, Australian industrial designer David Caon collaborated with Yohei Ito of pottery manufacturer Fudogama to explore the possibilities of Mino Yaki ceramics. Together they created a console and lighting piece from modular ceramic elements. “The material drove most of the decisions in the design, especially in terms of form and scale,” says Caon, who embraced the randomness of the glazing process in favour of its “deeply beautiful and emotive” surface. In Tokai, he was surprised to discover that the craftsmen surrounding the process were “young and energetic”, rather than the older, more serious group he had expected. The collaboration reinforced Caon’s belief in putting more faith in a fabricator's advice and not trying to control every detail. The precision lies in the form and structure of the modules, while the Oribe glaze is deliberately left unconstrained. “I hope people get a little lost looking at all the different ways the glaze has reacted across the individual modules,” he says. Websites: @caondesignoffice, fudogama.com Chair in Japanese Nuki and Dami style, The Everyday at the Atelier: Eugene Kangawa x Mayuki Kato Japanese contemporary artist Eugene Kangawa worked with Mayuki Kato of pottery manufacturer Shingama, drawing on the brushwork and tonal variation of the Japanese underglazed porcelain craft Seto Sometsuke Yaki. “The diversity of expression that comes from clay, the handwork of the brush, and the variations created by heat were especially compelling,” says Kangawa. “In particular, the variations within the deep indigo blue were fascinating.” The collaboration evolved through experimentation, with the kiln undertaking tests it had never tried before, while deliberately retaining “a diversity of forms and moments.” For Kangawa, the process reinforced his belief that craft is intrinsically connected to the geology, history and everyday life of a place. “New discoveries often seem to lie within the process of trial and error,” he explains. He hopes the finished work encourages people to recognise that even techniques passed down for generations can still leave room for new findings. Websites: the-eugene-studio.com, store.singama.jp Kasane: Philippe Malouin × Shigeyuki Ando Shigeyuki Ando of Ando Cloisonne and British-Canadian designer Philippe Malouin joined forces to explore the architectural potential of Owari Shippo cloisonné (a type of enamelware). “The first thing that struck me was the precision of the work and the depth of the enamel,” says Malouin. “It somehow feels very precise and technical, but also obviously handmade.” The project took shape around a practical limitation: the kiln's maximum size. Rather than work against it, Malouin designed a series of boxes that could be stacked to form a larger, totem-like object. The pattern began as “very casual marks” drawn randomly with a felt marker, which Ando and his team translated into silver wire and black enamel. Visiting the Tokai region gave Malouin a deeper appreciation of its craft traditions: “I already had a huge amount of respect for Japanese craft, but being in the Tokai region made me understand how closely these techniques are connected to a particular place and to the people who practise them.” Of the finished piece, he says: “I hope that, at first, people see something quite simple and calm. Then, when they get closer, they start to understand how complicated it actually is.” Websites: philippemalouin.com, ando-shippo.co.jp Grid Unwoven: Lanzavecchia + Wai × Takanori Senda Grid Unwoven brings together Takanori Senda of Warabi Paper Company with designers Francesca Lanzavecchia and Hunn Wai of Lanzavecchia + Wai. They have reinterpreted the traditional Japanese shōji – a lightweight sliding screen traditionally made with a wooden lattice and translucent paper – through the material qualities of Mino Washi, a handmade Japanese paper. “We came to see washi not as a surface, but as a living material that holds light within itself,” say Lanzavecchia + Wai. Working with Senda revealed how its fibres, density, and translucency could become architectural qualities. “We were interested in imagining what would happen if that order were touched by nature, as if a ripple or a raindrop had disturbed the grid. The wooden structure begins to bend and soften, while the washi and light amplify this sense of movement,” they explain. Their experience of Tokai also reinforced the connection between Japanese craft and its landscape: “The rivers, the kozo, the workshops, the people all shape the final work. We loved seeing how craft is not separated from everyday life there. It is embedded in homes, architecture, and the landscape itself.” The turning point in their creative process came at a visit to Senda's workshop: “We realised washi could extend far beyond the traditional sheet, into architecture and interiors. That understanding shifted our ambition, from designing a screen to creating a quiet spatial experience.” Website: lanzavecchia-wai.com, warabipapercompany.com Kataginu: Bethan Laura Wood x Hiroyuki Murase British designer Bethan Laura Wood collaborated with Hiroyuki Murase of Suzusan, transforming the colour and texture of Arimatsu Narumi Shibori – a traditional Japanese textile technique that creates patterns by folding, stitching, binding or clamping fabric before dyeing – into illuminated sculptural works. After researching textile shades and volumes, Wood was intrigued to create a family of lighting that retained elements normally removed during the process. She worked with Suzusan to develop colours that would respond to light: “I discovered that the soft, gentle pastel pink transforms into an almost neon colour when lit.” She was particularly drawn to the interplay between control and chance in the technique, from the delicacy of traditional threadwork to the organic effects of reactive dyes. Working directly with Suzusan allowed the project to evolve through testing and experimentation. “It was very important for me to get to visit the company in Tokai to see how they make their work and be able to discuss different directions and possibilities,” she says. “I really enjoyed seeing the crafts in the flesh and getting to have a go…and of course the yummy food.” Websites: bethanlaurawood.com, suzusan.com Yamollo: Atang Tshikare x Tomoyuki Matsuda Created by South African designer Atang Tshikare and Tomoyuki Matsuda of Itogo, Yamollo is a sculptural lighting work informed by the structure and colour of Iga Kumihimo braided cords. “The braiding process made me think about sculpture as a living line rather than a fixed object. I became interested in how repeated strands could create volume, movement and shadow, allowing light to become an active material within the form,” says Tshikare. The precision of the Kumihimo art form also reminded him of African hair-braiding and craft traditions, “where repetition and rhythm are used to create meaning and structure.” A trip to Tokai deepened his appreciation of the patience, discipline, and intergenerational knowledge embedded in Japanese craft, while showing him how preservation and innovation can coexist. The collaboration ultimately became a cross-cultural exchange, with Tshikare preserving the integrity of the Kumihimo technique while exploring it in a new sculptural context. “For me, respect comes from understanding rather than imitation,” he says. “The work is ultimately about finding common threads between different cultures, histories and ways of making, and recognising how craft can become a bridge between them for a brighter future.” Websites: atangtshikare.com, itogo.co.jp Find Craft x Tech at Medieval & Renaissance, Room 64b, The Simon Sainsbury Gallery, V&A South Kensington, as part of London Design Festival 2026. Exhibition runs 12 - 30 September 2026. Free entry. Find out more at craft-x-tech.com and londondesignfestival.com.

item.title: Elinor Dashwood's guide to Devon: wild moors, rickety antiques and historic pubs for the ultimate Jane Austen escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.06
There are few places in the world I know and love quite as much as Devon. I spent much of my youth growing up in the county that’s sandwiched between Dorset and Cornwall, exploring its woods, rolling hills and beaches, as well as its creaking old pubs and other assorted watering holes. With ancient lore baked into its bones, it’s little wonder this corner of the West Country has captured the imaginations of writers for centuries. Among all that verdant countryside, there really is magic at every turn. Jane Austen knew it. She spent time in Devon with her family in the early 19th century and, later, set much of Sense and Sensibility there. After leaving behind the grandeur of Norland, the Dashwoods move to Barton Cottage, on a fictional estate a few miles from Exeter. Their new abode may be considerably more modest than the home they have left behind, but its surroundings are thoroughly romantic: nestled in a valley, backing out onto high hills, and winding lanes, bucolic downs, woods, knolls and streams all around. It is nothing if not idyllic. With a new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility heading to cinemas this September, I decided to explore my hometown through the eyes of the book's heroine, Elinor Dashwood (played by Daisy Edgar-Jones in the upcoming film). From windswept walks to antique hunting, these are the places I think a modern-day Dashwood would frequent – and possibly fall in love along the way. Explore Dartmoor National Park Much of the Devon landscape you’ll see in this year’s adaptation is filmed in Dartmoor National Park, where vast stretches of open moorland are punctuated by granite tors, swirling rivers and plenty of wildlife – birds of prey, otters and, yes, Dartmoor ponies. Much of the production was based around Princetown, Tavistock and Gutter Tor near Yelverton, with Edgar-Jones knowingly referring to filming on “stormy Dartmoor” in a recent interview. There are countless walks through the national park, whether you want a gentle ramble or something more dramatic. AllTrails is particularly useful for finding routes on the go, but whichever direction you head in, expect sweeping views and the kind of wild landscape that feels made for an Austen heroine. Follow the antiques trail in Ashburton For furniture, art, books, trinkets and beyond, there is nowhere quite like Ashburton, home to more than 10 antique shops clustered together on the informally named Ashburton Antiques Trail. One can easily imagine Elinor Dashwood picking up a neat walnut writing desk, a stack of books or a pair of candlesticks here, alongside any number of other treasures she happened upon. Start along North Street, stopping at The Shambles, The Globe, Catherine Waters Antiques and Denis Perry Antiques and Interiors, where you’ll find everything from sizeable pieces of furniture to smaller decorative treasures. Continue along East Street for East Street Antiques and Alchemy Antiques, before ducking into the tiny shops on St Lawrence Lane, where rummaging is very much part of the fun. You’ll find pieces spanning the centuries – the 19th included – and at all manner of price points. Eat at Emilia Once the antiques have been acquired, there’s no better place to refuel than Emilia, a tiny Italian restaurant and wine bar on Ashburton’s East Street. The menu is designed for sharing, with plates spanning pappardelle with duck ragu and braised pork to pickled fennel and plenty of good bread to mop up olive oil, all eaten on chunky wooden tables. While it’s true that Elinor probably wouldn’t have been particularly au fait with Italian cuisine, it’s a lovely, rustic, cosy visit for anyone in the area – somewhere I'm fairly certain a modern-day Dashwood would surely adore. Wander around RHS Garden Rosemoor If you were to picture the perfect Austen-worthy garden, RHS Garden Rosemoor might be it. Like Barton Cottage, it sits in a valley, and encompasses everything from carefully designed formal gardens to sprawling woodland filled with ancient trees. It’s an ideal place to wander, lost in thought – a pastime of which any Dashwood sister would surely approve. Thanks to clever planting, there is something to see in every season, although late spring and summer are particularly lovely. Don’t miss the two rose gardens, home to more than 2,000 roses, both old and modern, which provide as much fragrance as they do colour. The cottage garden, complete with thatched summer house, is similarly enchanting. Together, they make for a very pretty way to while away a few hours. Go horse riding When in Rome, do as the Romans do – and in Devon, many would consider horse riding a crucial part of country life. In the novel, the Dashwood sisters sadly have to give up their horses when they leave Norland for Devon, but with a little artistic licence – and given that Elinor is depicted on horseback in Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation – it seems safe to assume she’d take the opportunity to ride across the moor if she could. Close to Widecombe-in-the-Moor is Shilstone Rocks, a family-run riding centre where I learned to ride way back when. As well as mastering the basics in its – mercifully sandy-floored – arena, you can head out on hacks across the surrounding moorland. Few things make you feel more immersed in the Dartmoor landscape. Have lunch at Riverford Field Kitchen While we don’t know Elinor Dashwood’s modern culinary preferences, I’m willing to bet she’d be a farm-to-table kind of woman, preferring local produce for its taste and health benefits. Riverford Field Kitchen, on Riverford’s organic farm near Buckfastleigh, feels like an obvious choice. Here, organic vegetables take centre stage in generous, seasonal dishes, which are brought out to the whole restaurant at the same time. With dried flowers punctuating wood-clad walls and much of what’s on the plate grown just outside, it’s an excellent – and delicious – way to get your five a day. Stay at Glebe House Once a vicarage, Glebe House is now a Georgian guest house set within 15 acres of beautiful East Devon countryside overlooking the Coly Valley. There’s a kitchen garden, where produce is grown before making its way onto guests’ plates, an outdoor swimming pool and the sort of pastoral views Elinor could happily lose herself in. Inside is just as charming. With interiors that nod to Charleston, the rooms are layered with pattern, paintings, wooden armoires, antique furniture and inviting fireside spots made for reading. It’s colourful and characterful rather than overly polished – exactly the sort of country house one imagines a Dashwood sister settling happily into. Have a pint at the Pilchard Inn Given Elinor’s fondness for walking and the outdoors, she’d be impressed by the enormous beach at Bigbury-on-Sea, particularly at low tide, when great stretches of sand and rock are exposed for exploring. It’s then that you can walk across to Burgh Island, the island famously associated with another female writer, Agatha Christie, who used it as inspiration and a setting for some of her novels. Perched on the island overlooking the sea is the tiny Pilchard Inn. Dating back to 1336, it’s an atmospheric, slightly ramshackle pub that has welcomed fishermen, smugglers and countless other characters over the centuries. Today, it makes an excellent stopping point for a pint and a bowl of chips before heading back across the sand. Browse the Devon and Exeter Institution As an avid reader, Elinor would have loved the Devon and Exeter Institution, a historic independent library on Exeter’s Cathedral Green. Founded in 1813, just two years after Sense and Sensibility was published, it is home to two spectacular Georgian library rooms, lined with books and topped by cupolas. Today, visitors can buy a day membership or join one of the Institution’s free guided tours on Wednesday afternoons, providing the perfect excuse to lose an hour or two among the leather-bound books – including some of Austen’s oldest works. Explore Killerton For another dose of history, head to the National Trust’s Killerton, a grand Georgian country house just outside Exeter. Surrounded by thousands of acres of farmland, woodland and orchards, the house is also home to the National Trust’s largest fashion collection – an archive of more than 20,000 items spanning centuries of dress. Think 18th and 19th century clothes – the sort of garments Elinor herself might have worn – alongside pieces belonging to Queen Victoria and 20th-century couture. Not everything is displayed at once, but changing exhibitions offer a fascinating glimpse into the way people have dressed over the centuries. For a heroine known for observing the world around her rather carefully, it feels like a fitting final stop.

item.title: Inside the £1 billion renovation of London’s most glamorous new hotel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.04
If you peer through the leafy canopies of Green Park, you’ll spy a grand mansion proudly standing watch. From its Piccadilly vantage point, Cambridge House has welcomed some of the capital’s grandest residents across its threshold, from Queen Victoria and Lawrence of Arabia to author Ian Fleming. For more than two decades it was home to Prince Adolphus, Duke of Cambridge, then became the townhouse residence of prime minister Lord Palmerston, before finally acting as a base for the Naval and Military Club (otherwise infamously known as the In & Out Club). Now, this 18th-century landmark is entering its newest lease of life – this time, as a magnificent, marble-draped hotel. Condé Nast Traveller has the exclusive first glimpse inside the Cambridge House, Auberge Collection, and we can confirm it’s as glamorous as you’d expect. Think marble-veined hallways, Palladian-style courtyards, majestic sweeping staircases and gilded suites, complete with views across Piccadilly and sprawling Green Park beyond. Fresh off the back of their work on The Twenty Two, Burlington Arcade and Admiralty Arch, British businessmen and hoteliers the Reuben Brothers have embarked on a £1 billion regeneration project for this area of Mayfair, turning this Georgian mansion into one of London’s glitziest hotels – Auberge Collection’s debut hotel in London. “Our vision for the Piccadilly Estate is to preserve what makes this part of London so special, while giving it a renewed sense of purpose,” reads a statement from the Brothers. “Cambridge House is an exceptional piece of London’s heritage, and its restoration has been approached with the care and respect that such a building deserves. We have sought to retain the character and integrity of the house while bringing a fresh perspective to the way it can be experienced today.” Leading the design team were Jean-Louis Deniot (Waldorf Astoria NYC) and Laura Gonzalez (Casa Monti in Rome, Byblos in Saint Tropez), bringing together modern, sleek interiors with decadent trimmings and regal allure in equal measure. In the Augusta Suite, for example, shades of duck egg blue and soothing cream tones are offset by dazzling chandeliers, gold-rimmed mirrors and plush furnishings, while the Adolphus Suite – an ode to the building’s original Duke of Cambridge resident – is a chic, grey-toned affair. On the ground floor, Major’s is rumoured to be London’s hottest new dining space. The team behind Carbone and Torrisi have created the ultimate American chophouse-style restaurant in the restored Georgian ballroom. Diners can expect towering seafood platters, formal caviar service, and an impressive steak selection from British farmers and hunters, all served in one of Mayfair’s most glamorous dining rooms – or outside in the jasmine-fringed courtyard. The signature bar is also causing a stir in London's drinking scene, with Gonzalez guaranteed to deliver a fittingly lavish space for guests to sample bottles from an impressive wine cellar. Major's will have a cocktail menu featuring no fewer than 10 takes on the martini – perfectly suitable for a former Fleming drinking den – while the bar itself is sure to have a stellar drinks menu, too. There will also be a wellness club and spa area. Spread across three floors, the bathhouse will feature hydrotherapy facilities, heated swimming pool, six treatment rooms, a gym, and a relaxation lounge. Later in 2027, the hotel will unveil a members' club. Cambridge House, Auberge Collection is set to open its doors in early 2027, with room rates starting at £1,250. “For us, this is about more than restoring an important building,” says the team at Reuben Brothers. “It is about giving Cambridge House a new chapter, one that respects its past, embraces its future and ensures that it remains an important part of London for generations to come.” For more information, visit auberge.com/cambridgehouse.

item.title: El Niño is returning – here's how it could affect your travel plans
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.03
El Niño has officially arrived – at least according to Japan – and some forecasters are suggesting it could eventually develop into a rare “super” event capable of dramatically altering weather patterns across much of the planet, from the safari plains of East Africa to the coral atolls of the Indian Ocean. For travellers, that could mean everything from a quieter Atlantic hurricane season to worsening wildfire smoke in Southeast Asia, stress on reefs in the Pacific and floods, landslides and transport disruption across parts of the Americas – with the most significant impacts likely to emerge from late 2026 into 2027. Previous El Niños have brought major devastation across continents. From 2015 to the following year, severe drought affected parts of southern Africa, Ethiopia and Central America, vast fires burned through drought-stricken Indonesian forests and peatlands and exceptional ocean heat contributed to the longest global coral bleaching event then recorded. More recently, the strong El Niño recorded in 2024 helped propel that year to the highest global temperature yet measured, with extreme rainfall and flooding killing more than 180 people in southern Brazil and displacing around 600,000. In June 2026, the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) stated that “In Europe, this El Niño could be strong enough to flip the pattern: instead of colder-than-normal autumn temperatures that typically accompany it, Europe may experience warmer-than-normal conditions, with that warmth building towards spring 2027”. The House of Commons Library reports that the meteorological effects of El Niño on Europe could result in more extreme winter weather in the UK in 2027. Jump to… In an update issued on Wednesday, 10 June, the Japan Meteorological Agency became the first major national forecasting organisation to confirm the onset of the phenomenon, declaring that El Niño conditions had been present across the equatorial Pacific since spring 2026. Sea surface temperatures in the agency’s closely monitored Niño 3 region were already 1.2C above normal during May, while unusually warm water beneath the Pacific continued to spread eastwards and the trade winds above it weakened, laying the foundations for what could become the dominant climate story of the next 18 months. That's significant because other global agencies have so far stopped just short of formally announcing that an El Niño event is underway – but the World Meteorological Organisation now puts the probability of El Niño developing between June and August at 80 per cent, rising to around 90 per cent or more through the autumn, and has told governments that the time for preparation has already begun. What makes people so apprehensive of El Niño is that it rarely stays where it starts. A patch of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific can eventually influence everything from rainfall in Kenya to drought around Victoria Falls, wildfire risk in Indonesia and winter storms in California. “We need to prepare for a potentially strong El Niño event,” World Meteorological Organisation secretary-general Celeste Saulo warned this month, pointing to the prospect of worsening drought, heavy rain and heatwaves both on land and at sea. UN secretary-general António Guterres was blunter, saying El Niño would “pour fuel on the fire of a warming world”, allowing its effects to travel farther and strike harder. The most alarming forecasts raise the possibility that the event could eventually cross into “super El Niño” territory, an unofficial term generally applied when temperatures in a key part of the tropical Pacific rise at least 2°C above normal, with such events occurring only around once every decade or so, and historically leaving a trail of droughts, floods, fires and failed harvests across several continents. “When you have an El Niño over what climate change already brought, the risks are enormous,” Francisco Aquino, head of the climate centre at Brazil’s Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, told Reuters. Piers Forster, professor of physical climate change at the University of Leeds, meanwhile described the developing event as a potential “window into the future” – a preview of weather extremes that may become increasingly ordinary as the planet continues to warm. Here's everything travellers need to know about this year's El Niño weather system. What exactly is El Niño? El Niño is a recurring warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific that can disturb weather thousands of miles beyond the ocean where it begins. Under usual conditions, easterly trade winds push warm surface water westwards towards Indonesia and northern Australia. Cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the depths off Peru and Ecuador, while the warmer western Pacific produces some of the world’s most dramatic tropical rainstorms. During El Niño, those trade winds weaken, and the great reservoir of warm water begins sliding back towards the east, suppressing the cold upwelling off South America and dragging the principal zone of tropical thunderstorms across the Pacific with it. That interferes with the Walker circulation – the vast loop of rising and sinking air above the tropics – and sends a series of atmospheric ripples around the planet, with results that can appear entirely disconnected from their source. Is El Niño now officially underway? According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, yes. On Wednesday, 10 June, the organisation said El Niño conditions had been present since spring 2026. Sea surface temperatures in its monitored Niño 3 region were 1.2°C above normal during May and warmer-than-average water extended beneath much of the equatorial Pacific as the trade winds over the central Pacific had weakened. Japan now considers it virtually certain that El Niño will persist through the northern hemisphere autumn. Other global agencies have been more cautious, although they are moving towards the same conclusion. NOAA’s latest full assessment continued to classify the Pacific as neutral while giving El Niño an 82 per cent chance of emerging between May and July and a 96 per cent chance of persisting into the coming winter. The World Meteorological Organisation placed the probability at 80 per cent for June to August, rising to around 90 per cent or more after. Why is this particular El Niño attracting so much attention? Most international models currently suggest that the event will become at least moderate, with a strong event also possible. Some longer-range projections extend into the much rarer territory sometimes described as a “super El Niño”. That's generally used for an exceptionally powerful event in which temperatures across an important section of the central tropical Pacific rise roughly 2°C or more above average – and only a small number of modern El Niños have reached comparable strength. All three became associated with severe and simultaneous weather disruption across several continents. Yet the most extreme projections for 2026 remain just that. NOAA has said there is still substantial uncertainty over peak strength, with no single category dominating its probabilities. Stronger El Niños also make certain consequences more likely rather than guaranteeing them. The amount of heat already sitting beneath the Pacific explains why forecasters are watching so closely – and the WMO has urged governments to prepare for a potentially strong event capable of worsening drought, heavy rain and heatwaves on land and at sea. When will travellers begin to notice the effects? The first visible signs for travellers may be slightly subtler – unusually dry conditions in Bali, greener-than-usual safari landscapes in East Africa, or a quieter Atlantic hurricane season than forecasters had expected. El Niño usually develops between spring and early summer, strengthens through autumn and peaks between November and February. Its effects often then continue through the following spring or summer, while slower consequences – such as depleted reservoirs, damaged reefs, altered river levels and stressed wildlife populations – may last considerably longer. During summer and autumn 2026, travellers could begin seeing the first shifts in tropical cyclone activity, Southeast Asian rainfall, wildfire conditions and the Asian and African monsoons. From around October, attention is likely to turn towards East Africa’s short rains, drought risks in southern Africa and Australia, and the possibility of heavy rain across Peru and Ecuador. The influence on the US, Canada and parts of East Asia usually becomes clearest during the northern hemisphere winter, particularly between December and March. Yet its effect on global temperature may peak later still. El Niño releases heat stored in the tropical Pacific into the atmosphere, meaning the year after an event develops can be exceptionally warm. The strong 2023-24 El Niño helped push 2024 to record global temperatures, and the return of the phenomenon has already raised concerns that 2027 could challenge those records again. What could happen to travel during the 2026–27 El Niño? The potential impacts are wide-ranging and vary dramatically by country. The same climate pattern that brings blue skies to Bali could contribute to flooding in Peru, while travellers enjoying greener safari landscapes in Kenya may be doing so during the same season that drought grips southern Africa. Across Indonesia and parts of maritime Southeast Asia, suppressed rainfall could initially look like ideal holiday weather, but as the dry season deepens, the same conditions can produce water stress, forest and peat fires, and smoke capable of spreading into Singapore and Malaysia. East Africa may face the reverse problem later in the year. Stronger October to December rains could turn safari landscapes a magnificent green while reducing roads to mud, flooding airstrips and complicating transfers to remote camps. Southern Africa may become hotter and drier, improving wildlife visibility around shrinking waterholes in the short term but placing animals, rivers and communities under increasing strain if drought persists. According to analysts, at Victoria Falls, reduced upstream rainfall could eventually reduce the thunderous curtain of water pouring over Victoria Falls, although the effect would be delayed by the vast size of the Zambezi catchment. Coral reefs are another major concern. The world has only recently emerged from the most extensive global bleaching event recorded, during which heat stress affected more than 80% of reef area – and further Pacific warming could expose already weakened reefs to another damaging season before they have had time to recover. Does El Niño mean the weather will be bad everywhere? No – and some destinations may experience conditions travellers actually consider favourable. The Caribbean could have fewer hurricanes, California ski resorts could receive substantial snowfall and drier weather may produce long stretches of sunshine across Indonesia. The danger lies in the point at which favourable weather becomes excessive – for example, with snow closing mountain roads, rain carrying away bridges crossing it, or sunshine becoming drought. Could El Niño affect safaris in Kenya or Tanzania? Quite possibly – and not necessarily for the worse. One of El Niño’s most consistent signatures is heavier short rains across East Africa between October and December. The East African savannah can look extraordinary after rain as dust settles and grasslands turn emerald green – with migratory birds arriving in huge numbers. Yet tracks that are easily navigable in August could become axle-deep mud by November, and small bush airstrips may temporarily close after particularly heavy downpours. During the 1997-98 El Niño, exceptionally heavy rain caused widespread flooding across East Africa, washing out roads and bridges in Kenya and leaving parts of the country difficult to reach. The most recent event offered another warning, as across Tanzania, the rains of 2023 and 2024 damaged 63 bridges, more than 800 kilometres of road and hundreds of culverts. Could El Niño affect the Maldives? The Maldives sits atop one of the world’s most celebrated coral reef systems, making it one of the destinations most exposed to El Niño’s effects beneath the surface rather than above it.
