During the enormous 1997-98 event, sea temperatures rose so dramatically that large areas of coral across the Indian Ocean bleached, and scientists estimate that some Maldivian reefs lost more than 90 per cent of their shallow coral cover. The good news is that many reefs have since recovered remarkably well, but the bad news is that they are now entering another potential El Niño after enduring the most widespread global coral bleaching event ever recorded between 2023 and 2025. Marine life remains spectacular even on reefs that have experienced bleaching, but conditions may vary dramatically between atolls, and some reefs could face renewed stress if ocean temperatures climb significantly during late 2026 and early 2027. More widely, the Maldives may experience warmer seas, periods of unusual calm and changes in rainfall patterns, but it is unlikely to see the kind of extreme droughts or floods that could affect parts of Africa, South America or Southeast Asia. What could happen in Japan during El Niño? The country that first declared El Niño’s arrival may end up feeling relatively modest impacts compared with many tropical destinations. Historically, El Niño winters in Japan have tended to be warmer than average, which can be good news for city-break travellers exploring Tokyo, Kyoto or Osaka, but less welcome for ski resorts that are dependent on deep snowfall. The bigger concern for travellers may be summer heat. Japan has already experienced a succession of exceptionally hot summers in recent years, and El Niño’s tendency to boost global temperatures could make future heatwaves more intense. Could Thailand have a better winter than usual during El Niño? Thailand often sits on the drier side of El Niño, and during previous events, rainfall has decreased across much of the country while temperatures climbed higher than average – which means more reliable beach days in Phuket and Krabi and fewer interruptions to island-hopping itineraries. Yet there is another side to the story. The powerful 2015-16 El Niño contributed to one of Thailand’s most severe droughts in decades, with reservoirs reaching critically low levels and agricultural regions facing water shortages – so ultimately, what feels like perfect weather for a holiday can create serious challenges for the communities living through it. Should travellers to Bali and Indonesia be concerned? El Niño often brings Bali some of its most glorious weather: weeks of blue skies, lower humidity and uninterrupted sunsets. The problem is what can happen when the dry season refuses to end. The devastating Indonesian fire seasons of 1997-98 and 2015 were both closely linked to strong El Niño conditions, with vast areas of forest and peatland burned, producing smoke that spread across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia. The smoke often originates hundreds of kilometres away, yet visitors can still feel the effects through disrupted flights and deteriorating air quality. Could El Niño affect European holidays? Europe sits far enough from the tropical Pacific that El Niño’s influence becomes considerably weaker and less predictable. However, strong El Niños often contribute to record global temperatures, and Europe has become increasingly prone to severe heatwaves regardless of what happens in the Pacific. The summer after the 1997-98 event was, at the time, the hottest year ever recorded globally, and the 2015–16 event helped produce another global temperature record. The most recent El Niño contributed to 2024 becoming the hottest year in modern measurements. Mediterranean destinations that were once comfortably warm in the shoulder seasons of June or September may increasingly become the sweet spot, while July and August edge further into heatwave territory. Could El Niño affect Mauritius, Seychelles and Zanzibar? During the 2016 bleaching episode in the Seychelles, between 69 and 99 per cent of coral was bleached at monitored locations, followed by an estimated 50 per cent reduction in hard coral cover – and another marine heatwave would affect those ecosystems as they recover from earlier damage. Mauritius has also experienced El Niño-related bleaching, including its first recorded mass event in 1998, although mortality was considerably lower at many sites than in the Seychelles. The 2023–24 El Niño, meanwhile, brought above-average rain to Tanzania across two successive rainy seasons, contributing to severe floods, landslides and extensive damage to roads and bridges.

item.title: 21 best hotels in Mykonos to book for a slick and stylish stay
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.03
Though you wouldn’t know it now, it wasn’t until the 1980s that Mykonos opened its first luxury hotel on the island’s south coast – and thus began the influx of the best hotels on the island. While this hotel, Myconian Ambassador, still stands, Mykonos today has become synonymous with luxury: hotels, restaurants, beach bars and beyond. It's best known as a place to party, but there’s a lot more to this Greek island, with beats-until-dawn bars mainly confined to the (actually fairly small) area of Mykonos Town. More than ever before, visitors are starting to notice everything Mykonos has to offer away from the late-night dining and dancing scene and are choosing to explore the island’s wild, less-crowded coastlines instead. Where tourists wander, hoteliers follow: over the last few years, there’s been a boom in openings along the island’s south-east coast, from Kalafati beach, where you’ll find Cali Mykonos, to Elia beach, where Four Seasons Mykonos is set to open, the second Greek property from the brand, following its 2019 Athens Riviera launch. See our edit of what to pack for three nights in Mykonos here. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Mykonos - Best for luxury: Four Seasons Mykonos - Best for honeymoons: Amyth of Mykonos - Best beach location: Myconian Sunrise Relais & Chateaux Hotel - Best for a girls' trip: Fouquet's Mykonos - Best boutique hotel: Deos Mykonos - Best for families: Santa Marina, a Luxury Collection Resort What are the best areas in Mykonos to stay in? For all of its hype, Mykonos is relatively small. The island is only 10 kilometres, so wherever you stay, you're pretty close to the action and beaches. Some of the hotels on this list are found along the popular Ornos Beach on the island's southwest. If you want to be based around some hubbub, this option has plenty of shops, restaurants and bars nearby. To be in the thick of the party scene, look to hotels like Mykonos Theoxenia and Bohème, located right in Mykonos town. If you'd prefer to be far removed from it all, Cali Mykonos is hidden away in the reclusive (and exclusive) coastal village Kalafati. When to go to Mykonos The height of the season is July and August, but things are already hotting up in early summer when the fresh produce is better and there are less crowds. If you favour a slightly slower pace, with more comfortable temperatures and less crowds, book a trip to Mykonos in either of the shoulder season months: May or September. How to get to Mykonos Flights from London: Mykonos has an airport serviced by domestic flights from Athens and direct flights from the UK. EasyJet flies directly from the UK to Mykonos; Olympic Air and Aegean Airlines fly to Mykonos via Athens. By ferry from within Greece: Mykonos is easy to reach from Athens' two ports (Piraeus and Rafina) by boat, especially in summer when ferry companies add to their scheduled journeys. Car ferries tend to be comfortable but slow, taking approximately seven hours to get to the island, while modern high-speed catamarans and Sea Jets are more than twice as fast, but not as steady in rough seas. You can also reach Mykonos via other Greek islands if you want to island-hop. How we choose the best hotels in Mykonos Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: The world's busiest airport is no longer Dubai
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
The world's aviation landscape looks a little different this year, with South Korea's Incheon International Airport outranking Dubai International as the world's busiest for international passengers. According to preliminary data from the Airports Council International (ACI), released by Incheon, the South Korean airport served 38.4 million international passengers during the first six months of 2026. Once confirmed by the ACI in its World Airport Traffic Report (to be released next month), the airport will now rank as the world's busiest for the first time since opening in 2001. Dubai International Airport is expected to place outside the top five this year, despite ranking first for international traffic for the past 12 years. The decline in international footfall follows the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which reconfigured the globe's skies when it began on 28 February, with ACI data showing the UAE travel hub fell from 7.4 million passengers in February to just 2.5 million in March. Incheon also reported an 18 per cent increase in transfer passengers this year, as many who previously transferred in the Gulf on their way to Europe had to rethink their route amid airspace closures. This year, London Heathrow is set to rank in second place, recording 37.79 million passengers in the first half of the year, followed by Singapore's Changi Airport, which has seen 34.53 million international passengers pass through its terminals during this period. It's not just the war that's contributed to Incheon's sharp rise in numbers. According to the airport, an infrastructure expansion (which was completed in 2024) has enabled it to handle a larger traffic load – now serving 101 airlines flying to 158 international destinations. And with a growing global interest in Korean culture, from its TV shows to its music, food, beauty and fashion, it's little wonder the airport has continued to climb the ranks, placing fifth in 2018 to being named third busiest in 2024 and 2025, and now reaching the top spot. Before the conflict, Dubai's global status as a tourism hotspot and destination for transfers was increasing year on year. In April, it was named the world's busiest airport for international passengers in 2025, with 95.2 million international passengers landing in the city over the course of 12 months. The figure marked an increase of 3.1 per cent from 2024, and a 10.3 per cent rise from pre-pandemic numbers in 2019. In February, the emirate was also named the world's best-connected city by Mozio, which compared the journey time from arrivals to a central landmark in 50 of the world's most-visited cities. With tensions continuing and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) extending its conflict zone advisory for the Gulf until 31 August, it remains unclear when air traffic in the region will return to its pre-war levels.

item.title: The best family-friendly hotels in Sicily, recommended by a parent of three
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.43
The Sicilians are, by and large, remarkably welcoming of bambini, who are embedded in their psyche as a blessing, not an inconvenience. As such, the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily are also some of the island's most lauded. Expect cooing, overly expressive signs of affection and a society that is unabashedly pro-children, being integrated into every facet of life. Even the most elaborate hotels welcome children warmly – perhaps not the sort whose parents turn a blind eye to their darlings smudging pistachio cannoli filling into Zoffany upholstered sofas, but here, first-rate kids' clubs buy parents plenty of off-duty time. Time, that is, to enjoy a sun-dappled terrace framed by crumbling columns and palms, a haze of distant blue ring-fencing the green hills braided in olive groves and vineyards, and the irresistible waft of orange blossom and freshly baked arancini washed down with crisp Etna wines. Sicily is a wildly romantic island, layered in history, wrapped in surreal blue waters, caught in the crosshairs of civilisations, and intensely varied in its landscape, cuisine and culture – depending on which region you pootle a few kilometres over to. Wild spirits can run free on the island’s abundant argiturismos, free of the formalities and precariously balanced 17th-century busts of the high-end hotels. Where you choose to stay depends on your children’s ages, proclivities and really, how you like to holiday. This is our edit of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily. Editor's picks of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily: Best for luxury: Villa Sant'Andrea, A Belmond Hotel Best for children at different ages: Veruda Best for teens: Bracciallieri Best kids' club: Veruda Best all-inclusive: Mangia's Costa Ragusa Borgo 5 tips for visiting Sicily with children Prepare for the heat Small children will struggle outdoors in Sicily in peak summer from about 11am-4pm. Unless they’re aligning with Sicilian siesta law or are under a shaded kids’ club, it would be wise to consider shoulder season for pre-schoolers. What’s more, many of the Baroque Sicilian towns and cities’ ancient cobblestones aren’t designed for prams, so remember to bring a good baby carrier, backpack or hop on one of their sweet family train rides that introduces children to grand Baroque architecture, pointing out the best gelato spots, chocolatiers and the gargoyles peering down from atop their palazzi. Pack smart Invest in a wide-brimmed sunhat and long-sleeved, long-legged swimsuits for tinies to save their skin from the fierce Sicilian sun. Always check with your hotel for minimum kids club age, and what time their restaurant opens – what's worse than a 7.45pm restaurant opening time when you’re children are used to eating at 5pm and being tucked up two hours later? Hire a car Unless you’re staying solely in Palermo or Catania (where Sicily’s two airports are based), it’s worth hiring a car to explore, though don’t expect the rental company to procure age-specific carseats (even if this has been agreed). I have experienced this hiccup numerous times and on my last trip, invested in two Cybex foldable Solution G2 carseats for peace of mind. Even if you book a smart transfer with hotels, you really have to emphasise the ages of your children and reconfirm to avoid the booster seat for a six month old scenario. Embrace day trips Older children and teenagers will enjoy exploring Siciliy’s maze-like towns and villages, diving into its Slim Aarons-looking pools and aquamarine swimming spots, and hopping on boat trips for uninhabited islands and caves. The beauty of Sicily is that, no matter where your hotel is located, much of the island can be explored via day trips, though families would be forgiven for indulging a little Dolce Far Niente, poolside or under the shade of the citrus trees. Take your time Having travelled to Sicily as a family multiple times, the best formula for a successful 10 days or two-week break is, unquestionably, combining a family-friendly hotel with a villa stay. Hotels provide parents with all the pampering they’re so desperately in need of (the spa facilities, the elevated dining, the kids’ club or babysitting), then a villa serves up all that precious family time and, crucially, the privacy to let children run wild and the room space to ensure everyone’s banking ample sleep. It works particularly well for multi-generational groups and opens up new areas of the island for everyone to explore. How we choose the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. This is our edit of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily. For more inspiration on where to stay in Sicily and Italy, visit About the author Rosalyn Wikeley is a regular contributor to Condé Nast Traveller and a ski and Sicily expert. Former Creative Content Editor for the publication, Rosalyn has written for the Financial Times, the Telegraph, The Times, Vogue, House & Garden, the London Standard and consulted on content for leading luxury brands and hotels. She beelines for Sicily's Baroque South East every Autumn to seek out new hotels and arty enclaves, and also writes extensively on Paris, family-friendly stays and skiing.

item.title: Inside the secret Yorkshire art walk that’s harder to get into than Glastonbury
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.32
I love walking. As a Cotswolds countryside resident, my once-concrete jaunts across east London have been swapped for crunchy grass stomps through cow-laden fields or floating across rolling hills just out my front door. I also love art. Exhibitions and retrospectives are often what dictate my travels. A recent dash on the Eurostar brought me to a speedy 48-hour whip around the late David Hockney exhibition at the Louis Vuitton Museum in Paris, in between long bistro meals and a snoop around the city’s latest new hotel opening. So when a few art-obsessed friends returned from what they called the most incredible walk of their lives up in the North York Moors, but said that they couldn't really tell me why, I was immediately intrigued. I began researching and uncovered an outdoor art walk where tickets to gain access to were as hard as heading to Glastonbury. The walk is, rather intriguingly, called Hanging Stones. I'd heard about artist Andy Goldsworthy from my mother. The contemporary English land artist has been shaping, morphing and discerningly using his hands to form large scale works using natural materials we might often overlook in everyday life: stones, snow, rock, leaves, iron, twigs, mud and more. One of his most talked-about pieces involved transporting 13 one-tonne snowballs from Scotland and placing them on the streets of London during a hot summer's day. He challenges and inspires conversation about our world and its precious land, and for his ongoing project up in Yorkshire – commissioned by the David Ross Foundation – he shifts the focus to the raw beauty of the Moors. To get tickets, eager hikers need to set reminders to check the website. Slots open at hangingstones.org – it’s currently booked out for the rest of the year, but new releases come out regularly. It costs £10 per adult; under-18s and students go free. There’s a maximum of four groups of six allowed each day. On the day, collect your laminated map and keys from Sevenford House B&B, then head to the Milburn Arms in Rosedale Abbey where the circular walk begins and ends. Allow five to six hours... you’ll need it, and wear proper boots (once you have your slot, I’d advise against trying to change it, so prepare for all weather conditions) and bring your own food and water – there are no facilities en route. My husband and I set off up north for a six-mile hike through farmers' fields and dormant heather hills to to pick up an instruction guide and a set of dangling keys… Here's everything we found along the way. To Goldsworthy, the whole walk is an artwork in itself. There are ten stone outbuildings, some rebuilt from ruin, all immaculately beautiful and each with its own installation inside. The tenth, titled Heygate Thorns, is currently in the works, but there’s a tiny window Goldsworthy left for you to have a special glimpse. My favourite stretch was the uphill push to the furthest point you reach before looping back, which is surrounded by hazy gorse and heather. There’s magic in unlocking giant padlocks and not knowing what’s inside. The signposts felt straight out of Lord of the Rings; little slits of eyes hammered into stone are your earmarks to keep you on your way. Don’t forget to look up. The light can change everything. Goldsworthy makes the mundane something joyful to look at. Perhaps the perfect picnic spot, or keep on pushing to the highest point of the walk for a chapel- like shelter on a particularly blustering day.

item.title: 7 best bakeries in Bath for brioche buns, sourdough loaves and sticky cinnamon treats
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.27
The best bakeries in Bath mean different things to different people. When my late great aunt came on what felt like a state visit from Scotland to stay with us in Bath each year, for example, she’d insist on tea at the 18th-century Pump Rooms. There was the chandelier opulence that she liked, the harpist, and the starched white tablecloths. But mainly it was her annual Bath bun fix that she was after: soft, round and topped with oversized sugar crystals. Bath has form when it comes to bakeries. There were the brioche-like Sally Lunn buns, first touted around the abbey in the late 17th-century, and then came the sugar-loaded Bath buns during Bath’s glittering Regency years. But fast-forward nearly 350 years, and there’s been a flurry of new bakeries in Bath over the past decade or so, where the stacks of sourdough and trays of sticky cinnamon buns alone justify a trip to this corner of the West Country. The frontrunner is Landrace Bakery on Walcot Street, opened in 2019 and the kind of place I unashamedly plan a trip into town around (getting in early enough to time it right for a cardamom bun for breakfast and holding off a sad piece of toast at home beforehand so that I can savour every bite). But a bun for breakfast is just the start. In a city that’s all walkable with hills at every turn, the need for pick-me-ups is plentiful. So here is our guide to the best bakeries in Bath for coffee and a sugar hit when you start to flag. Landrace Bakery Best for: a cardamom bun The grand dame of Bath bakeries, Landrace was opened by Andrew Lowkes on artsy Walcot Street with sourdough made using speciality grains milled at Westcombe Dairy in Bruton. Get there early for a warm, straight-from-the-oven cardamom or cinnamon bun, with a smooth Roundhill Roastery flat white collected through a hatch on the street. Or grab a table in the ground-floor Caff, where the shelves are lined with loaves, and you can settle in for a pastry armed with your book (croissants filled with Somerset-grown apricot jam perhaps, or a Danish packed with lovage and Lamyatt cheese from Westcombe Dairy). And when you haven’t managed to bag a table upstairs in the restaurant for dinner, from 5pm (Tuesday-Saturday) the Caff serves up 18” pizzas loaded with local ingredients. Address: 59 Walcot Street, Bath, BA1 5BN Website: landrace.co.uk Morso Bakery Best for: savoury pastries In one of the smartest corners of town, a two-minute hop from The Circus, Matt Puchowski and Georgia Barton have opened Morso, years after dreaming of doing just that. The bakes are all vegan (but the pair are low-key about this; you’d be hard-pressed to guess), with coffee from Wiltshire roaster Colours Coffee, a sunny courtyard and benches out the front spilling over with coffee drinkers. You won’t miss it – the front is a cheering apricot colour – and if you can hold out until lunchtime, the savoury pastries are deliciously inventive (try the Danish flavoured with gochujang, maple and confit garlic). Address: 4 Saville Row Bath BA1 2QP Website: instagram.com/_morso_bakery/ Green Street Best for: sandwiches Next to the neon sign glowing in the window at Green Street are hunks of local, grass-fed meat and strings of garlic, with in-the-know locals dashing to get their hands on a rotisserie chicken roll with caramelised shallots for lunch. This is a place that’s big on provenance: the bread is all made at their prep kitchen in Bath before being delivered at the crack of dawn, and the sandwiches are filled with meat cooked from the butcher counter. If you’re passing in the morning, pick up a coffee (Triple Co, roasted in Bristol) and one of their in-house baked croissants, cruffins or, best of all, brown butter cookies. Address: 10-11 Green Street, Bath, BA1 2JZ Website: greenstreetsandwiches.com Society Café Best for: carrot cake At the end of The Corridor, Bath’s 19th-century shopping arcade, you’ll find some of the best coffee in Bath at Society Café (it has another outlet on Kingsmead Square if you’re in that part of town), with beans from Origin Coffee Roasters in Cornwall and deliciously full-fat milk from Bruton Dairy. Stools line the bars at the windows with locals and tourists eking out their flat white with one of the café’s pastries (delivered from The Newt in Somerset), traybakes from the Wild Flour Cake Co in nearby Timsbury, cookies from Bakervee in Bath or its showpiece carrot cake made by Alice Cakes (a recipe they’re most often asked for but can’t divulge…) Address: 19 High Street, The Corridor, Bath, BA1 5AJ and 5 Kingsmead Square, Bath BA1 2AB Website: society-cafe.com Brume Bakery Best for: old school buns This autumn, in a Grade-II building on the cobbled Kingsmead Street, Brume Bakery will open, the brainchild of Bath locals Joe and Tori Hill, who between them have worked for go-to Bath dinner spot the Beckford Canteen, Soho Farmhouse and The Newt in Somerset. Where once there was a fish and chip shop, there will now be the couple’s long-held vision of a Parisian bistro-meets-bakery. Expect sourdough, baguettes and focaccia made using stoneground British flour, as well as croissants, cheesecake, tiramisu and nostalgic-making stacks of iced buns. Address: 38 Kingsmead Street, Bath, Somerset BA1 2AA Website: instagram.com/brumebakery Colonna & Small’s Best for: coffee When husband-and-wife Maxwell and Lesley Colonna-Dashwood opened Colonna & Small in 2009 it was a coup for Bath’s coffee-connoisseurs. The couple had discovered the third wave coffee movement – treating coffee as a craft rather than a basic commodity – in Melbourne the year before and brought this vision to the West Country. Nearly 20 years later coffee is treated just as seriously here (Maxwell is a UK Barista Champion). But that doesn’t mean it’s an intimidating place to get your caffeine fix, with chattering huddles of friends around pared back tables and laptop-wielding workers at the bar. Grab the spot in the window to watch Bath life trundle past, charged with one of their billowing croissants from Hobbs House Bakery to refuel you. Address: 6 Chapel Row, Bath, BA1 1HT, Website: colonnacoffee.com BRaC Best for: focaccia sandwiches On those trips to Bath when you ditch the to-do list and timings go out the window, wandering just out of the centre of town along the River Avon to BRaC is worth the step count. Founded by chef Sam Wylde, the bakery bakes all its focaccia in-house each morning, alongside its baps and a changing line-up of treats (expect Basque cheesecake, chocolate torte and lemon meringue). Milk is from Frome-based Ivy House, eggs from Fenton Farm near Taunton, meat from Ruby and White butchers in Bristol, and blooms from Bath-based Flowers by Passion. Opt for the towering Pollo Caesar Focaccia sandwich for lunch, and when the sun is shining, get it to go and stroll the 10 minutes back up to the Royal Crescent to scoff it with a view. Address: Pegasus Leat, Nelson Villas, Nelson Place West, Bath, BA1 2BD Website: instagram.com/brac

item.title: 21 best UK autumn holidays to book this year
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.16
Autumn in the UK is a pretty special time. The last of the summer sun is lingering and the world outside is filled with a kaleidoscope of colour as leaves burn bright, while indoors, crackling fires fill rooms with a warm glow and blankets are laid out for curling up under. Choosing to holiday closer to home means no crowded airports, and no tickets or boarding passes to deal with. The weather is taken as it comes – get lucky and you might arrive at your destination to bright blue skies and sunshine, but it could easily transform into threatening clouds and drizzle in the blink of an eye. Spend days exploring the blustery landscapes spread across the UK or traipsing round cities and quaint villages, but be sure to end each excursion with a gut-busting roast dinner with all the trimmings. Here are our editors' favourite places to go for autumn in the UK, from picturesque villages in the Cotswolds to rugged coastal scapes in Cornwall. For more inspiration, see our guide to where to go in Europe in autumn.

item.title: D.C.’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Started as a Pop-Up
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.39
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. When chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy opened Alfie’s as a pop-up restaurant in 2016, they didn’t expect the road to a brick-and-mortar location to last nearly a decade. The temporary D.C. location where the duo served northern Thai cuisine to the city’s tight-knit service industry and other regulars was open for just a few months. After that, Ahn and McCoy began operating it as a roving concept all around the world, but now they’re finally returning to D.C. with a permanent venue in Georgetown. Now the team is settled into a new 25-seat venue tucked in an alley off of Georgetown’s M Street serving Thai dishes made with Mid-Atlantic ingredients and natural wine produced just over the river in Virginia. Still, elements of the pop-up — like its run-and-gun service and chalkboard menu that shifts based on what local purveyors have in season — remain. We caught up with McCoy to learn more about how the team has shifted this scrappy pop-up model into a brick-and-mortar concept while keeping that dynamic energy intact. Liz Provencher: Why did you decide to launch Alfie’s in a pop-up format? Alex McCoy: We [already] had a permanent space in Petworth that we were building out [for our brick-and-mortar restaurant]. There was another restaurant space down the street that was slated to be demolished, so we talked to the landlords and they were like, “It’s yours until your space is ready or our project starts.” We thought it was a great opportunity to train our staff, test the food, and work through the menus while our spot was in construction. It was in a quiet part of town, and we just really wanted to have fun with it, but it ended up becoming this cult sensation. We were packed for months in advance. We had Vogue writing about us. Bon Appetit called it one of the top new restaurants in America. But it was really only about six months total that we had the place open, which is kind of wild. We closed the pop-up in 2017. That Petworth space didn’t end up working out for us, so we had to look for a new space. In the meantime, we were doing pop-ups in New York, D.C., London. We spent a lot of time overseas and some of the bigger pop-ups were in London with our buddies at Carousel. In that time, we were always looking for a new venue, and it was the time in Europe that really evolved the brand into what it is now. How did that time on the road shape the concept and operation plan? After COVID… everyone was struggling to try to figure out how to make restaurants work. With operating and staff costs going up, people were coming up with these creative service styles with [fewer] servers and less table service and more QR codes. The math isn’t mathing, you know? It seemed to me that the model should be similar to the way things operate in Europe with these little hole-in-the-wall places in Paris and London. Chefs don’t own six or seven restaurants; they’re in there [in one place] with one or two people. Not only was that the heart and soul of what Alfie’s always was, but it felt to me to be the way forward with the brand. After we did our last pop-up in London, we found this funky little spot in Georgetown, which is a neighborhood that feels the most European of anywhere in D.C. to me. It’s this incredible 25-seat space in an alleyway behind the hustle and bustle of M Street. It’s a little gritty. You step down into the alleyway and you have to dodge cars. It’s a really cool, funky space with a lot of character. So immediately it was like, this is the spot. This encapsulates the vibe and the ambiance and the feeling and the energy of what we’re trying to do. Have things changed since running the restaurant as a pop-up? It’s very much still a pop-up mindset. Justin, myself, and Ian, who is our sous chef, we’re 90 percent of the staff at this restaurant. From a cooking perspective, twenty-five seats is perfect because it gives us this opportunity to really [pore] over small batches of food. If we’re making a curry for the day, we’re [only] making 30 orders. We’re able to look at the menu on a daily basis and assess based on what ingredients come in. If our local fishmonger has five beautiful seabreams that he’s bringing in, we’ll just throw them on the menu because we have that ability to be scrappy and change things up and make adjustments and not have to retrain the staff and everything. That also plays into Thailand’s market culture, which is the ethos of our brand. We want to challenge ourselves to make dishes utilizing what’s available around here: rockfish, soft shell crab, foraged asparagus from the Eastern Shore, morel mushrooms, things like that. Does your drink menu also play off of local ingredients? When you go to France or Italy or another wine-producing region, you go to a bar or restaurant and you’re drinking what was made in the town or right around it. You don’t often see that in D.C., even when Virginia wineries are making spectacular stuff, literally 15 to 20 minutes away by car. The majority of our wines by the glass are from Virginia and we have more than 2,000 local producers by the bottle too. Our bottles, for the most part, are between $35 and $75. We only have a couple that top that. I think a lot of people go out to eat dreading the check. But I want people to come in and just get lost in the experience and not have to worry that they can’t take a chance on something that they haven’t tried before because it’s too expensive. They don’t have to be thinking about the price of everything they’re eating and drinking while they’re here. Alfie’s also has a wine club. How does that work? Alfie’s has always [drawn] a lot of regulars, and we’ve always tried to facilitate this vibe of being your other living room. If you love wine, we want this to be a place that you want to spend a lot of your time and cater that a little bit more. Our wine club has 19 spots, and for a monthly fee of $150, you basically get a rack of your own [in the restaurant]. If you have a great collection at home, you can bring it in. Or if you have specific tastes and things that you enjoy when you come here, we can curate the wine locker for you so you can actually purchase wine at a steep discount that we don’t have on the list. If there are special selections that are too expensive for us to put on the menu, we can get those for you, and you’ll pay 50% less than standard restaurant prices. After releasing the first few days of reservations, you immediately had 700 bookings. Were you expecting that kind of reception? I wouldn’t say I expected anything. [But] I was hoping for it, and I kind of felt it. Sometimes in this industry, you can feel when something is gonna hit. Leading up to [opening] and seeing some of the interest on social media, it seemed like it was gonna go that route so we were trying to plan for it. Alfie’s scratches an itch that [D.C. diners] haven’t been able to scratch at least since 2020. The city is getting burnt out [by] small businesses being replaced by big corporate restaurant group spots, and we’re very much the antithesis of that. You walk in, and Justin and I are in the kitchen, so we can say hi to you and run food to the table. I think it’s a vibe that D.C. hasn’t had in years.

item.title: Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.72
Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Old Raj gin looks like the kind of thing you’d find at the back of your grandfather’s drinks cabinet; its mercantile font and black-and-white portrait of a colonial officer are from another age. Launched in 1972 by Scotland’s oldest independent whisky bottlers, Cadenhead’s, the saffron-laced gin spent decades being resolutely uncool. So I was astonished to find, on a recent trip to New York, that it’s now a cult Martini pour. William Elliott, bar director of Brooklyn’s Maison Premiere, was an early adopter of Old Raj. “We were hunting down obscure, overproof [high abv] gins for a tableside Martini and were struck by its quiet intensity,” he says. “The luxurious application of saffron gives it a tonal and textural quality that was a clear upgrade from the brutishness of most London Dry-style gins.” Old Raj is bottled at two strengths: 46 per cent (Red Label, £30) and a bracing 55 per cent (Blue Label, £34). “The 55 per cent abv version is the must-have,” says Nima Ansari, spirits buyer at Manhattan’s Astor Wines. The fact Old Raj is owned by the company that distils the Campbeltown single malt Springbank is also, he says, a plus for spirits connoisseurs. Blue Label is what they use for Martinis at Maison Premiere and Le Veau d’Or on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. You’ll also see it on the list at Gallaghers Steakhouse, Death & Co and Frenchette, where it’s served in a Martini twist with vermouth and tomato water. “I first came across Old Raj while working at Small Victory in Austin, Texas,” says Jojo Colonna, bar director at Four Horsemen’s buzzing Italian I Cavallini in Brooklyn. If a customer requested Blue Label, he says, “it was a sign of an intentional Martini drinker”. Old-style, high-strength gins have been making a comeback among Martini connoisseurs. “At the higher abv, the spirit holds on to more of those botanical oils and aromas,” says James Stevenson, founder of new Martini bar Brutes of Mayfair, where the house gin is Plymouth Navy Strength (£42), a 57 per cent abv homage to the high-proof gins once drunk by officers in the Royal Navy. “You still get a very dry, clean Martini, but with a much more oily texture, from the gin.” If you’re mixing Martinis with a high-strength gin, “stir with ice for longer than usual to allow for adequate dilution”, advises Kevin Beary, beverage director of Chicago’s Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club. Erik Delanoy of Elder in NYC also recommends using Old Raj Blue Label for a wet Martini with equal parts gin and vermouth. At Three Sheets in Soho, they favour The Botanist’s 50 per cent abv Distiller’s Strength (£42). “It’s still very soft and mellow,” says co-owner Max Venning. “Because it’s higher-proof, you can stir it down for longer and get the Martini really cold, without losing the lovely wild, floral botanicals.” Forget old-school stiffener – it’s now all about soft power. Comments

item.title: Secrets of the C-suite smoothie
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.17
Secrets of the C-suite smoothie Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Julia Baldet was a “burned out” 27-year-old pulling 100-hour weeks when she spotted the opportunity for a new kind of drinks brand last year. “I was working in finance, I was sick from stress, I didn’t have time to eat properly. But I also didn’t want something off the shelf from the supermarket.” The result was Elevate, a café in the City’s Royal Exchange that serves nutritionally enhanced smoothies in packaging that wouldn’t look out of place in a Space NK boutique. Bestsellers include The Glow (£8.90), a strawberry-pink mix of berries, yoghurt and skin-improving collagen. Muscle-boosting creatine – featured in the high-protein Lean Berries – “has also been trending”, says Baldet. A suite of £1.30 add-ons includes MCT oil (quick energy), lion’s mane (focus) pitaya (anti-oxidant) and prebiotic fibre. The brand recently opened a second café in Selfridges and is on target to hit £1mn in sales by the end of 2026. Functional nutrition is now one of the fastest-growing sectors in a wellness market worth $1.8tn globally. The rise of GLP-1s combined with an “always-on” culture means that more of us are skipping meals, and the comfortingly slurpable, customisable smoothie looks primed to fill the gap. Smoothies are also a cornerstone of the regime at Exalt, an “on-the-go nutrition” brand co-founded by Dan Wilson-Vaughan after 15 years in the banking world. Just like athletes, he says, deal makers are now looking to nutrition to give them the competitive edge. “Athletes want recovery and performance,” says Wilson-Vaughan, whose clients range from Premier League football clubs to City types. “Corporates traditionally needed a meal that actually replaces the one they skipped. They now want both.” What a lot of time-poor workers need most is protein, he says: “20g+ [a day] is a must alongside fibre and the right fats. We are also pushing the use of ashwagandha as a way of alleviating stress.” At Earthbar in Silicon Valley, the go-to smoothie is The Protocol ($14.95), a green, protein-packed blend of fruit, spinach and yerba mate (a natural source of caffeine, supposedly without the crash), plus blue spirulina, creatine, collagen and whey protein. There is also a choice of almost 50 further “add-ons”, including B12, probiotics and bee pollen, as well as L-carnitine, a supplement which some believe can help burn fat. As for whether we actually need all these add-ons, the jury is out. “Smoothies can be useful to deliver large amounts of a particular ingredient,” says James Collins, managing director of the INTRA Performance Group, which provides nutrition advice to both athletes and Fortune 500 CEOs. “However, we don’t recommend ‘functional smoothies’ for general, unstructured use. Marketing leads people to believe that a supplement can be the silver bullet for better health and performance without addressing the wider principles of nutrition, exercise and recovery.” Perhaps, just sometimes, all one needs to do is close the laptop and go out for dinner with some friends. Comments

item.title: Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.74
Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago When I say Chicago isn’t a celebrity town, that cuts both ways. We have limited tolerance for Instagram culture, we roll our eyes at round-the-block queues and, for most of us, the very notion of $20 trend smoothies triggers an allergic reaction. On the other hand, we can be provincial. At a recent concert at the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park, the Jumbotron cycled through drone footage of American skylines. At the sight of Chicago’s, the crowd exploded. At all others, including a glimmering and handsome New York City? Crickets. Chicagoans have a funny relationship to fame. Seeing a celebrity out and about is not just another Tuesday for us: it’s day-derailing. We’ll ignore the cardinal rule imparted by our peers on the coast and bug the hell out of them, then spend the rest of the day calling our cousins’ cousins. We keep our local celebrities close but feel inordinately stung when they decamp for another city. To better understand this hot-and-cold city, we spoke to eight cultural insiders who know it better than most. Some were forged in Chicago. Others enthusiastically adopted it. And many of them still choose to live here, even when New York and LA beckon. Jump straight to . . . Sandra Cisneros, writer and author of ‘The House on Mango Street’ (born and raised in Chicago; based in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Aon Center. After going to a concert downtown in Grant Park, we would walk over to what was the Standard Oil Building, now the Aon Center, on East Randolph Street. In the plaza’s sunken garden is the most fabulous treasure: wind sculptures by Harry Bertoia. They look like reeds, and at the dedication ceremony in 1972, the artist climbed inside the installation and “played” them. Bertoia was a furniture designer, too. When his sculptures were displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1975, it was the first and only time I’d seen a sign that said, “Please touch.” I like the idea that he thought about the poetics of these sculptures moving and making these wonderful sounds. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Hot dogs. If you haven’t had a Chicago hot dog, you haven’t had a hot dog. You have to have a bun with little poppy seeds on it, it has to be bundled in waxed paper and the french fries have to be good. Now, there are even vegan hot dogs. Recently, my family and I got some at Portillo’s late at night, and they were really good — I was surprised! One more thing I didn’t realise until two years ago that the flowers in Chicago’s public parks were so much a part of the city. To me, lilacs, peonies and lilies of the valley are the quintessential flowers of Chicago. Jeff Tweedy, musician and lead vocalist/guitarist of Wilco (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The parks. If you want to soak up what the city and culture are really like, I’d pick any of the Chicago Park District parks, like Independence in Irving Park or Gompers in North Park. Have a picnic and see how Chicagoans really recreate. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand “Dibs”. The concept of saving your parking spot, especially in heavy snow. Technically not legal, but ultimately, pretty fair and moral. If you’re the one who broke your ass shovelling snow, you should get to keep that spot for at least a day or so. What Chicago teaches you When you grow up in a smaller town like I did, there’s a belief that it’s a kinder way to live and that you can’t get that in a city. It’s not true. When I moved to Chicago, I knew more people in my neighbourhood than I did growing up — it’s all about block parties and meeting up with neighbours. Chicago has problems like everywhere else, but it’s a city that facilitates community. Rick Bayless, chef and restaurateur (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The National Museum of Mexican Art. Rather than establishing the museum downtown, the founders chose Pilsen — a predominantly Latino neighbourhood — and they chose to keep this world-class collection free to all. NMMA is not only one of our city’s best museums but an integral player in this vibrant community. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Storefront theatre. Yes, we have grand old theatres that host Broadway touring companies, and yes, we have the internationally acclaimed Steppenwolf, Goodman and Chicago Shakespeare companies. But Chicago is a city of neighbourhoods, and most of them are home to a host of storefront theatres. One of the best is TimeLine Theatre Company, which does historical pieces that have contemporary relevance. Hungry yet? Forty years ago, when we opened Frontera Grill, farmers’ markets hadn’t taken off in Chicago. Today, with local chefs championing local products, there are over 40 and growing. Now communities are hosting “alternative” farmers’ markets that start at 3pm or 4pm and sell until around 7pm on specific weekdays, rather than weekend mornings. Eve L Ewing, author, scholar and co-owner of Build Coffee & Books in Woodlawn (based in Chicago) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The South Shore Nature Sanctuary and Montrose Point Bird Sanctuary. Our city motto is urbs in horto — city in a garden. Away from all the noise and the hubbub, the marshlands and prairie are also part of our identity. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Community. The city is famously corrupt, but there’s a more generous way to understand the “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” way we do things, which is that Chicagoans look out for each other and take care of one another. If you’re my neighbour’s cousin’s pick-up basketball buddy, you’re in the circle and I’ve got to take care of you. The hill she’ll die on Everyone likes to share their (mostly ill-informed) opinions on Chicago pizza, but through and through we’re a taco city. Our ratio of great tacos per capita is off the charts. I grew up going to El Cid, a Mexican restaurant in Logan Square, while El Milagro in Pilsen both sells tacos and manufactures the best tortillas and chips. Enrique Mazzola, conductor and music director of the Lyric Opera of Chicago (divides time between Chicago and Paris) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Driehaus Museum. This small museum just off the Magnificent Mile focuses on the art, architecture and design of the American Gilded Age and the Art Nouveau period. Inside is a magnificent auditorium with interesting and diverse programming. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The walks. One of my favourites goes from downtown along the Lakefront Trail to Lincoln Park. Only a true Chicagoan can understand how beautiful this itinerary is. In general, I love walking around the city — I even walk to work at the Lyric Opera of Chicago and enjoy following the Chicago River every day. Bonus recommendation Wander around the boutique shops and cafés in the North Side neighbourhood of Andersonville. You’re still in Chicago but removed from the tourist areas and high-rises of downtown. Isaiah Collier, saxophonist and composer (divides time between Chicago and New York) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago 63rd Street Beach. The city has its madness, but it also has its tranquillity, usually by the water. Cats will get together here for drum circles — they’ve been doing it for decades. It’s therapeutic and uniquely ethnic. The overview of the city that you see from down there is kind of mythical, very cinematic. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Concerts at Pritzker Pavilion. No matter where you’re from in the city, I think we can all agree there’s something special about being able to witness a proper concert at Pritzker Pavilion. Not amateur stuff, but a full production from start to finish. It’s one hell of a location. A brutal truth We’re the most segregated major city in America. That residual effect has made people feel there are not enough opportunities. It can be disheartening for creatives. Grant Achatz, chef/creative director and co-owner of Chicago’s Alinea restaurant Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Primitive on Jefferson Street. It’s a massive showroom packed with rare antiquities from all over the world. I’m into medieval and Egyptian history, so for me it’s a rabbit hole I can lose an afternoon in. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The grit. When I showed up in 2001 with this weird, modernist way of cooking, this city embraced the risk and let me build. People here get that ambition runs quiet, that the winters bond everybody together, that nobody’s impressed with you until you’ve put in the work. You can’t feel any of that from a postcard. You’ve got to live here a while. Tasha, singer-songwriter and poet (born and raised in Chicago, based in New York) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Promontory Point. We just call it The Point. I don’t think people who aren’t from Chicago really know the secret, stunning beauty it has, especially on the South Side. There is nothing more romantic than jumping from the rocks at sunset on a sticky, hot summer day, the sky pink behind the city skyline, cicadas buzzing. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Being from the city proper. I love the way we bond over that. Not the suburbs. Not the surrounding counties. Definitely not Indiana. A love letter No matter where I end up in the world, Chicago will always be my home, the place I return to, the place that understands me, that holds my whole family and first gave me courage. Chicago forever. What do you love most about Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. And find more of our Chicago guide here Follow us on Instagram at @FTGlobetrotter Cities with the FT FT Globetrotter, our insider guides to some of the world’s greatest cities, offers expert advice on eating and drinking, exercise, art and culture — and much more Find us in Chicago, London, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Tokyo, New York, Paris, Lagos, Rome, Frankfurt, Singapore, Hong Kong, Miami, Toronto, Madrid, Melbourne, Copenhagen, Zürich, Milan, Vancouver, Edinburgh, Venice and Istanbul Comments

item.title: Rose Chalalai Singh’s dinner with the dervishes
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.51
Rose Chalalai Singh’s dinner with the dervishes Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I first went to Turkey four years ago and have gone back every summer since. I have friends in Istanbul – sisters Başak and Defne Kocabıyıkoğlu – who I met in Paris. Together they run Nackiyé, a family-owned fashion brand inspired by the eastern Mediterranean. It was Defne and Başak who introduced me to the whirling dervishes, a Sufi Muslim group founded in the 13th century by the poet Rūmī. They practise a form of meditation and worship called Sema, where they spin in circles while dressed in long, buttonless skirts. Defne and Başak’s great-grandmother, Seyyare, was the first woman to whirl at their family’s dervish lodge in Kutahya (now a mosque). We decided to host a dinner and go to a dervish performance afterwards. The first place I head to when I land in Istanbul – and the last place I go before I leave – is Pandeli, a legendary restaurant above the Egyptian bazaar. It’s an institution; everyone has been there, from politicians to tourists. Fergus Henderson told me it’s his favourite restaurant. The walls are fitted with beautiful blue tiles, and there are framed photographs and notes from all of its visitors; its founder Pandeli Çobanoğlu was a very elegant man. I suggested it as the location for our dinner. Defne and Başak weren’t sure it was going to be possible. In its 125-year history, Pandeli has rarely opened for dinner; the gates to the bazaar usually close at 7pm and it’s right near a mosque. But I asked them to try. A few days later, Defne called me up with the good news. In exchange for a donation to the mosque, they would give us the space for the night. We just needed to have good security on the gates. At 5am on the day of the dinner, we went out on a little taxi boat to go fishing in the Black Sea, just as the light was coming in. It was magical. We caught lots of horse mackerel, a pretty blue fish, and brought it to the restaurant. I coated it in a mix of ginger powder and toasted chilli from my kitchen in Paris, where I mostly use Thai flavours, and fried it almost like tempura. We served it over a bed of yoghurt with fresh herbs and a tomato salad dressed in coriander, dry lemongrass and some seaweed. Abdullah Sevim, the chef at Pandeli, cooked grilled lamb, aubergine and baby okra for a Turkish accompaniment to the fish – Istanbul has amazing vegetables. There’s also a seventh-generation spice store in the bazaar where I went absolutely crazy. I think I spent €800 on Turkish spices, including carob and blue nila powders for food colouring, and around 10kg of pistachios. We dressed the table with pink roses, embroidered napkins and matching pink Chini ceramics from Nackiyé (every plate was drawn, painted and gold-rimmed by hand). The 21 guests were all friends, including art director Katia Hakko and photographer Johan Sandberg. We drank rakı all night from a special narrow highball glass, before finishing the dinner with flan and cherry sorbet. The next night we went to see a dervish performance at Kasımpaşa Mevlevihane, a historic lodge that hosts ceremonies three times a week. It felt like a theatre for religion. The performance was about an hour long, and the dervishes turned to the sound of the ney, an ancient reed flute, which helps create a sense of contemplation. I loved the costumes – the camel-hair hats and swirling white skirts, which symbolise the shrouds of the dancers’ egos. It’s a beautiful act of devotion. Dervish dances are performed to Mevlevi music, which we also had playing at the dinner. Defne and Başak invited two classical Turkish music teachers from Haliç University to play a series of pieces on the ney and the kanun, a stringed instrument that produces a delicate shimmery sound. It is some of my favourite music because it is all about pleasure. What I love about the dervish dance is that it makes you feel calm and silent. It brings you into something that’s very focused. Comments

item.title: Want to eat like a real Chicagoan? Go to these three neighbourhoods
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.21
Want to eat like a real Chicagoan? Go to these three neighbourhoods Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago I’m sick of talking about Italian beef. I don’t even remember the last time I ate it — partly out of stubbornness. But Chicago is not only about dripping beef sandwiches or doorstopper deep-dish pizza. In the almost 20 years I’ve lived here, and 15 writing about the city’s food scene, I am more frequently on the hunt for a standout banh mi or jibarito. Pounding the pavement of my hometown, I’ve come to know the delicate shatter of a Cantonese chicken wing fried to perfection and the quivering wobble of just-set chawanmushi seasoned with wild local alliums. I’ve eaten the best Mexican food in Chicago, slurping goat birria stained red from chillies in a hole in the wall, or wolfing tender lengua tacos in the middle of a grocery store. I’ve wept over corn smut-filled ravioli that honours every iota of this lifeblood crop down to its hairy silk. Chicago is a city of immigrants, proud natives and hearty blow-ins. Almost a quarter of our residents are foreign-born, meaning you can feast aplenty on traditional Sonoran, Sichuan, Pakistani, Polish, Korean, Greek, Ethiopian, Laotian, Colombian dishes and more. You can also taste what it’s like for someone to have to straddle two identities and cultures. In order to experience Chicago’s best culinary thrills, you have to get out of shuffling distance of the beef sandwich and deep-dish chains, away from the tourist attractions dotted amid The Loop’s glistening monoliths. That’s the other thing you need to know about Chicago. It’s a city of neighbourhoods — 77 of them to be exact. Here’s how to eat across three of my favourites. Logan Square I’ve spent much of the past two decades living four-ish miles north-west of downtown in Logan Square, an intoxicating and maddening nexus of contrasts, home to wide, tree-lined boulevards and some of the city’s finest cooking. Low-slung stone structures housing indie cafés, dives, taquerias and a historic jewel box of a movie theatre butt up against ugly, sprawling apartment complexes with lower floors occupied by chains proffering $18 grain bowls. Gentrification has ebbed away some of the neighbourhood’s grittier bits and charm. But with reinvestment have come delights like the 606, a 2.7-mile, foliage-lined walking and cycling trail on a derelict former rail line. The Logan Square Blue Line station deposits you in the neighbourhood’s beating heart. A towering Doric marble column overlooks a circular plaza that has been refurbished to create more walkable space and redubbed La Placita in honour of the neighbourhood’s Latino heritage. On the other side of the plaza is Chicago’s original farm-to-table restaurant, Lula Cafe. Jason Hammel and Amalea Tshilds opened this indie icon in 1999, and now it spills across three storefronts, faithfully churning out inventive seasonal cooking and comfy standbys such as Pasta “Yia Yia”, aka feta-laced, cinnamon-scented bucatini. It’s thanks in part to Lula that the neighbourhood remains a magnet for dynamic, heartfelt seasonal cooking, and why I consider it prerequisite eating to understand what makes Logan Logan. We’ll (officially) start three-quarters of a mile north-east of Lula at Cellar Door Provisions. This decade-old slip of a restaurant has, at various times, been a café and bakery, tasting-menu restaurant and wine bar, all under the same name, and with the same corner perch on a leafy, residential street. It’s now a bistro, and it’s restless, scrappy and exciting. The hyper-seasonal à la carte dinner menu, from chef-owner Ethan Pikas and chef de cuisine Alex Cochran, changes constantly and occasionally startles. You may get red wine-braised lamb’s tongue with herbaceous salsa verde, a pert, luscious burger or grilled mackerel with preserved mussels in sauce Américaine. The wine leans light, bracing and a little weird. Some 350 feet away from Cellar Door is Superkhana International, an Indian-ish restaurant from chefs and co-owners Zeeshan Shah and Yoshi Yamada that blurs lines with joyful abandon. Is their tangy, creamy Palak paneer pizza (with creamed spinach, chilli oil and crispy shallots) pizza or naan? Is their Maggi noodles bolognese umami (that’ll be the Maggi liquid seasoning), warmly tangy (that’ll be the achar masala) — or both? Don’t overthink; just indulge. And always add shareable chaat, which cleverly rotates with our challenging Midwestern seasons. Like the hot-pink-painted Superkhana, Mi Tocaya Antojería, a 15-minute walk south-east, is a riot of colour and bustling energy, though the latter holds a bit faster to dogma in the name of preserving Mexico’s gastronomic heritage. To walk in — Spanish mingling with English, the sizzle of marinated carne and mole-soused tortillas chiming with the metallic maraca of shaking cocktails — is to enter a kind of multicultural Chicago utopia. At the heart of this place is the outspoken chef and proprietor Diana Dávila who recreates the regional Mexican cooking of her childhood, hair swept into a braided crown, laugh reverberating from the pass. A Chicago native born to Mexican immigrants, Dávila would be the first to tell you that her luscious mole negro, comprising some 30 ingredients (and lately enveloping braised pork shank and celery root), is “f****** dope”. Here costra (cheese-crusted) tacos taste like Mexico City and beets get roasted in coffee and heaped on garlicky Mayan pepita spread. Don’t be surprised if you spot beloved Chicago chef Margaret Pak stopping by for a post-shift steak burrito. The big-hearted co-owner of the excellent Keralan restaurant, Thattu, in neighbouring Avondale, swears by this comfy handheld meal, with good reason. Revel in its grilled skirt steak, local black beans, queso chihuahua and sour cream. I’ve been known to wax poetic on Giant’s crab tagliatelle to anyone who will listen. This tangle of al dente pasta slaps the taste buds with sweet, brackish crab, fiery chilli butter and acidity. For almost a decade, I’ve darkened the door of this narrow joint on West Armitage Avenue, bound for a bar stool in the back overlooking the tiny galley kitchen that radiates heat and sweat. Chef Jason Vincent’s boisterous little restaurant has a gift for exceptional, likeable food (think ruffly layered lasagne and pork schnitzel). For summer 2025, this restless crew of creatives upped the ante with a Test Kitchen menu. This is the brave, invigorating food they cook for themselves and that we get to eat: Laotian steamed fish, green garlic chawanmushi with bonito flakes and black sesame and pistachio-studded pâté en croûte with foie gras. Other excellent Logan Square restaurants - Omarcito’s Latin Cafe for tangy marinated steak sandwiches and crispy consommé-drowned chicken tacos, doled out from a bright yellow shipping container. - Bungalow by Middle Brow for thick rafts of sourdough bread and cleverly topped char-speckled pizzas, washed down with house-brewed beer and house-made natural wine — all made from ingredients grown in and around Illinois. - Osteria Langhe for unfettered northern Italian cooking. - The Radicle for late-night pizza and tinned fish snacks, washed down with aperitif-heavy cocktails. - Longman & Eagle for a stiff whiskey cocktail and superb smashburger. Uptown There’s a nostalgic grandeur to Uptown that you can almost conjure into a grainy old film in your mind’s eye as you gaze up at the soaring, Prohibition-era Art Deco buildings. “Of course, Al Capone drank here,” you think, scooching into a beat-up, half-moon booth at the longstanding Green Mill Cocktail Lounge, as you await Chris Foreman’s Friday evening jazz piano set over an eye-poppingly stiff Old Fashioned. A century ago, this booming nightlife and entertainment district even housed the studio that produced a Charlie Chaplin film, but it struggled subsequently for decades after discriminatory housing practices sent property values plummeting. Yet the institutional malfeasance and low rents produced a richly diverse demographic with a penchant for social justice. JOIN (Jobs Or Income Now), an activism group that challenged racist welfare practices, was born here. Vacant storefronts remain, but Uptown is rising (read: gentrifying), as evidenced by the arrival of a Target where a burnt-out rail and bus yard once stood, but also by the bold cooking making a home here. The wind blows a bit harder and chillier up here. All the more reason to pop in for pho in one of the outstanding Vietnamese restaurants concentrated on West Argyle Street. (For a handheld delight, consider the ham and head cheese banh mi on a shattering baguette at Nhu Lan Bakery.) But the stalwart Hai Yen, its stark greyscale facade hiding amid shinier Little Saigon storefronts, is the one Chicago chefs will send you to for bò lá lốt (lemongrass-scented beef and pork sausage grilled in betel leaf) and phở đặc biệt with beef in half a dozen guises bobbing amid slippery rice noodles. I like prefacing said beef injection with a few springy tapioca shrimp dumplings. I’m admittedly not the biggest fan of a tasting menu, but one of the few exceptions is Cariño, whose executive chef and owner, Norman Fenton, nabbed a nomination for Best Chef: Great Lakes at the 2026 James Beard Foundation Awards. This Detroit-born chef, who previously cooked at WILD Tulum in Mexico and then at Grant Achatz’s world-renowned cocktail lounge The Aviary and the inventive, Michelin-starred Schwa in Chicago, has a gift for zhuzhing the stuff of everyday nourishment with imagination and humour. The familiar flavours of tacos al pastor jolt the senses when reimagined as a marinated lamb tartare tostada. Cariño’s dozen-plus-course tasting menu ($200 per person) moved me and made me think, laugh and, yes, cry, just once. (See the aforementioned tear-inducing corn smut ravioli, filled with the truffle-like corn fungus huitlacoche, a Mexican delicacy.) If you don’t mind a 10pm dinner, Cariño performs a more affordable second act in the form of an eight-course taco omakase ($125 per person, including drinks), a masa-centric romp through tetelas, tacos and quesadillas set to a thumping, upbeat soundtrack. The crackly-edged, suadero carnitas taco will change you. Chicagoans can’t go too many days without an outstanding sandwich. Fortunately, Ragadan, a deliciously uncommon mash-up of Jordanian street food joint and Midwestern diner, has several cures for that. Owner Danny Sweis’s parents hail from Amman, Jordan. He was born and raised in his family’s diner in Oklahoma City, hence the menu’s OKC burger, with shaved onion caramelised right into the minced beef. Anything between bread is superb here, but the sandwich that keeps me biking five miles to get there is the falafel ka’ak. Craggy outside, achingly soft inside, the falafel pucks exhale warming spices, layered amid bright, crunchy veg, sharp pickles and silky hummus. And oh, that Levantine bread: wispy, airy, caked in sesame seeds, and sourced from the Latin American and European bakery Markellos. Ask for a za’atar mayo side for dipping. If you don’t, Sweis may deposit a little cup alongside your sandwich anyway. Other excellent Uptown restaurants - Kie Gol Lanee for soul-soothing Oaxacan cooking (get the chapulines if they’re not sold out). - Demera for expert traditional Ethiopian cuisine and aromatic house honey wine. - Sun Wah BBQ for the off-menu Beijing (Peking) duck, starting with the whole crispy-skinned bird and ending with duck-fried rice. - YooYee for lip-tingling braised beef soup with fat hand-pulled noodle ribbons. Chinatown At the corner of Cermak and Wentworth, a landmark red gate denotes the technical start of Chicago’s Chinatown. But you can smell and feel that you’re here the moment you emerge from the Cermak-Chinatown Red Line station. Chinatown breathes and bustles impatiently, its residents endlessly streaming by laden with plastic Thank You bags. It smells, surprisingly perhaps, like Portuguese tarts baking and five-spice and fish. This 30,000-strong community is spilling into proximate districts and evolving as younger generations make their mark. In 2022, Lily Wang and Joe Briglio decided to fix a problem in Chinatown: there wasn’t, and had never been, a dedicated cocktail bar here. The couple took the reins at the classic Chinese restaurant Moon Palace, a 50-plus-year neighbourhood fixture owned by Wang’s parents. They shifted the restaurant into a permanent takeaway operation and built a sultry bar, Nine Bar, where the dining room used to be. You walk into what resembles any other brightly lit, tile-and-wood carry-out, save for a formidable metal door. You’re then deposited into a dim, neon-lit lounge that feels both lively and intimate, bar staff deftly mixing cocktails that mingle Japanese, Chinese and tropical influences, from the MSG-laced martini to a Sichuan peppercorn-spiked margarita called the Paper Dragon. A few doors down, Yao Yao provides a decidedly bright and turquoise-hued contrast to Nine Bar. Tuck yourself into a booth and prepare for the day’s simplest order: pickled fish, a soup of sharp pickled greens and mild, tender bass bobbing in a deliciously tacky broth. Order it mild if you want to feel the Sichuan tingle without missing all the beautiful nuance. Even the smallest size is too large for two, so prepare for leftovers. I like adding toothy thin glass noodles for heft. They come in little knotted bundles. Because we must end on a sweet note, follow your nose to the oldest bakery in town. The family-run, cash-only Chiu Quon Bakery has been open since 1986. It was founded by Pui Yip and Cora Chiu with recipes that Yip brought from Hong Kong, and the second generation owns it now. I’ve never been here when there wasn’t a queue, though I’m grateful for time to ponder my order from the packed wraparound case. For starters, I’ll take an always fluffy, sweet-savoury BBQ pork bun, custardy Portuguese egg tart and a bouncy mochi ball. Uncomfortably full? Me too. I’d suggest a ramble through Ping Tom Memorial Park, a former rail yard turned native prairie park that hugs the Chicago River. Paved paths and raised boardwalks carry you through rewilded grasses and past colourful murals. Glance north at every available opportunity, then gasp. Is that not the most gorgeous view of the skyline? Other excellent Chinatown restaurants - Dolo Restaurant and Bar for traditional and modern dim sum. - MCCB for charcoal-grilled whole fish and twice-cooked pork with leeks. - 3 Sauces Hainam Chicken Rice at the Richland Center food court for, you guessed it, Hainam chicken rice: soft, toothsome poached thigh meat served chilled over chicken fat-flavoured rice. - Yummy Yummy Noodles to slurp shrimp wonton noodle soup. Which is your favourite neighbourhood restaurant in Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. And read more of our Chicago guide here Follow us on Instagram at @FTGlobetrotter Cities with the FT FT Globetrotter, our insider guides to some of the world’s greatest cities, offers expert advice on eating and drinking, exercise, art and culture — and much more Find us in Chicago, London, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Tokyo, New York, Paris, Lagos, Rome, Frankfurt, Singapore, Hong Kong, Miami, Toronto, Madrid, Melbourne, Copenhagen, Zürich, Milan, Vancouver, Edinburgh, Venice and Istanbul Comments

item.title: Affordable Alternatives to Japan's Most Crowded Destinations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 8.00
Japan welcomed more visitors in 2025 than ever before, and most walked the same ten streets. The crowding is real but concentrated: a few temples, villages, and viewpoints absorb most of it, while places offering the same experience sit half empty a valley away. Budget travelers hear a tempting promise: quieter must mean cheaper. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the quiet option adds a shinkansen leg or a rural bus that erases every yen saved on admission. The only way to know is to do the math, so this article does it for four popular swaps using prices checked in August 2026 from official sources. That timing matters: JR East raised fares on March 14, 2026, and Kyoto doubled its accommodation tax two weeks earlier, so numbers from older guides are quietly wrong. The pairings come from the Crowd-Free Japan Index, which matches 40 of Japan's most-visited places with curated quieter alternatives. Kanazawa Instead of Kyoto: The Savings Are on the Ground, Not the Rails Kanazawa is often called "little Kyoto," which annoys both cities, but the comparison holds where it counts. The Higashi Chaya geisha district is a smaller, calmer Gion where the teahouses actually let you in: Ochaya Shima charges ¥500 to walk through a working 1820s interior. In contrast, most Gion teahouses remain entirely closed to casual visitors. Omicho Market delivers the seafood-breakfast experience of Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, with locals still doing their shopping there, and entry to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, costs ¥320, compared with ¥500 for Kinkaku-ji or ¥500 for Kiyomizu-dera, each ticketed separately. The biggest savings come from where you sleep. Kyoto's average hotel rate hit a record ¥20,195 per night in 2024. Since March 1, 2026, the city has charged a ¥1,000 per-person-per-night accommodation tax on rooms priced at ¥20,000-49,999, double the previous rate. Kanazawa's tax on the same room is ¥500. | Cost item (August 2026) | Kyoto | Kanazawa | | Shinkansen from Tokyo, one way | ¥14,170 | ¥14,600 | | City bus, single ride | ¥230 | ¥220 | | Transit day pass | ¥1,100 | ¥800 | | Headline garden or temple | ¥500 | ¥320 | | Accommodation tax, per person | ¥1,000 p.p. per night | ¥500 p.p. per night | Note the first row: The train from Tokyo to Kanazawa costs slightly more than the train to Kyoto. The swap pays off in everything after you arrive and compounds with every night you stay. Shima Onsen Instead of Ginzan Onsen: The Clearest Budget Win in Japan Ginzan Onsen's gaslit street has become so popular that the town now meters its own visitors. In winter, day visitors park two kilometers out and ride a shuttle; evening entry requires a paid reservation (¥1,150 in the first season, capped at 100 people per hour), and after 8 pm the street closes to everyone but overnight guests. Those overnight stays start at roughly ¥25,000 per person with meals, and reaching the town from Tokyo costs about ¥13,000 by the Yamagata Shinkansen, plus a ¥1,000 bus that takes cash only. Shima Onsen, tucked in a Gunma river gorge, offers the same Taisho-era wooden-ryokan romance with none of the metering. Sekizenkan's main building dates to 1691, making it Japan's oldest hot-spring inn building, and it is often said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away; its budget rooms start at ¥10,450 per person. The riverside cave bath Kawara-no-yu is open to day visitors from 9:00 to 15:00 without charge. Best of all, a direct highway bus runs from Tokyo Station for ¥3,500 one way and ¥6,300 round trip, about three and a half hours. | Cost item (August 2026) | Ginzan Onsen | Shima Onsen | | Transport from Tokyo, one way | ~¥14,000 (shinkansen + bus) | ¥3,500 (direct bus) | | Night in a heritage ryokan | From ~¥25,000 p.p. with meals | From ¥10,450 p.p. at Sekizenkan | | Soaking without staying | Winter evenings ticketed | Free cave bath, 9:00–15:00 | One honest caveat: the bus runs once daily each way and must be reserved by 4 pm the day before. If you miss it, the rail route via Nakanojo costs more and takes longer. Book the seat, then relax. Ainokura Instead of Shirakawa-go: Let Your Routing Decide Shirakawa-go itself is not the budget problem; walking the village is free, the Wada House costs ¥400, and the viewpoint shuttle costs ¥300. The problem is that everyone arrives on the same reservation-only buses (¥2,800 one way from either Kanazawa or Takayama) and shares the lanes with them. Ainokura, a village of twenty thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses on a mountainside in neighboring Gokayama, is listed as a World Heritage site with a fraction of the foot traffic. It is also free to enter on foot, and the World Heritage Bus from Takaoka or Shin-Takaoka costs ¥1,100, less than half the Shirakawa-go fare. Whether that saves you money depends entirely on your routing. Traveling the Hokuriku Shinkansen anyway? Step off at Shin-Takaoka and Ainokura is the cheaper, quieter choice. Based in Kanazawa or Takayama with no plans northward? The extra rail leg to Takaoka eats the difference, so the direct ¥2,800 bus to Shirakawa-go wins. The best-value option for seeing both: the ¥4,000 two-day unlimited pass covers Ainokura, Suganuma, and Shirakawa-go on one ticket, and costs less than buying a single round trip separately. Related: Travelers looking beyond Tokyo and Kyoto can find more ideas in Go Backpacking's guide to Japan's Chubu region. Naoshima and Teshima Instead of teamLab: When Quieter Costs More Honesty requires one counterexample, because quiet does not automatically mean cheap. Tokyo's teamLab Planets charges from ¥3,600, with date-based pricing.
