The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to reclassify livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species of its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led American Prairie to cancel its public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here, and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: He Fell 500 Feet Down Mount Shasta. To Survive, He Took Off His Boots and Crawled Through the Night.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.38
The climber took off his mountaineering boots and walked through the night to a remote wilderness cabin to await rescue (Photo: Courtesy of Shasta-Trinity Forest Service) On September 10, a mountaineer from San Jose, California, summited Mount Shasta around 7:30 P.M. According to a rescue report from the Shasta-Trinity National Forest Service (STFS), that was the least eventful part of his climb. After his summit, the climber attempted to glissade down Avalanche Gulch, the most popular route to the top. Glissading involves sliding down a steep snowpack and is a technique some use to descend a mountain quickly. But he lost control and slid about 500 vertical feet down the slope. During the fall, his feet were severely injured. So, he took off his mountaineering boots and walked through the night to a remote wilderness cabin to await rescue. “However, he ran into trouble shortly thereafter,” the Forest Service wrote. “His cellphone died after summiting, and the climber’s friends became concerned when they were unable to contact him the following day.” Authorities have not released the climber’s name, age, or condition. When he failed to check in, the climber’s friends reported him missing to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office. Mount Shasta is one of California’s most popular peaks for mountaineers. Seven year-round glaciers cover its flanks, making it a perfect testing ground for budding mountaineers hoping to learn to use crampons, ice axes, and other mountaineering gear. The climber was in the Avalanche Gulch area, the classic mountaineering route to the mountain’s peak. It’s not an overly technical route, but it requires a 7,000-foot vertical ascent, with exposure to steep snow, ice, rockfall, and extreme weather, the Mount Shasta Avalanche Center (MSAC) wrote on its website. “The climb to the summit is steep and rigorous, requiring crampons, a mountain axe, helmet, and basic snow travel skills,” MSAC wrote. “Don’t consider this route a cakewalk.” According to MSAC, the best time to climb Avalanche Gulch is April through June, sometimes in July, and rarely August through November. In late summer, lower portions of the trail lose their snow cover, exposing climbers to loose scree, talus, and difficult hiking conditions. “Later season climbing will expose you to dramatically increased rock fall and is not advised,” MSAC writes. Mount Shasta Climbing Rangers, Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Search and Rescue, and the California Highway Patrol (CHP) began searching for the climber at 2 P.M. on September 11. Two hours into the search, responders said a hiker called them from Horse Camp, a historic base camp and alpine refuge located at about 7,900 feet. The hiker had found the missing climber—the latter of whom was barefoot. During his fall, the climber sustained significant lacerations and injuries to his feet. When trauma occurs at a high altitude, tissue can swell rapidly, making rigid mountaineering boots exceptionally painful. “The climber removed his boots due to painful swelling and crawled through the night, down the remainder of Avalanche Gulch to the Horse Camp Cabin,” the Forest Service wrote. “After evaluating the climber’s injuries, he was airlifted from Horse Camp to a nearby hospital for treatment.” The Forest Service notes there are several lessons to be learned from this incident. For starters, don’t begin such an ambitious hike so late in the evening. In mid-September, the sun sets around 7 P.M. in the area. “When climbing Mount Shasta or a similar objective, give yourself plenty of daylight to hike out,” a STFS spokesperson wrote. “This makes the descent safer, and if you or another member of your party needs help, it is easier for rescuers to find and assist you. Experts recommend climbers set a noon turnaround time when attempting Mount Shasta, even if that means they’re short of the summit. Always share your itinerary with at least one person, and give your friends a plan on what to do if you don’t check in. “The climber wisely notified his friends of his plan to climb Mount Shasta and made a point to check in and provide progress updates,” the STFS spokesperson wrote. When he lost contact, his friends contacted law enforcement to report him overdue and traveled to help with the search effort. When using electronic navigation, have a backup and be ready for rescue. Never rely solely on a GPS or phone to navigate—if the devices stop working, hikers need to use their own navigational skills to get home safely. “The Shasta-Trinity National Forest thanks the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office, SAR volunteers, CHP helicopter team, and the hiker who found the climber at Horse Camp Cabin for their assistance in this mission,” the spokesperson wrote.

item.title: A McDonald’s Toy, Pokémon Cards, and 25,000 Other Items Dropped in Yellowstone’s Geysers
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.29
An assortment of items collected from Yellowstone geysers shown on a table, includes an Uno card, Polaroid pictures, cameras, and race car toys (Photo: NPS and Jerrad Scoggins/500px via Getty Images) Visitors dropped more than 25,000 items into Yellowstone National Park geysers in 2026, setting a new record for the amount of stuff lost to the world’s most famous hydrothermal features. In all, scientists removed more than 20,100 pieces of trash, 5,600 rocks and sticks, and nearly 300 hats from the park’s hydrothermal areas in 2026, according to a September 14 report published by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). This year marks a new record for debris removal in the park, and comes on the heels of a busy tourism season. More than 2.64 million people visited Yellowstone between January and July 2026, nearly tying the park’s most-visited year in 2021, according to National Park Service (NPS) data. “The more foot traffic an area gets, the more trash will be there—but this is especially true in wide open geyser basins with narrow boardwalks,” Margery Price, the report’s author and a park physical science technician, told Outside. “Midway Geyser Basin in particular is our biggest hat collector.” Among the tonnage of lost personal items were more than a few wacky finds: 15 fake fingernails, eight miniature race cars, two rubber ducks and a McDonald’s toy from 2010—and that’s just the beginning. By mid-September 2025, Yellowstone’s geology team used poles, including one with a 16-foot extendable handle, strainers, hand rakes and shovels to remove more than 13,000 pieces of trash, 4,000 rocks and sticks, and 300 hats from hydrothermal areas. The 2026 haul marks a 50 percent jump over last year’s loot. Objects lost in 2026 include what you might expect to find near the world’s most-visited geysers: camera lens caps, hair ties, and too many sunglasses to count (OK, there were three dozen). More obscure objects also littered the hydrothermal features, like golf tees, Legos, dental retainers, and not one but three lapel pins given to passengers on Delta Airlines flights. Crews also found Polaroid photos of the same hydrothermal features where they were recovered, a two-inch copy of The Vampire Diaries, and a single UNO card. The 2026 cleanup covers nearly all of Yellowstone’s developed, front-country hydrothermal areas, Price told Outside. Crews work everywhere from smaller sites like Frying Pan Spring and Clearwater Spring to Black Sand Basin, Artist Paintpots, Mammoth Hot Springs, Midway Geyser Basin, and Old Faithful. Experts say human objects can irreversibly harm the natural ecosystem. “Foreign material of any kind can damage or permanently alter a hydrothermal feature,” Price wrote in the 2026 report. Trash can clog a geyser’s water supply or block its runoff channels. Restricting hot-water flow can also lower a spring’s temperature, change its color, and hurt the heat-loving microorganisms that call these features home. In extreme cases, debris can even alter a geyser’s eruption schedule. Early 20th-century visitors at Yellowstone’s Minute Geyser clogged its largest vent by tossing in rocks. Eruptions that once happened every 60 seconds and could reach up to 50 feet are now smaller and irregular. NPS says these rocks have since been cemented together by mineral deposits and can’t be removed without risking further damage. Yellowstone has been trying to undo that kind of damage for decades. According to USGS, the first major thermal clean-up effort began in 1942 when a park geologist found features choked with rocks, logs, and materials visitors tossed in. Todd Walton, director of sales and marketing for Yellowstone National Park Lodges and a former park guide, told Outside that visitors should be mindful of their belongings, taking special care with “anything that can get blown off by the wind, like hats and scarves.” “I’ve seen gloves, cups, and sunglasses also, he said. “Hold onto your stuff.” Price told Outside there’s no reliable way to estimate what percentage of lost objects crews recover because conditions vary dramatically from one spring or geyser to another. “Some areas are shallow, and we can see most if not all of what’s in them,” she said. “Others, it’s just not possible for us to retrieve stuff that is too deep, at a challenging angle, or too far out from the edge. Most things sink eventually—especially once they get saturated with minerals.” Yellowstone geologist Liam Rogers told Outside that dropped items can sink quickly—but sometimes come back up. In September 2018, Ear Spring erupted and expelled coins, cans, plastic cups, cigarette butts, and other debris, including coins later dated to the 1930s, according to NPS. If visitors drop something in or near a geyser, Walton said to stay on the boardwalk and contact park staff. “People don’t realize how dangerous it is in these areas despite the numerous warnings and signs saying so,” Walton said. Many thermal areas in Yellowstone are between 150 and 200 degrees Fahrenheit, and although the surrounding ground may look solid, it can quickly give way. Multiple visitors have died in the park’s thermal features over the years. In August 2022, the body of a 70-year-old man was found in the 140-degree Abyss Geyser in the West Thumb Geyser Basin, and more than 20 people have died from burns caused by entering the park’s thermal features since the park began counting.

item.title: “You Could See the Grimace on His Face.” A Climber Fell 200 Feet Off California’s Power Dome. His Friends Used a Shirt to Stop the Bleeding.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.62
On September 11, a climber fell 200 feet while ascending on a 700-foot-tall rock face known as Power Dome in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. He was bleeding heavily, and his friends used a shirt as a bandage while they awaited a helicopter rescue. A California Highway Patrol (CHP) helicopter flew within 15 feet of the sheer granite cliff and rescued the climber with a hoist evacuation system, officials said in a statement. Authorities have not released the climber’s name, age, or condition. “He was completely coherent and alert, despite a lot of blood loss,” flight officer and paramedic Scott Clays, who operated the helicopter’s hoist during the rescue, told Outside. “He just seemed very tough.” Power Dome is a 700-foot granite formation located near Courtright Reservoir, a popular climbing and camping area about two hours from Fresno, California. Authorities did not say which route the climber was on, but Power Dome has around 40 trad, sport, and toprope routes of varying difficulty. Around 12:45 P.M., CHP’s Coastal Division Air Operations said that it received an evacuation request for the fallen climber. During the climber’s ascent, he fell and hit the cliff face, Clays said. The climber lost a significant amount of blood from his injuries. His climbing partners removed his shirt and used it as a bandage to control the bleeding. Still connected to his ropes, the victim’s climbing partners lowered the man to a narrow ledge for rescuers to evacuate him from. “The ledge seemed to be shoulder-width,” Clays said, adding that it was about 200 feet off the ground. The Fresno County Sheriff’s Office, which assisted in the rescue, first sent in a drone to provide images of the climber’s condition and location. The CHP helicopter crew flew within 15 feet of sheer granite—the limit of their safety clearance—to execute a high-risk short-haul hoist rescue. Any closer, Clays said, and a “catastrophic” collision may have occurred. Responders used what’s known as a big-wall rescue to save the injured climber. The technique is often used in climbing-related accidents in Yosemite National Park and other parts of the Sierra Nevada. Here’s how it works: From the helicopter, a rescue technician dangles by a rope as the chopper inches closer to the wall—but not too close; any impact would be catastrophic, Clays said. During this time, the pilot hovers in place for 30 to 40 seconds in what Clays said is a constant battle with the wind to keep the chopper a safe distance from the wall. Once on the ledge, the rescuer disconnected his rope to stabilize and secure the injured climber for transport, and both were hoisted separately back into the helicopter. The climber was conscious and coherent when rescuers arrived, Clays said, and remained alert and helped keep himself steady while hanging from the helicopter. Once the helicopter delivered the victim to a waiting ambulance, Clays said he could see how much pain the injured man was in. “You could see the grimace in his face,” Clays said. “You know he was hurting.” In nearby Yosemite, where CHP crews train for similar big-wall rescues, records more than 100 climbing accidents each year.

item.title: Weighted Vests Aren’t New. They’re Just Humanity’s Oldest Workout, Rebranded.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.73
(Photo: Ayana Underwood/Canva) This article has been medically reviewed by Rachel MacPherson, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and ACE-certified personal trainer. One day at 3 A.M., a few weeks postpartum, I had my baby latched to my chest while scrolling social media in the dark. The algorithm had decided it knew what I needed: new moms in weighted vests walking through neighborhoods after dinner. The comments claiming they were “life-changing” were a good enough endorsement for me. I ordered one on Amazon at 3:17 A.M. My partner saw the box when it arrived, looked at the baby, and said, with the patience of someone who has learned to choose their battles: “Why would you need a weighted vest when you can just strap the baby to your body?” He had a point. But unfortunately, a weighted vest and a baby harness aren’t interchangeable. A weighted vest distributes weight evenly across the body, but my baby harness keeps my daughter’s weight concentrated at the front of my body where she sits. A front load shifts my center of mass forward. So, while my baby might feel great, my back doesn’t. Because using my baby harness as a substitute weighted vest was out, I grabbed the real thing instead. But I found myself asking two questions: Why and how did weighted vests and load-bearing exercise become a thing? And what were the benefits? I dug into the history of the weighted vest and interviewed a physical therapist and a former military specialist to get some answers. Here’s what I found out. Load-bearing training didn’t start with TikTok, or even the U.S. military. The Spartans called it the agoge. The agoge was a mandatory state-run program that peaked between the 5th and 4th centuries BCE and required boys, as early as age seven, to learn the art of battle. By the age of 20, they were considered members of the army, according to a 1983 historical paper about life in ancient Sparta. Some were hoplites, a type of Greek soldier who had to wear heavy armor and carry bulky weaponry for many miles. Their shields could weigh around 15 pounds and were about three feet wide. Armies have long assumed that a soldier who can carry weight over distance is more valuable than one who can’t. Cal Coblentz, a former survival, evasion, resistance, and escape specialist in the United States Air Force, said that, in his world, carrying an extra 50 pounds was a baseline. “In my survival training and missions, it wasn’t uncommon to have a pack that weighed over 100 pounds,” he told Outside. He also said carrying a heavy load built an invaluable sense of mental fortitude. To be clear: most commercial weighted vests do not go this high in weight. But wearing a weighted vest that adds a few more pounds offers several benefits. People in the military weren’t the only ones who figured out the benefits of carrying more weight. For years, before weighted vests became a fitness accessory, physical therapists used lighter versions to help people recover from injury and boost their cardiovascular endurance. Peter Mason, a Wyoming-based physical therapist who works with athletes, describes the clinical logic: an evenly distributed load challenges the body without isolating vulnerable joints. In older adults with osteoporosis, a vest introduces progressive loading during functional tasks without requiring grip strength or external implements, he said. For someone rebuilding after injury or managing bone loss, that distinction matters. When you add load to a walk with a weighted vest, the weight distributes the load across your body evenly rather than, say, carrying a set of dumbbells (or my 15-pound baby). Because the load sits close to your trunk rather than hanging from one hand, your postural muscles work harder to keep you upright, and no single joint takes the whole load. Moreover, wearing a weighted vest helps activate core muscles and improves lower-body strength. A vest also gives your cardiovascular system a workout. A 2026 study published in the journal Physiological Reports examined the cardiovascular effects of wearing a weighted vest in people with obesity. Some of the 51 participants wore a heavy weighted vest (15 percent of their body weight), and others wore a light vest (one percent of their body weight). Participants in the heavy-vest group showed increased heart rate and cardiovascular workload. There is an important caveat. Mason said that vests are a good option for general conditioning, but “they are not a substitute for high-load resistance training in athletes who need meaningful improvements in force capacity and resilience.” In other words, for an athlete who wants significant strength gains in their sport, weighted vest training won’t be as beneficial as resistance training with heavy weights. But for a new mom like me, a weighted vest is ideal because I can do bodyweight movements like lunges, squats, and push-ups while wearing it and boost my heart rate without putting too much strain on my body. Eventually, weighted vests were no longer limited to physical therapy practices. They gained popularity through many mediums and went mainstream. According to a 2025 Forbes article, the global weighted vest market is projected to reach $350 million by 2033. Professor and bestselling author Michael Easter wrote in his Substack, Two Percent—where he writes about the latest in fitness and health—that the New York Times credited his 2021 book The Comfort Crisis with kickstarting the weighted-vest craze. In May 2025, when Peloton added weighted-vest streaming classes to their workout library, instructor Rebecca Kennedy said in a Time article that members responded with something close to relief and that the “appetite for weighted vests has been really wild.” If you want to try weighted vests, Mason suggests starting with a vest that’s five percent of your body weight and doing one to two non-consecutive weighted-vest walking sessions per week. If you weigh 160 pounds, that means you’d start with a vest that’s about eight pounds. A reasonable upper target for most people is ten to 15 percent of their body weight, he said. (That would be a max of a 16- or 24-pound vest for a person who weighs 160 pounds.) The best way to gauge when you can take on heavier weight, he said, is to pay attention to how your body responds over time. If you’re using an eight-pound vest and your movement is solid, aren’t experiencing pain, and have minimal fatigue, you can increase the vest weight, he said. “Fit matters: the vest should be snug enough to minimize movement and friction, but not so tight that it restricts respiration, trunk motion, or natural gait mechanics,” Mason said. One other important callout is that a weighted vest might not be for everyone. Skip the vest, or talk to a clinician first, if you’re pregnant, recently postpartum, or managing pelvic floor symptoms like leaking or heaviness. The same goes for anyone with a known vertebral fracture, uncontrolled balance problems, or a spine condition. If you feel pain, dizziness, or pelvic pressure, take the vest off. Overall, weighted vests are trendy for a reason; they are a legitimate tool for boosting the cardiovascular benefits of a walk. But they are not a substitute for strength training. As for me, I’ll still strap my baby to my chest for a walk just to get her outside, then throw on my weighted vest when I need some extra oomph for my daily walk or bodyweight routine. About the medical reviewer: Rachel MacPherson is a certified strength and conditioning specialist, an ACE-certified personal trainer, and a PN1-certified nutrition coach. MacPherson has spent over a decade helping lifters trade bro science for actual results. She’s happily turned an obsession with evidence-based health into a full-time writing and strategy career, helping publications, wellness brands, and supplement companies tell smarter stories that people trust. She’s a stickler for science-backed training advice that respects the reader’s intelligence, with the ultimate goal of getting you under the bar with total confidence (or moving in whatever way feels best). Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Off-Road Vehicles Are Cool But Loud as Hell. Can Polaris’ New Transmission Fix That?
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.50
Overview: Outside tested the Polaris Xpedition, a side-by-side off-road vehicle, on 4WD roads in South Dakota’s Black Hills National Forest. The Xpedition features Polaris’ new NUMATIX Controlled CVT transmission, which uses air pressure to manage the clutch and reduce cabin noise by a claimed 40 percent compared to previous models. The vehicle has 114 horsepower, a 999cc engine, and 14 inches of ground clearance. The two-seat XP model starts at $40,499; the tested ADV5 model seats five and includes an enclosed rear cargo area. The rain storm comes on quick and turns to hail even quicker, so within a few minutes the dirt roads I’m driving in South Dakota’s Black Hills National Forest become bogged with thick mud and slick rock gardens. It’s perfect. I’m testing Polaris’ new Xpedition, an all-terrain vehicle designed to tackle tough 4WD roads while keeping the driver and passengers as comfortable as possible. The off-road capability is only half the story of this side-by-side. I’ve driven my share of off-road vehicles over the years, from four wheelers on my buddy’s farm to snowmobiles in Colorado and my cherished 4Runner built for overlanding. But the side-by-side is a unique category of off-road vehicle. Instead of the open-aired all-terrain vehicles that are designed to get one or two people from point A to point B through rugged terrain, the side-by-side is designed to tackle the same rugged terrain in relative comfort, with closed cabs and surprisingly plush seats. During the last several years, side-by-sides have gotten more posh, with climate control, power windows, sound systems, and infotainment screens. These side-by-sides are so capable, and so comfortable, that there are people in Utah and Arizona (where it’s legal to drive them on the roads) that use them as their primary vehicle. I know a guy that drives his side-by-side to the golf course on a regular basis here in North Carolina. But there’s always been one glaring issue with these enclosed-cab side-by-sides. They’re loud as hell. The engines have to work at such high RPMs to power these machines through technical terrain that your entire ride is accompanied by the high-pitch sound of an engine working overtime. Imagine a car stuck in second gear at 40 mph. That’s what these side-by-sides sound like, and that ever-present hum gets trapped inside the enclosed cabs with no place to go. The first time I drove a side-by-side, I thought the transmission was broken and the vehicle wouldn’t shift. Some side-by-side owners will muffle the sound through after-market sound-proofing, while others wear ear plugs. The loud noise of the engine is enough to turn some people off of the vehicles altogether, so Polaris decided to address the issue, taking a big leap forward in terms of comfort with their latest innovation, the NUMATIX Controlled CVT. This new transmission uses air pressure to manipulate the clutch and deliver a quieter engine at cruising speeds. I’m not going to pretend to understand the engineering principles behind governing the transmission with pressurized air, but I will tell you that the new Xpedition is noticeably quieter than the previous model. Polaris claims that their new side-by-sides with NUMATIX are 40 percent quieter than previous models. You can experience the difference first hand by toggling back and forth between Comfort mode (with the NUMATIX engaged) and Sport mode (NUMATIX disengaged) while driving. The difference is immediately apparent, especially when you reach cruising speeds on a dirt road. The vehicles aren’t as quiet as a minivan, but they are significantly quieter than any other side-by-side I’ve ever driven. What this means is you can hold a conversation with passengers in the vehicle. You can tell your daughter to get off her iPad without raising your voice. You can listen to an audiobook. I drove the Xpedition for several hours through the Black Hills and listened to music the entire time. The Xpedition has had a bluetooth-enabled speaker system for a while, but there was no point using it in the past because the engine noise drowned out anything you’d play. But with the NUMATIX engaged, I could hear every word and note from Tyler Childers as I dropped into big mud puddles and climbed rock gardens. (Side note: You should always listen to country music while driving off-road.) And the Xpedition still performs like a champ in rugged terrain, providing plenty of power to muscle through technical situations. It has 114 horsepower in a 999cc engine that offers plenty of torque for rock crawling, and 14 inches of ground clearance so you won’t get jammed up in the rock garden. For comparison, the race-inspired Polaris RZR Pro R4 has the same horsepower but in a 1997cc engine and 16 inches of ground clearance. So the Xpedition might not be the vehicle you’re looking for if you’re hoping to compete in the Baja 1000, but for the majority of off-road users, it has plenty of power to get us where we want to go. And that’s the real draw of these vehicles. They’ll go pretty much anywhere you want to go in a very user-friendly “point and go” package. You don’t have to be an experienced off-road driver to operate this side-by-side through the gnarly bits. Yes, you can get in trouble—I’ve seen people roll their side-by-side because they carried too much speed through corners with loose tread—but for the most part, these vehicles open up hard-charging, off-road adventures to average drivers like myself. Going from a 4WD vehicle, like my F-150 truck, to a side-by-side is like moving from a cruiser bike to a full-suspension mountain bike on technical singletrack. The terrain is so much less intimidating and you’re no longer limited by the tool at your disposal. That leads me to the ultimate question with a niche vehicle like this: Who is the new Polaris Xpedition’s target consumer? First, it’s for someone with money to spend. The Xpedition ain’t cheap. Starting at $40,499 for the two-seater XP, it’s no wonder some people use these side-by-sides as their daily driver. But there are plenty of people reading this column that have dedicated off-road vehicles, and the new Xpedition might be an option for those off-road enthusiasts that want a vehicle dedicated to exploring gnarly backcountry. The Xpedition goes places a 4Runner, or even a Jeep, can’t go. And it can haul plenty of your gear and your people along the way. The Xpedition ADV5 that I drove fits five (or four and a dog) and has an enclosed rear cargo area (36″ long x 47″ wide and 13″ tall) big enough for your Yeti cooler and camping gear. You can load your bike rack into the hitch and even put a roof rack on top. I’ve driven models of the Xpedition while toting rooftop tents deep into the Grand Canyon backcountry through narrow canyons I would never take my 4Runner. And with the new, quieter Xpedition, you can have a vehicle that offers that same kind of access and carrying capacity without having to wear ear plugs and scream over engine noise.

item.title: Review: Lems Trail Thrasher Pro Shoes
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.18
The Lems Trail Thrasher Pro is a zero-drop shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole for people who want a hiking shoe that is more robust than a trail runner but less technical than an approach shoe. With a large toe box, durable Nubuck upper, and waterproof membrane, the Trail Thrasher Pro is a versatile, durable shoe that works well for day hikes, wet-weather walks, travel, and everyday outdoor use. - Gender: Men's (Women's Available) - Weight per shoe: 15.2 oz - Wide sizes: No - Drop: Zero - Stack height: 16mm - Outsole: Vibram Megagrip - Waterproofing: Yes - Upper: Nubuck - Fit: True to Size Fit and Comfort The shoe’s most noticeable feature is its generous toe box, which lets your toes spread and splay naturally. The zero-drop platform lets your foot move more like it would barefoot, reducing fatigue and improving balance on uneven ground. Cushioning is modest but adequate. If you prefer more support or more underfoot padding like a max trail runner, these will feel too minimal. Break-in time is immediate. I could wear them right away without any fit issues. Protection I don't look at my feet when I hike, so I like good toe protection just in case I bash into a rock. Like all serious hikers, I've had my share of broken toes and toenails. The Trail Thrasher scores high in terms of toe and foot protection with hefty front-toe kicks and a nubuck upper that's unlikely to split or get shredded at the corners of the toebox. Waterproofing The waterproof lining helps keep feet dry when worn in wet grass, shallow puddles, and muddy conditions. The tongue and upper also help prevent water and trail debris from entering around the laces. Because this is a low-cut shoe, it cannot protect against water that rises above the collar. Deep puddles and stream crossings will likely leave your feet wet. The waterproof construction can feel warmer than a non-waterproof shoe in hotter weather, but warmer when there's a chill in the air. Nevertheless, for ordinary wet-weather hiking and daily walking, the protection is useful. Traction and Trail Performance The Vibram Megagrip outsole provides solid grip on packed earth, gravel, roots, and rocky inclines. The shoe is stable on maintained trails while remaining comfortable when the route varies between roots and rocks, gravel, or pavement. But the Trail Thrasher is not as flexible a shoe as many zero-drop trail runners and is much sturdier, somewhere in between a trail runner and an approach shoe. That takes a little time to get used to, but it's useful if you want to use them across a wide range of surfaces, from trails to gravel and pavement. Recommendation The Lems Trail Thrasher Pro is a comfortable and versatile choice for day hikers and walkers who prefer a wide, natural zero-drop fit. Its strengths include a zero-drop platform, a spacious toe box, waterproof protection, a grippy Vibram outsole, and durable construction. If it has one weakness, it's the styling. Its plain black look is not the most appealing, even compared with the outlandish color palettes of trail runners and other athletic shoes. Disclosure: Lems donated shoes for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. The non-waterproof version appears to come in much better colors, if that isn’t a must have feature for you I wonder if this would be a good choice for the Arizona Trail, maybe without the waterproofing because of the heat. I’m thinking a bit more resistant to grabbing sharp spiny things, better at keeping pebbles out, and sturdier instead of the mesh-toed Topos I use now. What do you think? If it’s hot, they’d be on the warm side.

item.title: Wild Thing Canister Stove Windscreen
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.58
The Wild Thing Canister Stove Windscreen works with most small backpacking stoves and small cook pots. This simple folding screen has a magnet that attaches to your gas canister and holds the screen in place. It provides plenty of ventilation to prevent your gas canister from overheating (and exploding), while improving stove efficiency and reducing boil times. - Weight: 2.65 oz - Material: Aluminum - Folded Dimensions: 3.75″ x 3.25″ x 1″ - Open Dimensions: 6.75″ x 3″ x 3.75″ What I like about this windscreen is that it works with all my canister stoves. Like most backpackers, I own a couple of canister stoves which I use in different circumstances or when the mood strikes me. Cook Pot Packability While a stove-independent canister stove windscreen is great, it's hard to know whether you can pack it, along with all your stove system components, into your cookpot for easy transport. I happen to place a very high value on this level of packability, as do most backpackers. Just because I can pack the Wild Thing Windscreen, a small gas canister, an MSR Pocket Rocket, and a plastic folding canister stand into an Evernew Ultralight Titanium Cookpot doesn't mean you can replicate my success with your cook system components. The problem is the shape of the Wild Thing Windscreen, which isn't very space-optimal, either folded or unfolded. While I could pack it into my cook pot above, I had to swap a larger canister for a smaller one to fit everything. Flat Cat Gear, which also makes canister stove windscreens, addresses this issue by emphasizing packability and fuel savings, but it limits the number of stoves and, in some cases, the stove-and-pot combinations it supports. Of course, you can opt to just use a Jetboil or a Wind Burner stove system, which hardwires the stove and pot combination, but those stove systems tend to be comparatively heavier. Assessement The Wild Thing Canister Stove Windscreen is a good choice for backpackers who want one windscreen that works with several small canister stoves. Its low weight, simple magnetic attachment, and broad compatibility are its main advantages. It can improve stove performance in windy conditions without committing the user to a stove-specific system. Its main limitation is packability. Backpackers who want to fit every cooking component into a single pot may prefer a more compact, stove-specific design. For users who value flexibility more than maximum space efficiency, however, the Wild Thing is a useful and well-conceived accessory. Overall assessment: Recommended for multi-stove users; less suitable for those who prioritize the smallest possible cook system. Disclosure: Wild Things donated a stove screen for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Thanks for this post, I’ve been looking for something like this for awhile!

item.title: Review: Tarptent Moment Tent Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.31
The Tarptent Moment is an ultralight, single-person tunnel tent with dual side vestibules that doesn't require trekking poles to pitch. If it's raining, you can set up the rain fly first, independently of the inner tent. You can also set up the rain fly and use it like a tarp shelter, without the inner tent. Finally, you can set up the inner tent by itself for stargazing in fine weather, though it takes a little extra configuration and isn't the main reason you'd buy this tent. - Type: Double-wall Tent (with Fly first option) - Poles: 1 (no trekking poles required) - Doors and Vestibules: 2 - Interior Pockets: 2 - Model tested: Siliconized polyester with carbon fiber pole - Weight: 29.85 oz / 846 g - Rain Fly: 15D 100% silicone-coated ripstop high-tenacity polyester (5000mm+) - Floor: 20D 100% silicone-coated ripstop high-tenacity polyester (5000mm+) - Inner tent dimensions: 84″ x 42″ (center) tapering to 24″ (ends) with 39″ of height - Outer (covered) dimensions: 102″ x 72 (center) tapering to 24″ (ends) with 42″ of height - Seam-Sealing: Required (have Tarptent do this for you) - Minimum number of stakes to pitch: 2, more recommended. I first encountered the Moment when I met Tarptent's owner, Henry Shires, in Scotland during the final days of my first coast-to-coast backpacking trip in the 2010 TGO Challenge, as our routes converged in Glen Esk on the way to the east coast town of Montrose. Henry tested a prototype of Tarptent's Moment Tent on that hike, and I've wanted to test the final product ever since. This was my chance. Variations The Moment is available in several fabric versions, including siliconized polyester, Dyneema Composite Fabric (26.05 oz / 738 g), and Challenge Sailcloth UltraTNT v1.5 composite fabric (31.5 oz / 893 g). It's also available with two different inner tent options: one with mesh walls for warm weather, and the second with solid walls to retain greater warmth in winter conditions. Similarly, there are three pole options: the carbon fiber pole works well in moderate conditions, while the aluminum poles are recommended for high winds or heavy snow loads. For three-season use, most US-based users will opt for the tent in whatever material you prefer, the mesh inner tent, and carbon fiber tent poles. I prefer a siliconized polyester tent over Dyneema because it's more compressible, and I don't feel the weight savings are worth spending twice as much on this tent. Dyneema tents also tend to let in a lot of light, which makes it hard for me to sleep on long summer days, whereas the inside of a silpoly tent tends to be darker. Fly First Setup If it's raining, you can set up the Moment rain fly before the inner tent, but you'll typically keep the two connected and set them up at the same time. The inner connects to the fly with toggles, so you can disconnect it if it's raining out and pack it first while staying under cover if you want to keep it as dry as possible. When you set it up again, you can raise the wet rain fly and reconnect the dry inner tent underneath: there are 11 dowels and two mitten hooks to connect. Most double-wall tents sold in the US don't have this capability, although it's fairly common on tents manufactured by European companies (Hilleberg, Exped, Terra Nova, and others.) To pitch the Moment, you insert a collapsible tent pole into the center sleeve to create the hoop. Then you pull the two tent ends out and stake them. You really only need two tent stakes to pitch the tent on soil you can get a stake into, although more stakes can be added to loops positioned along the hoop and perimeter of the tent. Each end of the tent forms a triangular space, created by short carbon fiber struts that slot into channels at the ends. These are called pitchlocks, and they create tunnels at each end of the tent for enhanced airflow. They also lift the tent ends off the ground and increase interior space. Without them, the rain fly would touch the ground, much like the sides of a pyramid tent, and shorten the effective length of the tent. Tarptent uses them on many of its other tents, and they're a signature feature unique to the brand. The ends of the pitchlocks are covered with solid fabric, secured along one side with Velcro. You can also roll the fabric open to let more air flow through the tent, without worrying about rain getting inside, because the ends of the inner tent are recessed. When packing, you can remove the carbon fiber struts that form the pitchlock from their channels, but most people leave them inserted and roll them up inside the tent body. Removing them makes the tent more compressible if you want to store it horizontally in a narrow backpack, but it increases setup time. To remove the center hoop pole in one piece, keep it sharply curved as you slide it out of the sleeve. This prevents the ferrules from separating, so you can pull it out in one continuous length before breaking it down and packing it up. It took me years to learn this trick (credit: Tim at Slingfin), and it really works. The regular setup time is incredibly fast with the Moment (provided the inner and outer tents are already attached), since you only need to insert the center pole and stake out the ends. It's really astounding. It's even fairly manageable in a stiff breeze, as long as you stake out one of the ends and keep the hoop close to the ground before staking out the second end. That said, you'd still want to add a few more stakes if there is any wind, using the numerous anchor points surrounding the body tent. While the Moment isn't a freestanding tent, its hooped structure makes it feel like one. To make it truly freestanding, you can add a long carbon fiber pole (extra $$) that arches over the length of the tent and slots into the end guyout points, so you can pick the entire tent up and move it around freely. This freestanding mode can be particularly useful for added strength for snow loads in winter, reducing flapping in high winds, or for places where it's difficult to stake down the ends of the tent, like a beach or rocky ledge. I don't consider it a must-have for normal use. Once erected, the tent opens along the center zipper, allowing you to open both vestibule side doors completely or partially for great airflow. The center zippers on both sides are reinforced at the bottom by buckles to take pressure off the zipper, since zippers are the most delicate part of any tent. Top vents also help vent water vapor, and magnets secure the vestibule doors when rolled up instead of old-school toggles. Unlike many ultralight tents, the sides of the Moment also reach the ground in the style of British tents. This blocks wind and rain and provides better heat retention. Many ultralight tents made for the US ‘audience' leave a much larger gap between the rain fly and the ground, which helps explain why the Moment and other Tarptent models, such as the Tarptent Scarp, are favored by UK hillwalkers and wild campers. Recommendation The Tarptent Moment is an excellent choice for solo backpackers who want an ultralight tent without relying on trekking poles. Its fast, simple pitch, two vestibules, excellent ventilation, and useful fly-first setup make it especially practical in wet and changeable weather. The ability to use the fly on its own also adds flexibility for winter trips, while the solid construction and low-sided design provide better protection from wind and rain than many ultralight tents. Spacious and comfortable, the Moment provides a versatile shelter for the discerning backpacker who wants to stay “in the Moment.” Disclosure: Tarptent loaned the author a tent. I had the first Dyneema version of this tent and loved it. I was super sad to sell it because it’s difficult to change clothes inside due to a lower ceiling height. It is a rock solid design in bad weather. I spent a couple nights on the shore of Lake Superior in October with the mesh interior and slept comfortably despite the cold wind. I had the cross pole for freestanding capability, and it’s extremely useful in rocky conditions like northern Minnesota. No stakes needed to drive into the impossibly rocky ground. In fact I rarely used stakes, just the poles. Great tent, just make the ceiling higher.

item.title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.79
‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food. The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended. “Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home. Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses. Ingredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work. Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli. Högbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from. At Gammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby, The Old Mill is now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed. At Bergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations. But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon and böckling (hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills. Driving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce. At Teve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930. Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs. At nearby Järvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.” In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie. Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses. Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb. It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious. It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too. The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. For more information visit gastrikland.se and destinationhalsingland.se. Högbo Brukshotell has doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&B Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: ‘I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine’: readers’ favourite foodie experiences in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.00
Simple sardines in the Algarve Last August, the smoky aroma of grilled sardines drifting over the beach in Portimão woke me up from my sunbathing on the beach. Attracted by the aroma of barbecued fish, we found ourselves in the old port where, for €12, I was served two delicious sandwiches on rustic bread of sardines in garlic and olive oil, with a small cold beer. I sat down, ate and chatted with locals on benches at simple communal tables. The important thing seemed to be to enjoy food together. The next morning, a reenactment of the fishing boats arriving loaded with fish, as they once were, was a real spectacle – complete with guitar playing, drum-banging and excited seagulls whirling and wailing above in the hope of a feast. Later, concerts and dancing animated the town as the party for the sardine festival went on well into the night. Cooking demos and dishes including sardine-based soup and salads, added to the enjoyment. I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine. Joe A family dinner in the Faroe Islands My wife and I visited the Faroe Islands a few years ago, where we took part in heimablídni, a concept where traditional Faroese food is served in a home. We found it to be one of the best ways to experience the Faroes and a unique experience to share a meal with a local family. Homecooked dishes showcase ingredients from the surrounding sea and mountains. We were served smoked salmon from the host’s own smoker, lamb, potatoes and traditional specialities, all accompanied with great conversation about Faroese life and traditions. Sitting around a family table makes the experience feel personal and authentic. Mike A vegan feast in Sicily As a vegan who loves trying local cuisine, the combination of warm hospitality and a high proportion of locals with a lactose intolerance makes Sicily the ideal foodie getaway. Having hiked to the top of Monte Pellegrino in 35C heat, we popped into a small nondescript street-food shop (the only place that was open) and were delighted to find panelle – delicious crispy chickpea-flour fritters served in sesame bread. We ate them overlooking Palermo harbour. That evening, we tried Haiku, a vegan restaurant with reimagined classics based on dishes such as carbonara and tiramisu. It was so good we kept ordering more and more courses until we could barely move. Esther Strong spirits and small plates in Greece The city of Volos is famous for its Tsipouradika – tavernas that serve tsipouro, a strong spirit made from pomace, the stems, skins and seeds that are left over from wine making. It comes plain or infused with botanicals and anise, and is served with ice and water. Each glass you order arrives with a different small plate or meze. It could be grilled peppers, sundried octopus, a spicy cheese spread or smoked mackerel. You take pot luck as to what the patron fancies dishing up that day. Barbara The perfect snack to pair with Lithuanian beer In Vilnius, we came across the ultimate food pairing for the fantastic beers available there in the form of kepta duona – deep-fried rye bread with garlic and cheese. Every bar has a slightly different version – raw, roast or confit garlic with cream, melted or simply grated cheese. A heavenly snack that could easily become your main meal. Natalie Vegan delights in the patisseries of Paris Being an unfortunate combination of a foodie and a vegan, I was prepared for a weekend of staring longingly into patisserie windows when heading to Paris earlier this summer. I was not prepared for the unbridled joy awaiting me at the Land & Monkeys boulangeries/patisseries scattered across the capital. It began with an outrageously creamy raspberry petit gateaux from its Montmartre branch, followed by the unbelievable fluff and flake of a croissant aux champignons in the Marais the next day. A parting madeleine for the Eurostar on our last day was the pièce de résistance. Elinor Pasta with pears in Bologna It was in Bologna, Italy’s self-proclaimed food capital, where I sampled the city’s signature dish of tortellini. We stumbled across Rosarose Bistrot, enticed by tables with red-checked cloths set in the middle of a cobblestone road. I enjoyed shells stuffed with tangy gorgonzola cheese and chunks of caramelised pears, a fruit I would usually avoid, but I placed trust in the regional delicacy. The fruit’s sweetness blended harmoniously with the strong cheese flavour; crispy and soft fried bread known as crescentine, was used to soak up the remaining sauce. It was only right to mark this culinary experience with a small tortellini keyring from a nearby gift shop, filled with various merchandise emblazoned with the pasta shell. Caitlin Catalonia’s ultimate slow-food festival Last year, I discovered the ultimate slow-food festival – the Snail Feast of Lleida (L’Aplec del Caragol), 100 miles west of Barcelona. Over a long weekend, there was music, dancing, cooking and feasting, all in celebration of the tiny mollusc. Entrance to the festival is free, and visitors can enjoy traditional snail dishes in tents, local restaurants or simply in the town squares. I had two helpings of snails a la gormanda, cooked in a sauce of spicy paprika and herbs. Since attending the festival, I have been treading carefully in my garden in case I harm what I discovered are delicate and delicious creatures. Helen Heavenly cakes in Slovenia Having travelled by train from Bristol down through the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Italy, we reached our penultimate stop, Lake Bled. We’d been awed by the beautiful Swiss alpine scenery, but Bled took it up a notch. After a day of cycling from Bled to Lake Bohinj and back, we refuelled on the local delicacy, Bled cake, a sumptuously smooth set custard encased in the lightest of mille-feuille pastry and topped with whipped cream. Imagine an English custard slice, only a million times better. It was so welcome after a day in the Slovenian mountain air, we made it a holiday habit. A Bled cake a day until we had to come home! Sara Winning tip: delicious seafood soup in Spain Few meals linger in the memory like a proper Asturian sopa de pescado y marisco (seafood soup). After kayaking 10 miles down the Sella River, my reward in the town of Arriondas wasn’t a humble bowl of soup – it was a whole pan! Every flavour shone through in a broth packed with white fish, prawns and sweet crab claws, so extraordinarily rich it almost brought me to tears. I devoured it all, skipping the rest of the courses without regret. Years later in Gijón, history repeated itself. Even my soup-sceptical husband declared it the best he had ever tasted. In Asturias, fish soup isn’t a starter. It’s an obsession in a pot. Oksana Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Burrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, Italy
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.45
‘I don’t eat mozzarella outside Puglia,” says our friend Savio. “It’s not the same.” Savio is a very opinionated foodie, so I take his words with a pinch of good Puglian sea salt (see below). He was adamant about the superiority of the stretched-curd cheese from his home turf. Puglia is also the birthplace of ingredient du jour burrata, which originated in Andria, a few miles from Savio’s home town of Barletta. Andria forms one part of the triangular Barletta-Andria-Trani (BAT) province, but despite the cheese connection and Barletta having miles of palm-backed, sandy beaches, it is often passed over for better-known parts of Puglia. So I asked Savio’s company, Unexpected Italy, an app that calls itself the antidote to overtourism, to organise a trip to the area. About a century ago, in the hills outside Andria, farmer Lorenzo Bianchino was snowed in and couldn’t get his milk to market. To save what he could, he revived an old technique for preserving butter (burro, hence burrata), stuffing cream mixed with mozzarella scraps (stracciatella) in a casing of the stretched-curd cheese. There are now several burrata makers in Andria, the most famous being Caseificio Olanda, which offers demos, tastings and a museum. Late one morning, we watch Riccardo “Dino” Olanda, son of the founders, work his magic. He adds almost-boiling water to the curds, then mixes with hands red from doing this every day. As he stretches and massages the curds, a smooth velvety mass forms. “See how it’s shiny?” he says. “Means it’s ready.” Working quickly, he squeezes out round lumps between thumb and forefinger into the familiar mozzarella balls. This action is mozzare, hence the name. He also makes little knots and plaits before moving on to burrata. Taking a warm mozzarella ball, he works it into a hollow bag with his fingers then fills it with cream and stracciatella before tying the top with string. Afterwards, a dairy-heavy meal totally worth the cholesterol and calories: mozzarella and burrata to start, then bread with chunks of caciocavallo (a stretched-curd cheese), and a dessert of heart-shaped fresh ricotta with strawberry jam or cocoa. And, I have to say, Savio is right. The mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a gorgeous cheesy, umami flavour; the salt and flavour leached out by the whey the cheeses later sit in. How will I ever settle for Tesco Finest after this? Over the next few days, eating our way around the province’s restaurants and food producers, I wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way round. Barletta sees few foreign tourists, but it is full of Italian life. There are lots of independent shops, a Norman castle and cathedral to visit, and every evening people pour into the bars, clubs and gelaterie of the sette strade, seven parallel streets in the old town. Down the coast, Trani, with its sea-facing romanesque cathedral and pretty harbour, attracts some tourists, but they are not in evidence at 7am when the fishing boats return. The men complain of rough seas and a poor catch, but from the back of the boats they’re soon selling mullet, octopus, skate, fat sea snails, monkfish and palombo (small shark) to restaurateurs and fishmongers. Thirtysomething Nicola says he went out at midday and got back at 3am. When does he sleep? “Never.” A fifth-generation fisher, he began helping on the boats aged six. We’ll eat fish later, but today is for pizza. Portento in Barletta is run by food nut Luigi Lacerenza. He has us try so many local products as antipasti – caprino goat’s cheese tasting of green mountains, grilled caciocavallo from an old couple who make just six a week and small-batch salami – that we’re almost too full for pizzas. But they are wonderful: one with sausage, olives, oyster mushrooms and yellow tomatoes; another with aubergines and grated cacioricotta. In Cerignola, west of Barletta, Rosario Didonna used the money he won on a TV standup competition to turn his family’s deli into a cosy, wood- panelled restaurant, U’ Vulèsce (dialect for “peckish”). Rosario knows fishers by name, works with small farmers and wine producers, and invites nonne from all over southern Italy to demonstrate recipes in his kitchens. We start with tasty goat prosciutto and plum-sized local olives called bella di Cerignola. Then an unforgettable prawn tartare served in sea urchin shells, hairy crab spaghetti (“the juice is better than lobster”), octopus with bean puree, and sea bass with orange mayo. He waves away our thanks: “I’m doing the best job in the world!” Nicola Barbera at Masseria Barbera, a farm restaurant in the Alta Murgia national park, is equally inspired, but rather by what grows on the estate founded by his great-great-great-great-grandfather Riccardo, who fought with Garibaldi. Exuberantly bouncing us around the farm – it produces 90% of what the 100-cover restaurant needs – he shows us olives and vines, but also the “weeds” growing around them. “They’re eatable,” he says, grabbing handfuls of peppery rocket, and bitter but delicate wild chicory. From the abundant kitchen garden, he makes eight varieties of tomato sauce. We tuck into a lot of this for lunch: a pie with white onions, anchovy and sultanas; courgettes with mint and garlic; spaghetti with yellow tomatoes. (“I call it bastard sauce,” says Nicola. “Those tomatoes take three times as long to pick.”) Then, something I never thought I’d eat: grilled donkey fillet. I feel bad about the patient, mild-tempered beasts, but this is healthy, low-fat food, never intensively farmed. It’s also the best meat I’ve ever tasted. Good food is made better by good olive oil, and producers here include Muraglia, known for organic oil in hand-painted, rainbow-stripe ceramic bottles, and Sabino Leone, offering tours of its ancient groves and oil mill for €15, plus tastings. This area also offers plenty to do between meals. Barletta was the home of Italian painter Giuseppe De Nittis, who hung out with Degas and Manet, and took part in the first impressionist exhibition in Paris, in 1874. Over 200 of his works are now displayed in the 16th-century Palazzo della Marra (€6). At Europe’s biggest salt pan, Salina Margherita di Savoia, there’s an expanse of peaceful ponds with a snow-white salt mountain to climb. Another day, an exhilarating ebike ride in the Alta Murgia with Filippo Tito of Cycling ’n’ Trek, through dense forest to peer with awe into an old bauxite mine that resembles a mini grand canyon. We get back ravenous, but in this corner of northern Puglia, that’s a blessing. Where to stay Until this century, Barletta had little tourist accommodation. Pick of the few B&Bs is Antica Dimora (doubles from €97), a restored 17th-century palazzo run by Lilly and Riccardo Manna. There are three smart bedrooms with lots of plants and breakfast features different local specialities each day. Lama di Luna (doubles from €230) is an organic farm in deep countryside, with six rooms set around an 18th-century stone courtyard. A well and solar panels make it energy and water self-sufficient; half of its 200 hectares are left wild, the rest are planted with olives, vines, almonds and cherries. There’s a cinema, a library and a large pool shaded by 600-year-old olive trees. Where (else) to eat Barletta’s 60-year-old Mosé bakery is revered for its krapfen filled doughnuts and sourdough croissants. There are also chocolates, ice-cream and cakes, all housemade, and great coffee. Puglia has hundreds of gelaterie but experts rate Scoop in Canosa (which is called Puglia’s “Little Rome” for its catacombs, temple ruins and Roman bridge). Francesco Di Nunno makes ice-cream with local seasonal ingredients: raspberry and strawberry sorbets are available only in early summer; percoca yellow peach until mid-August. There’s affordable fine dining at chef Luciano Matera’s Il Turracciolo in central Andria. Highlights for me are broad bean and chicory “meatballs”, bright green inside; a “hidden mushroom” under baked eggy topping; and pasta discs with whole and pureed green beans and peas. At A Sud dell’Anima, chef Nadia Tamburrano uses modern techniques and hyper-local ingredients to make food of astonishing quality for a small hilltop town (Minervino, population under 8,000). Her antipasti explode with flavour thanks to house-cured capers and homemade mustard, syrups and purees. A main of sweetbreads wrapped in intestines feels a bit out-there, but is delicious, the intestines crispy as crackling. The trip was organised by Unexpected Italy, which offers personalised itineraries for Barletta and the surrounding area Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Solo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.02
I did my first solo hike during a sunny September, seven years ago. After a summer of feeding and ferrying four noisy teenagers (and their friends) around, I was exhausted. But despite being bone tired, I had barely moved. I yearned, above all, for time on my own, for the chance to walk without interruption (and at the pace I chose), and for the silence of some empty wilderness. But I was nervous. Not of being on my own, but of what might happen to me with no one around to help (breaking a bone, encountering a psychopath, being chased by a bull, getting fatally lost). I could have found a companion or joined a group, but my need for silence and solitude outweighed my fears. It seems that many women feel the same: in the UK, the proportion of women solo hiking surged by 27% between 2020 and 2022. In America, 41 % of female hikers report regularly walking alone. And yet many women, although keen to do something similar, feel intimidated. According to researchers at the Munich University of Applied Sciences who are studying solo female walkers, 30% of women interviewed said they would like to hike solo but are hesitant. In truth, women have long enjoyed a tradition of solo walking. From religious pilgrims to goat herders to 19th-century adventurers, there have always been women wandering, radically alone, through wild landscapes. But for those new to it, I’d say the best way to overcome your fear is to do it – and I’ve learned some simple ways to make the experience fun, not daunting. That first solo hike followed a French canal. It was beautiful but sometimes felt a little too abandoned. It was also bereft of facilities, and frequently involved a long, complicated walk to my accommodation. So here are some of the things I now look for in a route: no discomfort-inducing stretches of urban wasteland; wide open landscapes (ridgeways, cliffs and hilltops are favourites); excellently waymarked, well-maintained paths (like national trails); navigation-lite routes that follow rivers, (lively) canals or coastlines; and countries/regions with a tradition of hiking. I do my research with care, and I’ve always returned home exhilarated, revitalised and high on my own bravado. I’ve learned to avoid the trails where I might feel uncomfortable. I know now which landscapes calm me, and which trails are (almost) impossible to lose my way on. For the last seven years, I’ve walked solo every autumn. Indeed, autumn is the perfect time for a liberating, empowering and restorative (solo) hike. Falling leaves improve visibility, temperatures are pleasant, and the days are still long enough to ensure I can reach my destination before dark. Importantly, there are lots of other walkers around – but without summer’s hordes – and the landscape is autumnally crisp and colourful. If you’re new to solo walking, start with a single day. If you want to try walking for multiple days, consider paying for your luggage to be transported (or use a specialist tour operator who will plot your route, arrange accommodation and move bags). Otherwise pack as lightly as possible. Take a non-digital map and a stick/walking poles, and let someone know your arrival time. Study every aspect of your route – including transport options and the weather – before you set off. FOUR GREAT ROUTES FOR SOLO HIKERS The Bernese Oberland, Switzerland The Swiss Alps are one of my favourite places to walk alone. Swiss women are keen solo hikers (so no one bats an eyelid at yet another single woman), the waymarking is superb and the scenery is jaw-dropping. Because this is a nation of farmers and hikers, there are always people (and a phone signal) around. And yet – because of the mountainous terrain – there’s often a genuine sense of wilderness and solitude. The Bernese Oberland is overrun with tourists in summer, but come to this Unesco world heritage site in autumn and you’ll be walking, calmly, in the footsteps of dozens of 19th-century women who once came here specifically to hike alone. Base yourself in the car-free villages of Wengen or Mürren, and expect to find farm-cafes with homemade cakes and honesty boxes in the remotest of spots. The South Downs Way From Eastbourne To Kingston, near Lewes Time 2 days Distance 19 miles The UK has plenty of well-kept trails, but top of my list is the (expansive, clearly signposted) South Downs Way. In summer the Eastbourne to Alfriston clifftop stretch heaves with tourists, but in autumn you’ll share the panoramic views – dazzling sea, dramatic chalk cliffs – with a handful of dogwalkers. Just a few steps off the trail are cultural hotspots like the pretty village of Alfriston, Charleston Farmhouse (museum home of the Bloomsbury set), and Rodmell, where you can visit Virginia Woolf’s house. So you’ll never feel completely disconnected. The Cleveland Way From Saltburn To Filey Time 4 days Distance 52 miles The Cleveland Way was the UK’s second official national trail, meaning the route is well maintained, the signage is excellent and the scenery is glorious, covering coastline and windblown moors. The moors can feel bleakly exposed in the wrong weather, so opt for the four-day coastal section, Saltburn to Filey, with its quirky towns and villages. This is Yorkshire so expect plenty of conversation with passing walkers and the chance to feel romantically windswept – an intoxicating blend for the solo hiker who wants to feel alone in nature, but not too alone. The Fishermen’s Trail, southern Portugal From Praia da Luz To Sagres Time 3 days Distance 27 miles The Fishermen’s Trail is far too hot in summer, but when I went (November) the temperature was just right, the sea was warm enough to swim in, and there were enough solo female hikers to feel pleasantly companioned. With some rocky scrambling to make one feel suitably youthful, and sufficient sandy coves to squeeze in a siesta, this route (a chain of old fishing villages) also has abundant, inexpensive accommodation and fresh seafood galore. Like other sea-hugging routes it’s (mostly) impossible to get lost – just follow the coastline. I’ll leave the last word to writer Mathilde Blind, who (aged 19) walked alone through the Bernese Oberland in 1860 (no phone, no GPS, no bra, no waterproof trousers): “For once I felt truly free.” Annabel Abbs is the author of The Walking Cure and Windswept: Why Women Walk. She was a guest of InnTravel on its Coastal Algarve and Fishermen’s Trail route, and of MACS Adventures on its Highlights of the Bernese Oberland route. Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Air Canada’s Aeroplan program: The ultimate guide to earning and redeeming points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.48
Air Canada’s Aeroplan program: The ultimate guide to earning and redeeming points Editor's Note Air Canada's Aeroplan loyalty program is one of the most valuable Star Alliance airline programs — and it's one worth knowing, even if you don't travel to Canada. Aeroplan still uses published award charts for most partner flights, a rarity in a loyalty world increasingly driven by dynamic pricing. Plus, it charges low fees on award tickets and lets you add stopovers to one-way tickets for just 5,000 extra points.
