item.title: Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Which card is best for Delta loyalists?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.26
Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Which card is best for Delta loyalists? Editor's Note If you ask a Delta loyalist what credit card they have, they'll more than likely respond with either the American Express Platinum Card® or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card. Either of these cards makes a great case for a spot in a Delta fan's wallet; despite that, they have enough differences to make it important to carefully consider your traveling style before committing to one or the other. Committed Delta flyers will likely find the Delta Reserve more appealing, but travelers who place a high value on flexibility and lounge access may get more out of the Amex Platinum. Here's a full comparison of the key similarities and differences between these two cards, so you can choose the right premium card for your Delta flights. Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: At a glance | Card features | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Annual fee | | | | Welcome offer | Find out your offer and see if you're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) | Earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (A 21-plus day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply.) Offer ends Nov. 4. | | Authorized user fee | | | Quick picks by traveler type | Best for | Card | |---|---| | Travelers who don't exclusively fly with Delta | Amex Platinum | | Travelers who frequently redeem points for hotel stays, in addition to flights | Amex Platinum | | Travelers who exclusively or almost exclusively fly with Delta | Delta Reserve | | Travelers who often fly on Delta with a companion | Delta Reserve | Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Welcome offer Currently, new Amex Platinum cardmembers can find out their offer and see if they're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, this welcome offer is worth up to $3,500. Meanwhile, new Delta Reserve cardmembers can earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (A 21-plus day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply.) Offer ends Nov. 4. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, the miles in this welcome offer are worth $600. Amex restricts cardmembers to earning one welcome bonus per card per lifetime, so it's important to get the best offer you can. If you frequently fly with a companion or travel often domestically on Delta, the current Delta Reserve offer may be one of the strongest we've seen on the card for you. If you're able to get at least 150,000 points on the Amex Platinum, that's a stellar offer and worth applying for. Winner: Amex Platinum. The value of the Delta Reserve's welcome bonus is contingent on you flying frequently with the airline within the U.S., while the Amex Platinum's is both more valuable and more flexible. Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Benefits Statement credits | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Standout statement credits | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | The Delta Reserve differs some from other premium airline cards in that many of its key statement credits are not explicitly tied to flying. This makes it a closer competitor to the Amex Platinum, known for its array of merchant-linked statement credits. It's harder to justify the Delta Reserve's annual fee with statement credits alone compared to the Amex Platinum. Provided you maximize the Platinum's hotel* and Resy statement credits, you'll already be ahead of the card's $895 annual fee. *For use on Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings; THC bookings require a minimum two-night stay. Conversely, even if you use the full amount of the Delta Reserve's Resy, Delta Stays and ride-hailing statement credits, you'll still be around $90 short of breaking even on the card's $650 annual fee. If you're not comfortable with a card's value hinging on booking at least a couple of flights with Delta each year in addition to maximizing its statement credits, the Amex Platinum is the safer bet. Lounge access | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Lounge access | Access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection for eligible cardmembers, including: Enrollment is required for select benefits. **When traveling on same-day Delta flights; 10 visits per calendar year; resets Feb. 1; unlimited visits after $75,000 in spending in a calendar year. | Enrollment is required for select benefits. ***15 visits per year when traveling on a same-day Delta flight; resets Feb. 1; earn unlimited visits by spending $75,000 in a calendar year on your card. | The Amex Platinum is always my recommendation for anyone looking for a premium card with great lounge access. Eligible cardmembers have access to Centurion Lounges, Delta Sky Clubs, Priority Pass lounges and more. It's hard to beat what the Amex Platinum gives you here, but the Delta Reserve offers solid lounge access for an airline card. Typically, airline cards offer lounge access only to their associated airline's lounge network, but the Delta Reserve also includes access to the Centurion Lounge. Of course, you must have a same-day flight with Delta to access a Centurion Lounge, but you're likely flying Delta often anyway if you're thinking of opening its top-tier card. Given that the Amex Platinum offers Sky Club and Centurion Lounge access for eligible cardmembers, along with a roster of other lounge options, I view it as the winner here. The only exception is if you plan to visit Sky Clubs more than 10 times per year, since the Delta Reserve offers up to 15 visits per year. Delta-specific benefits | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Delta-specific benefits | None, unless you select Delta as your qualifying airline for your up to $200 per calendar year airline incidentals statement credit | | Here's where the Delta Reserve really pulls ahead of the Amex Platinum. With perks like free checked bags, priority boarding and a companion certificate for round-trip travel on Delta to select destinations each account year, the Delta Reserve offers a lot more by default than the Amex Platinum for Delta fans. You can select Delta as your qualifying airline of choice for the Amex Platinum's up to $200 per calendar year airline incidentals statement credit and use that amount to cover charges like checked bag fees and seat upgrades. That's what I did this year, using the full amount of this statement credit to cover checked bag fees and Sky Club guest passes for a trip to Mexico. Even so, there's a good chance Delta loyalists spend more than $200 with the airline in a year. Plus, the Amex Platinum's airline statement credit won't grant priority boarding or a companion certificate. Winner: When comparing the benefits of both cards as a whole, the Delta Reserve is the better choice for frequent Delta flyers. Its annual companion certificate, higher number of Sky Club visits in a year and day-of-travel perks are a better fit for Delta fans than what the Platinum offers. That said, if you care more about statement credits and lounge access, the Amex Platinum makes a more compelling case. How to earn and redeem rewards with the Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve Despite what you may think, the Amex Platinum makes a more compelling case with its earning rates than the Delta Reserve, with a couple of exceptions. Earning rewards | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Earning rates | | | This comparison highlights what is, in my opinion, one of the Delta Reserve's biggest shortcomings: A low earning rate on Delta flights. Earning only 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta flights isn't the best rate, given the card's $650 annual fee. I can think of just a couple of circumstances where I'd suggest someone go with the Delta Reserve over the Amex Platinum if maximizing earnings on Delta purchases is the key goal. Since you can transfer Amex Membership Rewards points to Delta SkyMiles, it's not like you're locking yourself out of Delta's loyalty program by going with the Amex Platinum. One exception is if you're anticipating spending more than $500,000 in a calendar year on Delta flights, but I expect the grand majority of cardmembers will not hit this spending cap. Another is if you're chasing Delta status and want to earn bonus MQDs on your purchases. Neither card is a great choice for everyday spending. If you want to maximize your earnings on everyday purchases and use those rewards for Delta flights, another Amex card like the American Express® Gold Card is likely a better choice than either of these cards. Redeeming rewards You can redeem Membership Rewards points in a variety of ways, including for statement credits, travel, gift cards and to pay for purchases through PayPal and at Amazon.com checkout. Delta SkyMiles can be used to book flights with Delta and partner airlines, such as Air France-KLM, Virgin Atlantic and Korean Air. In addition, you can use SkyMiles for upgrades, premium purchases in Sky Clubs and more. As I mentioned earlier, Membership Rewards points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles. They can also be sent to 19 other airline and hotel partners, including Delta's airline partners, such as Air France-KLM and Aeromexico. This is where you'll get the most value for your Membership Rewards, and why TPG values Membership Rewards significantly higher than Delta SkyMiles (as per our September 2026 valuations). I always recommend redeeming SkyMiles for flights, since that will give you the greatest value. I transferred 84,000 Membership Rewards points to Delta SkyMiles earlier this year to book three one-way tickets from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Cancun International Airport (CUN). Winner: Amex Platinum. You can transfer your rewards to Delta SkyMiles, plus over a dozen other programs in the event your travel plans involve flights or hotel stays outside of Delta's booking system. Its earning rates are also more compelling. Can I have both the Amex Platinum and the Delta Reserve? If you're prepared to pay over $1,500 in annual fees for both cards, then yes. Having both the Amex Platinum and Delta Reserve makes a lot of sense for Delta fans, since you'll receive the flexibility of the Amex Platinum alongside the Delta Reserve's Delta-linked perks. You'll also be able to earn two welcome bonuses, provided you haven't held either card before. That's a huge stash of rewards for your future Delta flights. That said, neither of these cards will make sense for you if you aren't traveling at least a few times each year. While you may be able to make the Amex Platinum's annual fee work with its statement credits, you'll likely get just as much value from a mid-tier credit card. Should I get the Amex Platinum or Delta Reserve? If you're almost always or always flying with Delta, the Delta Reserve more than likely makes the most sense for you. However, Delta loyalists can still benefit from the Amex Platinum's lounge access, superior earning rate on airlines booked directly or through Amex Travel (subject to a spending cap) and up to $200 per calendar year airline incidentals statement credit. Ultimately, the decision comes down to the value you place on flexibility. Bottom line The Amex Platinum and Delta Reserve are close competitors. There's a strong case to be made for either card having a spot in a Delta fan's wallet, but it also can make a lot of sense to have both at the same time. You can't really go wrong with either choice, but their high annual fees mean you'll want to pick the better of the two for your situation: - If you're a Delta loyalist chasing status, frequently visit Sky Clubs or often travel with a companion, choose the Delta Reserve. - If you want extensive lounge access, high earning rates on flights (subject to a spending cap) and points flexibility, go with the Amex Platinum. To learn more, read our full reviews of the Amex Platinum and Delta SkyMiles Reserve. Apply here: Amex Platinum Apply here: Delta Reserve For rates and fees of the Delta Reserve, click here. For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click here.

item.title: Worth the upcharge? Flying Singapore Airlines premium economy
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.91
Worth the upcharge? Flying Singapore Airlines premium economy Quick take: Singapore Airlines is a comfortable way to fly long distances if you can't find business- or first-class awards that work for your budget. Pros - Comfortable seats have a lot of recline. - Passengers can preorder "Book the Cook" meals. - There's great entertainment and free Wi-Fi for KrisFlyer members. Cons - There are few seats per plane and high award prices. - Some seat features are not ergonomic. - Certain elements, like plastic cups, don't feel elevated. I first flew Singapore Airlines premium economy over a decade ago, shortly after the carrier introduced the new cabin. Although I've since flown Singapore Airlines premium economy on a handful of short routes within Asia, I was excited to try the service again on a longer jaunt. So, when I saw an award ticket on the eight-hour route from Melbourne to Singapore, I cashed in some Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer miles for a ticket. While my flight was between Australia and Asia, Singapore Airlines has installed the same premium economy seats on its long-haul Boeing 777s, Airbus A350s and A380s. In other words, the plane I flew is similar to what you'll find on the airline's longest routes, as is the service on board. Here's my experience flying Singapore Airlines premium economy, and how you can book it for yourself. How much does it cost to book Singapore Airlines premium economy? The cost of a long-haul flight in Singapore Airlines premium economy depends on the route, dates and whether you're flying round-trip or one-way. My one-way flight from Melbourne Airport (MEL) to Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) would have cost $2,784.25 Australian dollars ($1,995), which was pretty steep. An economy ticket would have cost AU$1,457.25 ($990), so my ticket was around twice as expensive. Just for context, a business-class ticket on my flight would have cost AU$4,246.25 ($3,042), just over $1,000 more than premium economy. In terms of mileage prices ... it gets more complicated since Singapore Airlines introduced semi-dynamic "Access" pricing. Let me try to snapshot it for you, though: | Cabin | Cash price | Saver award | Advantage award | Access award | |---|---|---|---|---| | Economy | $990 | 29,000 | 60,500 | 87,000 | | Premium economy | $1,995 | 53,500 | Not published | 94,500 | | Business | $3,042 | 72,000 | 103,500 | 160,000-213,500 | | First | $4,251 | 98,000 | 178,500 | 331,000 | As you can see, mileage prices vary not just widely, but wildly. You could get a first-class ticket that costs over twice as much as a premium economy ticket for just a few more miles if you found a Saver award (one was available the week I flew) versus an Access award in premium economy. In my particular circumstances, I could only find Access awards in all classes on the date I needed to travel. That meant an economy award would have cost 87,000 miles, but a premium economy ticket that would have been twice as expensive in dollars was just 7,500 more miles. So, I decided to book premium economy. I was hoping a business-class saver-level award would become available, but the lowest those fell to was 192,000 miles — most definitely out of my budget. All told, I spent 94,500 KrisFlyer miles plus AU$114.25 ($77.65). That pegged my per-mile value at 2 cents apiece, which is well above TPG's September valuation of Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer miles at 1.3 cents each. To think about it a different way, I got a ticket that would have been $1,005 more expensive for just 7,500 more miles. So the value of each additional mile I redeemed was more like a whopping 13.4 cents. Don't have a ton of Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer miles? It's easy to stock up on them since the program is a 1:1 transfer partner of the following credit card rewards programs: While it still pained me to spend over 94,000 miles on my ticket, it still felt like an OK deal given the eight-hour flight duration, the ready availability of award tickets and the ease with which I can earn KrisFlyer miles. Checking into and boarding Singapore Airlines premium economy Singapore Airlines premium economy passengers can enjoy the following priority services at the airport: | Dedicated check-in | Yes | |---|---| | Luggage allowance | Two checked bags up to 23 kg (50 pounds) each or up to 35 kg (77 pounds) total | | Lounge access | No | | Does the airline participate in TSA PreCheck? | Yes | | Priority boarding | Yes, Group 3 | I arrived at the Melbourne airport exactly two hours before my 9:15 a.m. flight and found only a few other passengers waiting in line to check in with agents. There were dedicated lines for economy, premium economy, business class and first class, so I stepped into the lane for premium economy and was helped immediately. My bag was tagged, my boarding pass was printed, and I was directed to security and immigration. Unfortunately, Singapore Airlines premium economy passengers do not receive lounge access, but there are a few Priority Pass options for folks with access to that network. I stopped by the Aspire lounge for a cappuccino, but then went to the gate for boarding, which started right on time at 8:30 a.m. How comfortable is Singapore Airlines premium economy? Singapore Airlines' premium economy is between the business-class and economy cabins on the 777. Passengers can board through the main door, which is just forward of the main business-class cabin — the same door the economy folks board through. | Number of seats | 28 | |---|---| | Cabin layout | 2-4-2 | | Seat pitch | 38 inches | | Seat recline | Up to 8 inches | | Seat width | 19.5 inches | | Screen size | 13.3 inches | The premium economy cabin comprises 28 seats total in a 2-4-2 pattern. There are three rows of two seats each along either side of the cabin and four rows of four seats running down the center. For families of up to four, those center sections are ideal, while couples should enjoy the two-seat sections. The seats have 38 inches of pitch and are 19 1/2 inches wide between armrests, which feels much roomier than the 18-inch-wide economy seats (which are in a 3-3-3 pattern). That said, my bulkhead seat was effectively an exit row place and felt a little narrower due to the curvature of the cabin wall. There are just two manual (non-electronic) buttons to control the seat: one to recline the seatback up to 8 inches, which feels very expansive, and one to raise the legrest. My bulkhead seat's legrest had an attached pop-out footrest, though those in the other rows have footrests attached to the seat in front, which might affect the size of the bag you can put there. The tray tables are stowed in the center consoles between seats. There is a cover you have to open to access them, and the finger hold you use to do so is blocked by the table when it's deployed, so it can be a bit of a rigmarole. However, the tray table itself is very substantial and easily fit my MacBook Air plus a beverage with no issue. Beneath the control buttons, there is a corded touchscreen remote for the entertainment system, plus a small stowage cubby for little items like classes or a phone. There is a larger shelf next to the legrest where my computer could fit while I charged it. Speaking of plugs, there was an easily accessible USB-A port in the island where the entertainment monitors were stowed. There was also a universal power port embedded next to the seat's legrest. A second USB-A plug behind the armrest was handy for keeping wires out of the way. Just above that was an adjustable attached reading light. There were no USB-C ports, unfortunately. Premium economy passengers share five lavatories with the 184 folks in economy. Two were behind the first economy cabin, to either side of a small galley. The other three were at the back of the plane near the larger galley. Though they did not get too busy during most of the flight, there were huge lines for all of them after meal times. That said, the crew kept them very clean throughout the flight. Amenities in Singapore Airlines premium economy Each seat in Singapore Airlines premium economy came stocked with a medium-size pillow in eye-catching orange and a light fleece blanket. Since there weren't individual overhead air nozzles and the cabin was temperate, I didn't need my blanket. Amenity kits are available on request and include: - An eye mask - Slippers - Lip balm - A pouch made from recycled paper fabric The seat's entertainment screen measured 13.3 inches across diagonally. It offered hundreds of movies and TV shows, including recent releases like "The Devil Wears Prada 2," "The Mandalorian and Grogu," and "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie." Among the TV shows were "Dutton Ranch" and "House of the Dragon." The screens on most seats were mounted in the preceding seatback and tilted up or down slightly for better viewing when reclined or upright. The screen for my bulkhead seat was stowed in an island between the seats and popped up on a metal arm, then swiveled right and left from there. So, I couldn't use it for takeoff and landing. Some wear and tear meant it sort of sagged downward on the unattached side, but it didn't really impede my viewing. The center bulkhead seats have their monitors mounted on the cabin wall in front of them. The airline provided basic noise-canceling headphones that plugged into a jack near the USB port at the back of the armrest. It wasn't easy to plug the headset in, but once it was, the positioning meant the cord was mostly out of the way. Singapore Airlines offers Wi-Fi on its 777s. You can purchase a paid plan at the following rates: - One hour: $3.99 - Three hours: $8.99 - Full flight: $15.99 Business-class and first-class passengers, as well as elite PPS members, receive free Wi-Fi. Even better, if your KrisFlyer account is linked to your reservation, you can access free, unlimited Wi-Fi on multiple devices at once by entering your last name and seat number. I found the Wi-Fi good enough to do a little web surfing, but uploading a short video clip to Instagram took over an hour. Fast.com clocked the speed at 280 Kbps. How was the food in Singapore Airlines premium economy? Although there were no predeparture beverages, the attendants came through with the first beverage service and passed out packets of mixed almonds and cashews about 20 minutes into the flight. Passengers could choose from a selection of soft drinks, water, juice, beer and small bottles of spirits. The small, but respectable, wine list included: - Charles de Cazanove Brut Champagne - Craggy Range sauvignon blanc from Martinborough, New Zealand - St. Hallett Faith Shiraz from Australia's Barossa region On my eight-hour daytime flight, the meal service in premium economy included lunch and a light pre-landing snack — pretty much the same as you'd find in economy. However, premium passengers could take advantage of the airline's famous "Book the Cook" service (bookable up to 24 hours in advance), though the options were more limited than those in business and first class. I "booked the cook" in advance, selecting poached chicken with ginger and spring onion relish over steamed jasmine rice and served with Chinese cabbage and carrots. The whole meal was served on one tray and accompanied by a starter of melon and prosciutto over arugula, a garlic roll with butter, Arnott crackers with cheddar cheese and an apple cake with lemon curd. It basically felt like an economy meal, but the plateware had a ceramic-like finish, which elevated the look, and the metal cutlery did the same, though the cups used in premium economy were all plastic. The dish was flavorful but not super substantial. Still, it made for a tasty light lunch. Among the options available on the regular inflight menu were: - Stir-fried seafood with black pepper sauce and Chinese greens over rice - Braised lamb in brown sauce with crushed peas and mint, roasted carrots and Kipfler potatoes The other preorder "Book the Cook" dishes included: - Seafood casarecce in cream sauce - Malay-style nasi lemak coconut rice with spicy sambal prawns, anchovy, roasted peanuts and hard-boiled egg - Braised lamb in red wine sauce with buttery mashed potatoes and seasonal vegetables - A selection of special meals for specific dietary requirements Because I'd ordered ahead, my meal was served first — about 20 minutes before other passengers, and just 30 minutes into the flight — so I was finished by the time meal service began for everyone else. That meant sitting around with an empty tray for quite a while, but it was picked up when everyone else's was. About 90 minutes before landing, the second meal service was more of a "refreshment" according to the menu. It included a choice of: - Chicken and mixed vegetable pastie pie - Pea, pumpkin and chickpea samosas with chutney on the side I chose the samosa, and it was hot, delicious and not overly filling. Overall, both meal services were efficient, and the choices were interesting. Not only that, but flight attendants passed through at regular intervals offering passengers beverages (pretty much anything on the menu, not just coffee, water, or tea), which made the experience feel more like business class than economy. Would you recommend Singapore Airlines premium economy? Singapore Airlines premium economy remains an enjoyable experience with spacious seats, solid entertainment options and, thanks to the small cabin size, personalized and polished service from the flight attendants. Among the elements I most appreciated were the seats' significant recline, the option to use a pared-down version of the airline's signature "Book the Cook" meal preorder service and the free Wi-Fi. I do wish the airline would release more saver-level awards on routes, but given the small upsell compared to economy awards, redeeming a few thousand extra miles for tickets that would otherwise be significantly more expensive feels like a worthwhile splurge. item.title: This easy-to-miss Marriott site earned me 3,000 bonus points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.57
This easy-to-miss Marriott site earned me 3,000 bonus points There are the big and mostly obvious ways to earn points and miles — such as through credit card bonuses and spending, and, of course, on actual travel. But there are plenty of other easy-to-miss ways to earn rewards, too. From dining programs to Lyft rides, Starbucks reloads and so much more, you can earn points and miles in places you might not expect. And recently, for me, one of those places was on a private boat excursion in the middle of a bioluminescent bay during a trip to Grand Cayman. Taking good photos of the bioluminescent bay in the dark turned out to be ... impossible. But earning a few thousand Marriott Bonvoy points on the boat ride was shockingly easy. Here's how I did it: Marriott has what it calls a Marriott Tours and Activities site where you can book excursions around the world and earn, or even use, Marriott points in the process. Marriott doesn't operate these attractions and tours itself; instead, it serves as a third-party broker or aggregator. Some of the types of activities I've seen available to book through the site include: - Snorkeling trips - Walking tours - Boat and fishing trips - Food tours - Historical tours If you want to redeem Marriott points to cover one of these tours or activities, based on my test searches, you can currently do so at a rate of 0.4 cents per point. That means it would take 25,000 Marriott points to pay for a $100 activity. TPG values Marriott points at 0.75 cents each when used for travel (based on September 2026 TPG valuations), so that's not mathematically the all-time best redemption value with your Marriott points, but it is an option. But you can also earn Marriott points, like I did, at a rate of 5 points per dollar spent. Booking a private boat to see the bioluminescent bay in Grand Cayman for my group of five didn't cost any more per person than a group tour, so we booked that for $600, earning 3,000 bonus Marriott points we otherwise would have left on the table. In fact, booking directly with the company we used would have cost the same as booking via Marriott, so these were really just points waiting to be earned. Unfortunately, while the charge appeared on my statement as Marriott Bonvoy Hallandale Beach, Florida, it did not post as a Marriott purchase to earn bonus points on my Marriott credit card. Instead, on my transaction, it coded as entertainment - general attractions. So, you may want to pay with a card that offers a strong return on everyday spending or one that earns bonus rewards on entertainment. Bottom line Earning 5 bonus Marriott points per dollar on tours and activities isn't going to change the trajectory of your points and miles earnings. But I'm of the mindset that every point counts, especially when it doesn't cost anything extra to earn them and doesn't add any real hassle to my life. Marriott Tours and Activities checked all of those boxes for me. I paid the same price I would have paid by booking directly and walked away with 3,000 extra Marriott points for a pretty memorable boat ride to see the bioluminescent bay that I was going to book anyway.

item.title: Q3 Amex Platinum credits expire soon — here's how to use them
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.50
Q3 Amex Platinum credits expire soon — here's how to use them Editor's Note If you already have one of American Express' top-tier cards — or are considering applying — the real value comes from how consistently you use its built-in statement credits. As the end of the quarter approaches, it's worth making sure you've used your Q3 statement credits before Sept. 30, alongside any monthly statement credits that reset soon. This guide shows how to make the most of these benefits. Why this matters With a mix of monthly, quarterly and biannual statement credits, both the $895 annual fee American Express Platinum Card® and $895 annual fee The Business Platinum Card® from American Express can deliver hundreds of dollars in value each year (see rates and fees for the Amex Platinum; see rates and fees for the Amex Business Platinum). But that's only if you stay organized and use them before they expire. The consumer Platinum Card offers up to $75 in statement credits for purchases at U.S. Lululemon retail stores (excluding outlets) and online each quarter and up to $100 in statement credits for U.S. Resy-affiliated restaurants each quarter (enrollment required for both benefits). Similarly, the business version of the Platinum Card comes with a suite of ongoing statement credits that can deliver consistent value throughout the year. Advice for Platinum Card members With the up to $75 quarterly Lululemon statement credits and up to $100 quarterly U.S. Resy statement credits, Platinum Card members can extract up to $175 in value from their card's quarterly statement credits. It's essential that both new and existing cardmembers activate their Lululemon and Resy benefits in their Amex account before making any purchases to ensure these perks trigger correctly. Once you activate these benefits, use your card to spend: - Up to $75 at U.S. Lululemon retail stores (excluding outlets) and online: My advice is to click through a shopping portal and browse deals in the secondhand and "We Made Too Much" sale sections. Both online and in-store purchases are eligible for this statement credit (excluding outlets). - Up to $100 at a U.S. Resy restaurant: Look for a participating restaurant in your area; you don't need a reservation to be eligible to receive this statement credit. If you want to combine this quarter's statement credit with a future quarter's statement credit, a useful workaround is to identify a participating restaurant where you can purchase a gift card online. In practice, this allows you to "carry forward" value. You could purchase a gift card during this quarter to trigger the statement credit, then add more to the same gift card next quarter to use up the next statement credit. When you eventually dine at the restaurant, you can redeem the combined balance. This approach can be especially helpful if you don't plan to dine at a participating restaurant before your current quarter's statement credit expires but want to maximize the overall value across multiple quarters. Advice for Business Platinum Card members This is also a good reminder for both new and existing Business Platinum Card members to get up to $140 in value from the following statement credits before the end of the quarter (enrollment required): - Up to a $90 quarterly Indeed statement credit: Use this statement credit for U.S. purchases with Indeed. - Up to a $50 quarterly statement credit on eligible purchases with Hilton: First, make sure to enroll in the Hilton for Business program (for free). Then, use your card to pay for room rates and incidental charges at a Hilton property. Data points suggest you may also be able to receive the Hilton statement credit when dining at a restaurant or purchasing a product from a gift store located within a Hilton property, even if you're not staying at the hotel. I used my Q3 credit to cover $50 of the $59 cost of a high tea for a friend and me at the Urso Hotel & Spa in Madrid — even though we weren't staying at the property. Again, make sure you enroll in these perks first so your purchases trigger these benefits. A note on the semiannual hotel statement credit Both the Platinum Card and the Business Platinum provide an up to $300 semiannual hotel statement credit (up to $600 per calendar year). You'll receive the statement credit on prepaid American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings made through American Express Travel® when you pay with your eligible Platinum Card. (The Hotel Collection stays require a two-night minimum.) Dec. 30 is the deadline to use the second semiannual hotel statement credit (up to $300). If you haven't already used your up to $300 statement credit for the July-to-December period, now is a good time to do so. If you don't have immediate travel planned, you can use the current semiannual statement credit to book a prepaid stay into 2027. I've used my second statement credit for the year to book a stay in Melbourne, Australia, during the holidays. New cardmember? Get an instant card number If you want to pick up the Amex Platinum, you can apply online and get an instant card number for online purchases. You can add it to your digital wallet to use while you wait up to seven business days for your physical card to arrive in the mail. When you apply, you can find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) Then, you can immediately enroll in the statement credits that you can maximize before the end of the quarter. New Amex Business Platinum Card members can find out their offer and see if they are eligible for as high as 300,000 bonus points after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) Like consumer Amex Platinum Card members, Business Platinum Card members can receive an instant card number upon approval and start maximizing their quarterly statement credits immediately. An important note on contactless payments The terms and conditions for most Amex statement credits say something like this: "The transaction may not be eligible if the merchant uses a third-party to process or submit the transaction to American Express (e.g. using mobile or wireless card readers)." In practice, this means it's not guaranteed that every eligible purchase will trigger a statement credit, depending on how the transaction is processed. I ran into this issue twice when using the semiannual up to $50 Resy statement credits at U.S. Resy restaurants on my (now canceled) American Express® Gold Card — neither transaction posted within the standard eight- to 10-week time frame (enrollment required). After waiting 10 weeks, I contacted Amex via chat and had the statement credits manually applied. Because of this, it's worth keeping an eye on your account. If a statement credit doesn't appear within 10 weeks, reach out to Amex to have it reviewed. And before dining, you may also want to check that the restaurant can process your payment directly (for example, via the card terminal) or ask staff to manually input your card details. Bottom line By being strategic about timing, those with the Amex Platinum or the Business Platinum can take advantage of their statement credits before the end of the quarter. Remember to enroll in benefits before making purchases, track your statement credits throughout the year and follow up if any don't post within several weeks. Finally, I encourage new cardmembers to apply now, jot down their instant card number and immediately add it to their digital wallet.
